COLLECTING AND STORING THE EGGS. The eggs should be collected at least once daily; in warm, moist weather twice daily is preferable. They should not be kept in a hot room or exposed to the sun's rays. The store room should be cool and dry, and free from objectionable odours. A dairy is excellent for the purpose, but failing that a larder or well ventilated cellar would be suitable. It should be remembered that few food products are more susceptible than eggs tn taint by strong smelling substances, and to ra;,d deterioration when im- properly stored. All abnormal eggs, double-yoked, large, dirty, small and cracked eggs should be utilised for home consumption.
If it can be avoided, fertile eggs should not be marketed. In warm, moist weather they may undergo partial incubation, and, in any case, form the great mass of bad and deteriorated eggs.

div.head: EXERCISE FOR LAYING HENS.
div.p: EXERCISE FOR LAYING HENS.

It is very important indeed to maintain lay- ing hens in a lean, hard condition, and to achieve this result the birds should be encour- aged to take plenty of exercise. This is not always an easy matter during the winter months, for on many days the birds are scarcely able to venture into the open. It is a. capital plan, and one I have adopted for several years past, to have a scratching shed attached to the Muse, for then the birds can obtain all the needful exercise without going into the open. The floor of this place should be littered with straw or chaff, and the grain always scattered amongst it. This plan encour- ages exercise better than anything else I know of. Not only does it keep the birds healthy and in good condition, but it acts as a preven- tive against feather-picking egg-eating, Sz.c., vices more often than not caused by idleness.

div.head: YOUNG HENS FOR LAYING.
div.p: YOUNG HENS FOR LAYING.

On many farms the bulk of the laying stock is far too old, and as a consequence of little use for egg production. It often happens that because the pullets have laid well during their first season they are retained until they are three or four years old. A hen is always far more prolific during her first and second sea- sons; after this age the supply gradually dim- inishes until she does not pay for the food she consumes or the space she occupies. A hen will lay so many eggs during her life-time, and the greatest number are produced in the first season. The, second season is also productive, though the number laid depends largely upon whether, the hen has been forced the previous year. There are a few cases where ,a lien, hav- ing become fat and unproductive during the first season, will lay more eggs during the sec- ond, but such cases are obviously exceptional, and merely go to prove the rule. At any rate, it is generally agreed that unless a hen possesses 'some special value as a breeder she is not worth keeping for laying purposes after her second season, for in the third year there is a consid- erable falling off in the number of eggs pro- duced, and especially in, the case of birds that are kept in confined runs there • is more diffi- culty in keeping a bird healthy, and more risk of loss from disease.—" Expert," in "Farm and Home."

div.head: DRYNESS FOR CHICKENS.
div.p: DRYNESS FOR CHICKENS.

The most important point to observe in the care of 'young chickens is to protect them from slamp surroundings. The coops should there- fore be placed upon the highest part of the land, so that the fall of the land is from, and not towards, them. It is also highly important that they should face due south, the chickens thus being protected from the north and the

which is nothing more nor less than the turning of old woollen socks into mittens for the troo_ps. Mr. Pragnell, of St. Paul's Churchyard, started the industry, with the idea of finding employ- ment for out-of-work typists. An appeal to the public brought in over ten thousand pairs of socks and stockings, and from these over thousand pairs of mittens were despatched in a very short time to the troops of the Allies, and to the Fleet. Thin stockings and socks are un- suitable, and old golf stockings make the best mittens. Old and discarded woollen tam o' shanters can be made into splendid sleeping hel- mets, or into over caps for sailors on night duty in the North Sea. Wool is very scarce just now, and nothing made of it, not even the feet of old stockings and socks, should be thrown away, for high prices are paid by manufac- turers for all "kinds of cuttings and for old woollen materials.

Clockworking Revived. Few women give a thought to the origin of the clocks they wear on their stockings,. yet they have an interesting history, for they belong to an old branch of English embroidery called clockworking. . These decorations were inspired by the pendulums used for clocks during the seventeenth century. Clockworking was a geometrical embroidery, worked in wheels, in imitation of those used in clocks, hence the name clockworking. Crewels and silks, and sometimes gold thread were employed, and great ^s shown in the designs and in their ar- int. In fact, clockworking was a flour-

.6 industry in the seventeenth and eigh- ,,eenth centuries, and cashmere shawls and blankets were frequently similarly decorated. This interesting work has lately been revived. It offers a welcome change from floral patterns, which have been so universally used thy em- broideresses for a number of years.

Modified New Skirts. The new skirts have come in for much critic- ism, laudatory and otherwise. Their admirers claim for them that they are more graceful and feminine, and that they admit of much greater comfort in walking and in movement gener- ally, also that they improve the appearance of the feet, the greater fulness diminishing the apparent size of the pedal extremities. The more captious critics aver that as more material will be used, gowns will be more expensive, and that to bring last year's tailor-mades and after- noon frocks up to date will be impossible. As

div.head: CHAT and GOSSIP.
div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.
Red Women's Work.

British Columbia, Canada's Pacific province, and "last best West," has not been a whit behind other parts of the Dominion in the help it has voluntarily given the Mother Country in her hour of need. Despite the fact that a leisured class does not exist there, that the well- to-do lead strenuous lives, that every hour of every day is filled with manifold duties, most men and women have found time and oppor- tunity for united and individual service. The red women of the coast tribes equally with their
white sisters, made garments of all kinds for the troops, one Indian village alone sending numerous cases containing woollen comforts, the yarn for which they spun themselves. _By

means of these useful organisations of white farmers' wives, known as Women's Institutes in Canada, woollen garments were given out and despatched when -completed to the troops, and the Red Cross agencies. Where there were no institutes, Patriotic Leagues sprang up in their place.

div.head: Women Volunteers of British
div.p: Women Volunteers of British
Knitting had almost become war revived it, and now every woman anti

, plies the needles skilfully and unceasingly. The city of VanCouver gave two thousand of her sons to the first contingent of troops sent over to Europe, and others have followed. The women of the Patriotic Leagues are providing the families of. the soldiers with all necessaries. There is very little danger of an invasion of Canada from Germans in Europe, but those in the United States -are a menace. In view of this danger the women of British Columbia have formed a Volunteer Reserve Force, the mem- bers of which are prepared to take the place of men. The girls and women are already adepts in signalling, telegraphing, despatch riding, motor car driving, and nursing and cooking, as well as every other branch of the domestic arts.

div.head: WRITING FOR COMPETITION.
div.p: WRITING FOR COMPETITION.
MY DEAR CHILDREN,-

As you all know, I announced last week our new competition—an essay on "Which is better to live in, town or country? And why?" Well, one of my nephews at once wrote to tell me that he intended to send me an attempt (I am glad to hear this so soon, for it is a good sign !), but says he expects that everybody who enters the competition will write in favour of the country, and then they will have a better chance of Winning. Do you know why he thinks that? Why, because I said- -a .week or two ago that I always thought a day spent in the coun- try was better than a week spent in the town!

Now I want to make you all understand very dearly that it will not matter to me at all which side you take. You see, I don't judge your essays by what I agree with in opinions. Instead. I want good arguments, whatever sitie they are in .favour of, and I also want neat writing.
Has it ever struck you why it is important that your writing,should always be neat? Well, everything should always be made as beautiful as possible, for a. start—
thing of beauty is a joy for ever!

But don't you see that the neater you write the longer it takes you to do it? And the longer it takes, the more carefully is thought over that whicii you write. That is why the neatly-writ- ten essays are usually the nest!
Of course, I know there are some people so clever that they can write correctly, neatly and

"Beauty is woman's most important attri- bute. She who increases beauty is woman's greatest benefactor. Husbands, brothers, even fathers—in their inmost hearts beauty is the thing they desire most to see in their feminine relations." She laughed.

div.head: YOUNG KNIGHT-ERRANT.
div.p: A YOUNG KNIGHT-ERRANT.

On a cold morning in early spring, a little old man stood at the corner of a London street selling newspapers. He was thinly clad, and kept trotting up and down, trying to keep warm. But his voice was so hoarse from cold that the passers-by could hardly hear him. Some thoughtless boys jeered and laughed at him. But one—only about thirteen years old— looked at him for a few moments trnd then walked up to him. "I will shoat for you," he said.

The poor old man at first thought the lad was making fun of him. But all the same that lad began to call out "Chronicle !" "Tele- graph !" " News!" His voice- was so clear that nearly everybody noticed it, and in a very short time the old man had sold nearly all his stock. So grateful was he that he offered to pay his young partner, but the boy would take nothing. Instead, he went off with a smiling face, happy at having done a good deed in helping one who needed it.

div.head: FALLING LEAVES: A FABLE.
div.p: FALLING LEAVES: A FABLE.

"Go away, go away! want you here!' It was the Purple pansy who spoke, and she shook her velvety blossoms free from the leaves that were drifting down upon her from a neigh- bouring birch tree. "Don't you see you are hiding my flowers? They are not too plentiful, either, at this time of the year! how are people to see me if you come and cover me up?" "Hut where can we go?" cried the poor little leaves in distress. -".Gladly would we stay upon our parent tree, but she cannot keep with us any longer. And we .hoped that, though our work was done up there, we might still be useful on

the circular skirt may be too drastic a change, designers are showing a modification, which will probably meet with general approval. A very tight underskirt—not necessarily of the same material as the tunic, is shown, and over this is worn a full tunic whith sometimes has a double effect and falls nearly to the hem of the jupe; or a Highland tunic, which consists of a deep kilted basque, is added to the coat bodice.

The Vogue for Feathers. Feathers are to have an extraordinary vogue , when the time comes to disca,rd furs, and noth- ing is more becoming or more effective in the way of neck adornment than ostrich or mara- bout, which are to be the two leading favour- ites. Both will be used in natural tones, in the loveliest shades of the prevailing colours, and of course in black and white. RuChings of all kinds are to be used on the new skirts, as well as on other garments; the old-fashioned silk kind, frayed out at the edges, having found much favour with fashionable dressmakers. Fluffy frills, flounces and furbelows are also re- turning with other early Victorian modes. With regard to colours for spring wear, only subdued tints are considered in good taste. Navy blue, dark green, and shades of purple are to lead; later on pale soft shades will be seen. Grey and black is a favourite combination of ,the moment; sometimes black relieves gray, and vice-versa, but in ally ease the two colours are very cleverly contrasted as well as combined, and the effect is excellent.

Beautiful Spring Flowers. The war has not adversely affected the artifi- cial flower trade, to judge from the wealth of lovely blossoms prepared for spring and summer wear, for this is going to be a .flower season. The most beautiful specimens are made of vel- vet and silk, and are in every shade and tint. Sometimes Nature is faithfully copied, as in the case of the lovely pansies in the most ex- quisite colouring and the perfection of art. These, with nearly all the new flowers, are quite flat, and made in special wreaths, destined to trim the small hats that are as popular as ever. Sometimes the foliage and blossoms are utterly unlike anything in Nature, but they are beauti- ful, nevertheless, and will be seen to advantage on the silk hats, that are to take the place of the velvet so universally worn, and on the straws, later on. The purple clematis in numberless shades, and the roses of all hues, are especially lovely this year.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information in Popular
Language.
Excess in Tea.

- Tea, used to excess acts injuriously. Beware of drinking it when not freshly made; no tea is fit for drinking that has stood over five minutes. The misuse of tea is responsible for many forms of indigestion. Do not drink tea with meat, as the tannin has a chemical action 'on the meat which retards digestion, and con- tinued it may lead to severe dyspepsia. No young children should drink tea.

To Eat Porridge. . No true Scotsman ever eats sugar, syrup, or anything sweet with his porridge. He may use a little salt, and eat it with milk. If sweet- stuff is added to porridge fermentation is likely to arise, then there will be wind and acid risings. Also, oatmeal tends to make the skin itch; add sugar or syrup, and more or less you will want to scratch the body and limbs. Raw oatmeal may be eaten with benefit, either mixed with hot or cold water, or with fruit or greens; chew it well, and it digests well and nourishes well.—Dr. Allinson.

Baby's Outing. Fresh air is absolutely essential to a growing child, and it should have regular outings morn- ing and afternoon after the first three weeks, or even before in summer. Long hours of sleep out of doors are most advisable, and on days when the weather is not good, the child should sleep indoors well covered up, with the windows wide open. Rain, fog and strong cold winds are the only conditions which should prevent a healthy baby sleeping out of doors. Besides outings, exercise is necessary. This can be achieved by letting the child, after The first few weeks of life, have free play of his arms and legs after the ..bath. Fractures.

The symptoms are pain, swelling, deformity, loss of power, shortening, abnormal mobility, and the grating of the fragments of bone against each other. The last two symptoms one should never try to find, as any effort to ascer- tain whether they are present will lead7ko move- ment at the broken ends of the bone. .With regard to swelling, it is important that the medical man be sent for as soon as the accident occturs, or this particular symptom may become. so serious as to prevent him from being able to diagnose. In greenstick fracture, so commonly found in children, many of the above symptoms will be more or less absent. However, where there is doubt the case should be treated as one of fracture. -

"Useful, indeed! Pray, what use do you think you are to me?" replied the pansy, crossly. "Don't try to pretend you are think- ing of anyone but yourselves. But it's no use talking: I don't suppose you could ever under- stand how bad-mannered I think you are !" The little leaves were too sad to answer. After such a happy summer, it had almost broken their leafy little hearts' to part from the tree with which they had lived all their lives. And then—just as it had cheered them up so much to think that, after all, it was only a change se that they might be useful in another way—they had had this rude welcome from the pansy! It made them more unhappy than words can say. - But not far away there Was a fine clump of white pansies. "How . cruel !" they whispered, when they heard their • neighbour's words. "Poor little leaves! it is not their fault. wish we were not too frightened to call to them that they are welcome to come this way." You see, the white pansies were very shy and modest, and never put themselves forward before their purple . relation, who prided herself on being a Prize Pansy. But if the white flowers were not so large and fine, their feelings were gentle and kind. And just now they were, truly sorry- for the lonely little birch. leaves. However, in the course of the day the wind shifted a little, and the leaves' began to shower down on the white pansies. Faster and faster they came, but only to be received with kind .words of welcome.' "How glad I am of these!" thought one little plant; "I do not think I can live much longer now that the nights are grow- ing so cold. Let me do ply best to make others happy while I can." °

"Mother, mother!. look at this cutting from my pretty white pansy. It has kept alive all through the winter, and yet the purple ones are quite dead. I wonder how it is !" "Just see, darling, the heaps of dry leaves you have cleared away from it. I expect it is they who have sheltered your white panSy, and kept the frosts away. The purple ones .that have, died were almost uncoyered !" "How .wonderful !" cried the, child. " Why, mother, doesn't it seem as if they had been just tucked up in a nice little blanket?" So the white pansies' gentleness was rewarded, while the proud purple pansy sUffered, for her selfishness.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
BELGIUM 1NI) NORTH FRANCE.
British Help For _Agricultural
Restoration.

In view of the havoc wrought in the war- ravaged areas of Belgium and North-Eastern France, it is proposed to form a branch corn, mittee in each county, which will endeavour to obtain promises of seed, stock, &c., for the agri- cultural restoration of Belgium and North- Eastern France. Such gifts will be credited to the prospective counties. Communications have already been sent to the Chambers of Agricul- ture and agricultural societies. Lists already received from the Belgian and French Minis- tries of Agriculture show that the following will be required on a very extensive scale: Seed for cereals: Wheat, barley, oats and rye. Roots; Mangels, turnips, swedes, potatoes. Grasses and feeding crops, vegetables of all kinds, also fruit trees and bushes. Breeding stock: Horses, cattle, sheep, pigs, poultry. An estimate has been made that the total losa in the rural districts of Belgium is .t 56,000,000 of which vast sum the crops and stock repre- sent £30,000,000. In France the destruction has been almost as great. What this means is that the devastated areas of the two countries are about equal to all the counties of England north of the Trent up to the Cheviots and the Solway. The Central Committee has received a letter from M. Ferdinand David, French Minister of Agriculture, who says that "the stock will have almost entirely disappeared in the districts occupied by an enemy who has destroyed all that which he could not utilise or take away." It is cimfidently believed that there will be a large and hearty response to this suggestion, and when the time comes, we shall be able to ship to each country seeds of all kinds, fruit trees and stock, to an extent that will be worthy of our land, and contribute largely to- wards restoration of the devastated areas: Gifts large and small will be equally welcome. Seed for grain, legumes and roots can be given from a bushel to a ton; seed for vegetables from a quart to a sack; fruit bushes and trees from, half a score to a thousand; and stock from poultry to horses. Such as are unable to send seed, stock, &c., but desire to share in this great effort for restoration of the war-ravaged dis- tricts of France and Belgium, can contribute money in sums large and small, which may be applied in the purchase of seed, stock, &c., or for meeting the expenses of carrying out this undertaking, which must be considerable. The Central Committee for the Agricultural Restoration of Belgium and North-Eastern France is constituted as follows: The Marquis of Lincolnshire, ,K.G., G.C.M.G., the Right Hon. Sir Ailwyn Fellowes, K.C.V.0., Sir Rider Hag- gard, Capt. Charles Bathurst, M.P. (President , Central Chamber of Agriculture), Mr. Edward Brown, F.L.S. (honorary director), Mons. Alfred Duche (President French Chamber of Commerce in London), Mr. F. Percy Low, Prof. E. R. Matthews, Mr. Ernest Parke, Mons. M. E. Pollet (Consul-General of Belgium in London), Sir Robert Williams, Bart., M.P. (honorary treasurer); secretary, E. T. Brown. The offices of the Central Committee are at 39, Queen Anne's Chambers, Westminster.

div.head: HOME-GROWN SUGAR.
div.p: HOME-GROWN SUGAR.

Lecturing before the Royal Society of Arts, Mr. Edward R. Dayson, the well-known West Indian expert, calculated that about 700,000 acres of land in Germany and Austria are de- voted annually to the growing of beet for the English market—in spite of the condemnation, by the Royal commission of 1905, of the prac- tice of deriving 60 per cent. of any foodstuff from a single foreign source. He recommended pre- ferential tariffs within the Empire to foster the sugar-growing industry; and the cultivation of sugar beet in England bY a model State factory.
HOW GERMANY'S STATE FORESTS HELP THE FARMER.

A rescript of much interest has been issued by the Prussian.- Minister of Agriculture referring to the assistance which the State fcrests can give in the sujiply of food and bedding for cattle, says a "Daily Chronicle" correspondent. It is pointed out that since the war began the State forests have been thrown open .to farmers, and that they are free to drive their cattle into them. Evidently the farmers have not made adequate use of this privilege, for they are now instructed that the forests contain. enormous quantities of vegetable matter suitable for bed- ding—pine needles, dry leaves, and mould—and that if the farmers utilise these things they would set free large quantities. of straw to be used as fodder. There are also thousands of acres of oak forests, the ground strewn with acorns, which pigs ,esteem a great delicacy, and are excellent for fattening purposes. Finally, there are numerous clearings, capable, with care, of growing potatoes and other vegetables, and this land can be had in most cases for the asking. Only in rare cases' will a trifling rent be asked.

div.head: WOMEN AS FARM WORKERS.
div.p: WOMEN AS FARM WORKERS.

A letter in the 'Times," signed "Gertrude Elliot, Ginge Manor, Wantage," points out that formerly women milked and.did the bulk of the dairy work. "The elder ones will tell you how they milked fourteen cows daily. Now, in many counties, you will not find a single woman milker, and it is increasingly difficult to engage a dairymaid. All forms of dairy work are looked down on; women press into other employments and neglect one their mothers filled superla- tively well. Would it not be possible that an effort should be made in the counties where the habit of milking has not yet died out umoni women to instruct some of those now out of work in the art, and to .send them into the neighbouring counties? Might not facilities be given by those who own dairies to teach girls, and a few prizes be offered to those who learned to milk in the shortest period of time? If a few young ladies who are above foolish considera- tions of what is "fashionable" would learn in their home farms, and recruit milkers from among the village girls, they would be doing a national service. The position of the. dairy farmer is becoming daily more serious owing to the lack of milkers, and the time for calving is approaching fast. Frenchwomen have risen to the,occasion, brought in last year's harvest and seen to the cattle. Are Englishwomen less capable and less willing? Milking machines are being very widely introduced, but they are expensive, and many hundreds of farmers will be unable to afford them. It should als% be remember ok that the work of the machine. re- quires to be finished off by hand.",

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
SWEET PEAS.

Unfortunately, to a great many varieties which, when the flowers are mixed, even a specialist would fail to separate, distinct names have been given, with the result that many who purchase seeds are greatly disappointed when they find • That they have the same variety under, it may be, two or three different names. The list issued by the National Sweet Pea Society of too-much-alike varieties is a long one, and those who exhibit should carefully scan this, and thus avoid disqualification. The suc- cessful culture of sweet peas may be summed

up in a few words. Trench the ground deeply and manure freely. Sow thinly towards the end at the present month if the weather is favourable, but in any case in .March. Care should be taken to stake the plants before they get- too tall, and when in flower gather the blooms daily, and so prevent the formation .of seed. After the first flush of bloom is over, apply a top-dressing of manure along each side' of the row, and if the weather is dry soak thoroughly. • Such trouble will be rewarded in that, the plants will keep up a succession. of bloom for quite four months, and longer if the late summer and autumn are fine.—" Wick" in Fa I'M and Home."

div.head: GODETIAS.
div.p: GODETIAS.

These beautiful annuals are not so often seen as they ought to be, seeing how freely they flower and the many colour variations there are in the blooms. Another point that deserves attention is the long succession of bloom that is kept up, more especially where the plants have plenty of room to. branch out. They do not require rich soil. Seed may be sown in-the open air in April, care being taken to thin out to not less than a foot apart when the plants are tit to handle.

div.head: SALPIGLOSSIS.
div.p: SALPIGLOSSIS.

N umernus as are the hardy and half-hardy annuals now in cultivation; few, I think, are so effective when seen in a large group as tile sal piglossi, which, for the richness alone of the colour of the flowers, should always find a:place in the garden. The plants not only bloom very freely, but a succession of flowers is kept 1-11) for a long time. In the flowers we find almost every conceivable shade, from pure white, through yellow, purple, crimson, these being beautifully striped and marked with deep-col- oured veins.

div.head: OBJECT OF SUMMER SOIL CULTIVATION.
div.p: THE OBJECT OF SUMMER SOIL CULTIVATION.

When we cultivate the soil prior to the plant- ing ,of the erops it may be briefly said that we do so to sweeten and enrich it, and at the same time to put it into perfect mechanical • condition. In the summer our object is simply to ensure that the plants shall secure the full benefit of the work that was done, it may be, months beaire. Surface culture in the height of sunlit-ler does not necessarily mean entich— ment of the soil, but it most certainly means that it is maintained in a sweet state much longer, and apart from that, it secures to the plants growing in it practically all the food that was incorporated at the winter working, since it is not given the chance of escaping by capillary attraction, which is, of course, always proceeding. Further than this, it encourages sweetness through the free admission of fresh air following the water, and in some degree it adds to the fertility by the unobstructed pas- sage of rain water, which indubitably contains nutrient 'matters.-

HOEING AND FORKING. 'Whether the loosening shall be effected by the aid of the hoe or the fork. is entirely a matter for each cultivator to decide for him- self. There cannot be the slightest doubt that the Dutch hoe is the easier and quicker too/ for this particular 'purpose, but there are num- erous instances where it is difficult or even im- • possible to wield, and then recourse must be had to the small fork rather than allow th,e, surface to cake over and become almost as liara as the proverbial macadamised road. The hoe has one marked advantage over the fork, which is that it will do far better work in the sup- pression of weeds, but beyond this either tool may be ehosen at will.

Whatever is employed must be used so as to create the finest and \dustiest possible layer for 'a depth of an inch or thereabouts, since it is this condition that does such a mai•ked amount of good in the conservation of food. In dry weather it is, of course, imperative that water shall ,be given, and as soon afterwards as the state of the upper Crust will permit of it the loosening must be done, but it is necessary to wait until it has dried somewhat or the soil will be trodden down into close masses impene- trable by water or air. Let this be followed up persistently. and it will. be seen that- in land that was thoroughly prepar-d at the outset even .in the, &mightiest periods the plants will continue to make satisfactory progress for ,ft considerable. time.—" One and All Gardening."

div.head: HARDY EDGINGS.
div.p: HARDY EDGINGS.

Many people have an idea that the only plant suitable for edgings to beds in the summer flower garden are the lobelia, golden feather, an,d such like,ithat entail so much annual trouble and expense. Among hardy things that once planted increase in beauty year by year, and that only when they get too thick require to be divided and replanted, we may mention the white arabis, the aubritia„ the gentian, and snow in summer (Cerastium tomentosum), which when it gets unruly may be clipped over. Then, again, we have the many dwarfed hair bells, the creeping bugle (Ajuga reptans), in its purple-leaved form, and the pinks which when in flower give us for several weeks a delightful fragrance in the garden, and wbich when not in. bloom have neat foliage that, even in the dull autumn and winter days, is always pleasing. One, too, must not forget the thrifts, with their cushion-like form of growth and that flower so freely when well. established. Give the plants. mentioned, or some of them, a trial as. edgings and if the ground is deeply % dug and well man- ured, the results will, I am quite sure, be very pleasing, and the all too common lobelia an(i such like be cast on one side.—" Farm. and home."

div.head: PATRIOTIC DUTY FOR ALL.
div.p: A PATRIOTIC DUTY FOR ALL.
Safeguarding the Life and Health of the Future Generation.

div.head: GUILD OF HELP'S GOOD WORK.
div.p: GUILD OF HELP'S GOOD WORK.

"He endeavoured to struggle to the side of the Slough, but could not get out. But I beheld in my dream that a man came to him whose name was Help. Then said he: Give me thy hand'; so he gave him his hand and he drew him out, and set him upon sound ground, and bid him go on his way. Then I stepped to him that plucked him out And said: 'Sir, wherefore is it that this plat is not mended, that poor travellers might go thither with more security?'"

The foregoing quotation from Runyan's "Pilgrim's Progress" was printed at the head of the report which was laid before the members -a the Warrington Citizens' Guild of Help at their fifth annual meeting in the Town Hall on Monday evening. The Mayor (Alderman. Peter Peacock) presided over a numerous attendance, which included Mrs. Muter Wilson (of Man- (hester), the Rev. T. T. James, Alderman James Evans, and Messrs. F. G. D'Aeth (of Liverpool), F. A. Frost, H. Kingdon, C. E. Parker (chair- man of the Executive Committee), john A. ißansome (treasurer), and Wilfrid J. Rowland .(general secretary).

6611001 at the age of 13 years. One of the Dis- trict Committees is making a weekly allowance on the understanding that the eldest boy does not leave school until he is 14. .Another.family, consisting of father, mother and sir children, was found to be occupying only two beds, and one of the children was tuberculous.
Separate Beds for Tuberculosis Patients.

Although such inadequate bed accommodation may be comparatively rare, persons suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis often share a bed with others. To meet this difficulty the Guild made a new venture last year. Through the generosity of several donors (Mr. F. A. Frost, Mr. Grime, Messrs. J. and W. Dutton, and the Co-operative Society), the Guild was enabled to lend beds and bedding. This. scheme has been worked in conjunction with the Medical Officers' Department, which has kindly made itself re- sponsible for disinfecting the bedding, and, if necessary, storing it before it is passed on to another house.

div.head: HOW THE GUILD HAS HELPED THE MAYOR.
div.p: HOW THE GUILD HAS HELPED THE MAYOR.

Opening the meeting, the MAYA said that the Guild had rendered five years of steady service, and it was very gratifying to find that the. interest taken in it was well maintained. Speaking personally, he thought that This year, above all other years, it was absolutely neces- sary that they should do even further work, if .that were possible, for he felt certain that, -during the months that were ahead, there would be more cases to investigate and more .cases in which the assistance of a society like that would be appreciated and he of real soa vice. (Hear, hear.) First-band knowledge of the conditions of poverty were obtained by the various members visiting the homes,of the poor, and he learned that last year no fewer than 687 such visits were paid. He would like to express his own gratitude to the Guild for the assistance they had given him in .connection ivith cases of distress that had arisen through the war. He knew that they had also been of ;great service to the Soldiers' and Sailors' 'Families' Association. If ever a society (lid justify its existence in Warrington that Guild had done, and particularly so during the war period. (Applause.)
THE YEAR'S WORK
Material Help Where Needed and Deserved.

The annual report was then presented, the SECRETARY remarking that during the past year the Guild had tackled_ more eases than ever before. • The report read as follows The great conflict in Europe was the out- standing feature of 1914. Within three days of the declaration of 'war, a general meeting of the Guild was held, and an assurance was con- veyed to the Mayor that the Guild with its helpers was placed unreservedly at the disposal .of the town. A local Committee for the Preven- tion and Relief of Distress was quickly formed .at the Town Hall, on which the Guild was represented. A heavy burden naturally fell moon the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Asso- ciation, involving the need for much visitation. In the emergency, the Guild offered its services. During the first•three weeks our helpers carried out more than 360 investigations, reporting promptly and accurately. Meantime plans were made for dealing under one roof with all eases arising from the war, and the Parr Hall became the centre of administration with all the advantages of a staff driiwn from the Muni- cipal Offices. The Guild has ever since remained in constant -contact with the work at the Parr Hall, where representations have always re- ceived patient consideration.

The Problem Moral As Well As Economic. Among women there was some shortage of e!ullloYment, but this was only an intensifica- tion of a. chronic local difficulty. The question 44 the development of new local industries for girl labour was referred to the Committee for the Prevention of Distress. This problem is nth only economic, but moral. Gnild workers are frequently impressed with thc number of young girls who, with the sanetfon of their mothers, remain at home without definite duties.

Coming now to the case-work of the society, the following summary (which does not include the 'large number of cases brought forward from previous years) gives a general idea of the way in which cases were dealt with : Helped in material ways with work, food, clothes, medical comforts, convalescent treat- ment, ST., 139 (as against 80 last year); helped by advice and friendly visitation, 86 (41); re- ferred to local authorities or other societies, 41 (29); no help needed, 17 (); false addresses or gone away, 16 (21); help refused unsatis- factory cases, 25 (28); home inquiried for Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Association, 363.

Giving Baby A Start In Life. Attention to infant welfare has been more than ever necessary owing to the fact that many expectant mothers were separated from their soldier-husbands. Our lady helpers have brought cheer to lonely and depressed women by their visits, besides supplying nourishment. Milk, dried milk, Virol and barley have been sent to homes where the income was short. The Guild has in this way given many a baby a better start in life than it would otherwise have had. There is, however, constant need for care lest help -thus, given should enable a father to spend selfishly upon himself wl4t ought to go into the home. Sometimes it hasen necessary to say plainly why help has been withheld.

div.head: Problem of the Large Family.
div.p: The Problem of the Large Family.

Among the donations is a thank-offering of half-a-crown from a man, who thus expresses his thanks for a timely loan. He had a large family, and was suddenly obliged to incur an .expenditure of several pounds. The Guild granted him a loan free. of interest, and the instalments were repaid with unfailing regu- larity. A number of cases have come under the notice of the Guild during the past year where there have been six or seven children under the age of 14 years. Where the father only earns a labourer's wage, he and his wife have an almost impossible task-to feed and clothe their family. The cure certainly does not lie in occasional subsidies 'from charitable sources. But the question arises whether definite public aid can- not be given in some form to large families dur- ing the 3-ears of strain wheh there are, say, six or more children under working age.. trnder present conditions, overcrowding, shortage of food, ill-health, loss oJ independence, and loss of education through premature exemption from school are the resultants. Actual cases will show the problem in the concrete. In one family of eight children, four were found below the proper Standard of physical health. The eldest child in such a family frequently leaves
II Hill ' tenza has carried
your ,efences rebuild with ovril

div.head: BRITISH TO THE BACKBONE
div.p: BRITISH TO THE BACKBONE
Why He Fought?

As usual, some Of the necessary work of the society has been to refuse assistance. Tramps and loafers still impose on the public. One family had slept in four different towns during the week before they came to Warrington. Men in the prime of life accompanied by able-bodied sons have come begging at times, when most of our town industries have been short of labourers. A young Frenchman refused with scorn the offer to pay for a night's lodging because he wanted to have the money for drink. He announced that the entente was at an end. A local man repeatedly asked help while waiting for an operation, but when a bed was vacant he would not go into hospital. Another local cele- brity who was refused assistance by the secre- tary, was shortly after brought before the Police Court. He had been fighting another man to settle who was "the biggest moucher " in town.

div.head: "Look on that Picture and on This !"
div.p: "Look on that Picture and on This !"

On the other hand, it has been a pleasure through the Guild to pay railway fares for a patient to secure treatment at a special hos- pital; to start a lad fresh from -an industrial school in a skilled trade; to transfer a man earn- ing a- miserable remuneration to a position where he was paid a standard labourer's wage; t 6 tide men over short periods of illhess and un- employment; to give little comforts to an old soul who never has meat, but who makes won- derful use of the stump of a cauliflower.

div.head: "The Poor Man's Friend."
div.p: "The Poor Man's Friend."

In a number of instances the Guild paid ar- rears to secure Disablement Benefit. On two occasions complaint was made to the Insurance Commissioners about the treatment accorded by Approved Societies. In one instance maternity benefit was being wrongfully withheld. In an- other, Disablement Benefit was improperly post- poned, and the insured man treated with intol- erable rudeness.

These are but a few examples of the ways in which men's interests are being protected. Even from their own follies, such as reckless indebted- /nese, many people need to be saved, and the Guild has often been able to get them out of a morass and set their feet once more on sure ground, thus fulfilling its ideal of being the Poor Man's Friend.

div.head: MOTHERS' AND BABIES' WELCOMES.
div.p: MOTHERS' AND BABIES' WELCOMES.

A separate report on the Mothers' and Babies' Welcomes, which are situated in Academy-street and Catherine-street, set forth the fact that both Welcomes had again had a most successful year, the average attendance. at Academy-street being 15, and at Catherine-street 13. Babies had been weighed and health talks given as in other years. The Clothing Club was very popu- lar, and did excellent work. There were 76 members at Academy-street and 14 at Catherine- street. This year the Guild applied for and received a grant from the Board of Education, and they hoped to be efficient enough to receive it yearly, for it meant 50 per cent. of their working expenses. The treasurer's report again showed a balance on the right side, but as they had many more expenses to face this ,year, they hoped subscriptions would be renewed, and new subscribers found.

div.head: FINANCIAL.
div.p: FINANCIAL.

The balance sheet, which was appended to the report, showed donations and subscriptions dur- ing the year totalling £291 2s. 3d., and expenses amounting to ,t 334 2s. 3d. On the Ist of January there was a bank overdraft of £42 13s. 11d. The special fund for the Welcomes showed receipts amounting to £2O 13s. Bd., and a balance in hand of £6 19s. 4d.

div.head: ABOVE POLITICAL DIFFERENCES.
div.p: ABOVE POLITICAL DIFFERENCES.

Moving the adoption of the reports and bal- ance sheets, Mr. D'AETH indicated several direc- tions in which an organisation such as the Citizens' Guild of Help can be of help to the community, and referred with pride to the fact that there was no voluntary body doing social work that had ever been alluded to in so many Government publications as the Guild of Help had been. (Applause.) The Guild was, in fact, the one big movement in many towns to which the central public body could look for voluntary effort in a number of cases and diffi- culties that arose. To be successful a Guild of Help must be civic in its character; nobody could be more fitted to preside over it than the Mayor. It was essentially a• town society. It was not -a. question of religious matters, but anybody who was a citizen was qualified to join and should join. It did not infringe upon politics; indeed, it could only be a real success and do' the huge volume ,of work that was put before it so long as it did rise above political differences, and so long as everyone who possibly could came forward as a citizen to do their share. An enormous number of personal help- ers were needed to cope with the vast amount of work which came within the scope of the Guilds. Up till now the problem of the Guild had been very largely concerned with what he might call the abnormal person—the person who was sick; the person who had lost his charac- ter; the person who was in poverty. But now the Guild had begun to touch upon the broader aspect of social work; an instance of which they saw in Warrington in the shape. of the work amongst mothers. (Applause.)

div.head: EFFECTIVE "HUMAN NOTE."
div.p: THE EFFECTIVE "HUMAN NOTE."

Mrs. MUTER WILSON seconded the adoption of the reports, and, in doing so, touched upon the special, side of social work in which she is interested in Manchester; viz., the feeding of ,nursing and expectant mothers. It was, she said, the human note in the work which the Guilds did that made it so effective. Everyone nowadays talked of social reform, and although they did not all agree as to the causes of the state of affairs that called- for reform, and there was as yet no definite unity of action among them, yet the consciences of men and women were to-day awakened as never before, and there was a new moral energy, a now seriousness in everything in connection with the subject. . (Hear, hear.) She thought the people of to-day were realising more and more "that touch of nature which makes the whole world kin." (Hear, hear.) Too long they had been working to remedy the effects, and now they were beginning to realise that they would get the best results if they went to the Causes. Take the Temperance question, for instance. They had talked too much and too long about the men and women who " took too much to drink, and acted too little. They had had(their Bands of Hope, but had left the public-house to line every street. Warrington might be comparatively free from this--(laughter)---but in her own city it was almost impossible for a man or a woman with any taste for drink— either acquired or inherited—to be sober.
The Problem of the Drink:

She was in Salford the other day waiting for a tram, and from the point at which she stood she counted five public-houses, whilst, if she had wanted a cup of tea, or a glass of milk, she could not have got it without going some con- siderable distance. Year after year social workers went on fighting the effects of drink! Why, in the name of reason,, did not they re- move the cause of drink? (Ilear, hear.) There was a tremendous increase of late years in im- morality. It flowed like a bad stream froni-one

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915. MARKSMEN AND WAR. Ali INCREASED EDUCATION RATE.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915. MARKSMEN AND WAR. Ali INCREASED EDUCATION RATE.

end of the country to the other, and every big city was full of its victims. They tinkered away- at the problem with their rescue homes, but still paid all-too-scant regard to the fact that there were thousands of women in the country to-day who were forced to work for a sweated wage, and that where that was the case they almost invariably found alongside it a great deal of loathsome immorality. It was no use tinkering at the effects of immorality without removing the cause that made it necct, sary for so many women to seek that way of livelihood. (Hear, hear.) They wanted to help the victims of crime and disease. They did not find those victims in the big houses in the nice streets, but in the quarters where the houses were not fit for human dwellings; where whole families were penned together in dismal sur- roundings; where there was little, or no, sun- light and fresh air; where there was no privacy or decency! Palliatives Instead of Remedies.

To cope with the effects of all this horrible herding together they built prisons and sana- toriums. Why had they not the courage to go to the root of the matter and tackle the housing question? This century was going to be an era of preventive work. At last the people were waking up to the fact that preventive work was not only easier, but that it was much cheaper than a cure. (Hear, hear.) The biggest and infinitely the most important industry in this country was its child-crop, and, yet, how did they treat that crop? They had no right to ask women to go on producing children if they were to become mere 'bits of waste—mere human wreikage with no chance of a decent living or upbringing. (Hear, hear). Every child ought to have its birthright. The great cry in the past had been "Begin with the child !" but the cry to-day was "Begin with the mother !" The community that neglected its necessitous mothers paid a high price, and what wtts re- quired most at this time was a good constructive scheme of social reform that would procure for the next generation a minimum standard of health. (Applause.) - The Wastage of Child Life. -

Out of every thous-and children born 150 died before reaching their first birthday, and yet the nation had not seriously disturbed itself. Was there a farmer who would lose 150 sheep out of every thousand without using every means in his power to prevent the wastage? The com- munity ought to do everything in its power to save its children; they were its most precious possession. (Hear, hear.) Mrs. Wilson con- cluded a long address with an appeal to the men and women of to-day to give themselves to social -service. There was, she said, no work so satisfying; no work which left such a; nice taste behind it as the work that was done for those -who were not so happily circumstanced as 'one- self. "To cure is the voice of the past. To prevent is the Divine whisper of to-day." MORE MONEY THAN LAST YEAR. '

The TREASURER, referring to the balance sheet, stated that the total receipts last year were £291 Bs. 4d., as against £254 15s. the year before. Reports and balance sheets having been adopted, Mr. ROLAND WILLIAMS proposed, •the Rev. T. T. JAMES seconded, and those present carried, a hearty vote of thanks to the Mayor and to the speakers. Returning thanks, Mrs. MUTER WILSON said that in these days when they heard so much about patriotism, it might be well to remember that one could be patriotic in a very real sense by looking after the mothers of the little chil- dren who were to be the citizens of the future. Helping the children and the mothers was not simply a mother's duty, it was a human duty. It was the patriotic duty of the citizens of to-day to take care of the race of the future, just as much as it was the duty of the men who had gone out to the front to fight. It was as real a patriotism as any in the country. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR and Mr. D'Aurri also returned thanks, and the. meeting closed.

div.head: – MARKSMEN AND WAR—continued.
div.p: - MARKSMEN AND WAR—continued.

hoped that the regulations which will govern them will be well thought out, and be of such a nature as to be undoubtedly an advantage and stimulant. An ill-considered suggestion has got into print, that all rifle clubs shokuld be governed by the rules as 'applied bY the War Office recog- nition of Volunteer Training Corps.
Late Lord Roberts.

"I must not close my report without refer- ence to the death of Lord Roberts. It was he who ,stirred the country upon ,the question of formation of rifle clubs after the. Boer War, and whose ideal was "Every man a rifleman." It must have been gratifying to him to have seen the fruits of his labour justified, and his ideal on the road to realisation.
"Our best thanks and gratitude are due to our worthy President for his kindness in allowing us the use of the Old quarry, and for his great interest in the club generally." (Applause.)_
The report was passed n'em. 'eon..., on the motion of Messrs. J. W. Elliott and P. Harrison.
OFFICERS ELECTED.

The following officers were re-elected unani- mously to serve during the present year: Presi- dent, Lieut.-Colonel C. Lyon; vice-presidents, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Messrs. Vere B. Davies, J. .T. Whitley, Segar Owen and F. Warburton, and Lieut.-Colonel Fairelough; hon. treasurer, Mr. F. J. Grocott ; hon. secretary, Mr. A. Shep- herd; auditors, Messrs. F. Gandy and J. San- key.—Mr. Shepherd had desired .to resign his secretarial duties on . account of "advancing years," but the club decided that he was too valued an official to relinquish, and appointed Mr. Swinton to help him as assistant secretary. —ln accepting the position of president for an- otheik year, Lieut-Colonel Lyon expressed his great appreciation of the honour.
Mr. J. Towers was appointed armourer until Mr. J. Allardice (who belongs to the Terri- torials) could resume his duties. The com- mittee is as follows: Messrs. H. Baines, F. C. Ben-

!don, F. Black, A. Down, J., W. Elliott, W. J. Featherstone, P. Harrison, J. Hartley; S. James, It. Thompson, F. Tole and J. Towers. This committee will appoint the range committee, which last year consisted of Messrs. C. P. Day, P. Harrison and J. Towers.

div.head: BACHELORS AND RECRUITING.
div.p: BACHELORS AND RECRUITING.

The Chairman was heartily thanked for pre- siding, on the proposition of Mr. F. C. Bennion, seconded by Mr. F. J. Grocott. In returning thanks, the President referred to the uses of rifle clubs and. other topics connected with the war. He emphasised the necessity of training the "youngsters" in riflp shooting. Rifle Shooting, he said, was good all round, and it was to Lord Roberts that they owfd the existence of such clubs as theirs. If they had paid more attention to him perhaps they would not have had this war to go through. This lead on to the question of recruiting, and the' speaker declared that he had been astonished to find that, of the thousands who had enlisted where he was, sixty per cent. were married men. Where were the brichelors? He thought the parents, rather than wives, were more the cause of young men not joining the ranks. The wives seemed quite anxious to get them off. (Laughter and 4.4 ,

div.head: Appleton Rifle Club "Justifies its Existence,"
div.p: Appleton Rifle Club "Justifies its Existence,"
A YEAR'S USEFUL WORK.

The effect of the war upon amateur rifle clubs was strikingly illustrated at the annual general meeting of the Appleton Rifle Club, which was held in Atkinson's Cafe, Bridge-street, on Mon- day evening. The President (Lieut-Colonel C. Lyon) occupied the chair. A SUBSCRIPTION DIFFICULTY.

After formal business, the assembly considered the advisability of confirming a resolution passed by the committee, in respect to the re- duction of subscriptions to members of Train- ing and Volunteer Corps. The Chairman said that personally he would like to hear the treasurer's accounts before passing the resolution. Otherwise it was a little difficult to understand whether they could re- duce the subscriptions mentioned. The Treasurer (Mr. F. J. Grocott) said a few members of the committee had wished to re- duce the subscription to 2s. 6d., but the club would then be at a loss.

Mr. Melville asked what the effect of not re- ducing the subscriptions would be. The Treasurer replied that some would still join, but others would not; and they would have less "wear and tear" with the rifles. Mr. Melville: Then it would be a gain to the club not to reduce the subscriptions? The Treasurer: Yes, but not from the national point of view.

div.head: WOULD CONSCRIPTION DESTROY CAMARADERIE?
div.p: WOULD CONSCRIPTION DESTROY CAMARADERIE?

The Chairman said he was against anything thht would put any obstacle in the way of the Army. Everybody should be in the Army in some way or other. The professional soldiers did not really know Low to look at the Train- ing Corps, for they did not like to assist them. unless they were only for men who were phy- sically unfit for the Army, but who should be encouraged to learn to tise the rifle in °llse of the invasion of the country. He did not like to interfere with the Rifle Club; but it was, now becoming a very critical time for the voluntary army system, and if the men were not forthcom- ing and the war went on as it was now going on, there would be nothing for it but compul- sory service. And that was against the national spirit. The English were the best fighters, and the officers and men had a fellow feeling which did not exist in any other army—all through the voluntary system. If they had con- scripts they would have to be treated in a differ- ent.way, for that feeling could not be the same.

The question of reducing the subscriptions, continued the speaker, brought in all those points of view. If the subscriptions of those wily eligible for home defence were reduced it Would certainly be right, but able-bodied young men who thought that by joining a rifle club they were doing all that could be required of them, must not be encouraged at all.

div.head: NO REPLY TO THE CLUB'S OFFER.
div.p: NO REPLY TO THE CLUB'S OFFER.

The Treasurer said he believed the Training; Corps had been taking advantage of the munici- pal range. A Member: Well, we have asked them and they have not replied, so I think we should close our offer of a reduced subscription. The Chairman asked if the majority of the Training Corps were elderly men. • A Member: I think so.
Mr. F. C. Bennion then proposed that, as the committee had not been' replied to, the offer should be withdrawn.
Mr. F. Black- seconded, and the proposition was carried unanimously.
BIGGEST RECEIPTS IN THE CLUB'S HISTORY.
In submitting the Treasurer's accounts for 1914, the committee reported:

"It will be observed that the receipts are greater than any previous year, and also that there is a substantial balance in favour of the year's working.- Repairs and the upkeep of the range must be attended to, and .paid for out of this balance.

"The year has been an unusually busy one. The outbreak ef ,war brought many new mem- bers to the club, and the outdoor season was prolonged to the year end. It is gratifying to note that many new and oH members of the club have joined the Army, thus demonstrating the usefulness of obtaining the first instruction in the use of the rifle, and fulfilling the object for which the club was formed."

The revenue account showed receipts amount- ing to £124 2s. 7d. This total included: Sub- criptions £24 2s. 6d., 4th Battalion South Lan- cashire Regiment .X2O, National Service League £5, and Training Corps £2 14s. The sale of ammunition and other shooting requisites, and competition fees, made .up practically all the remainder—the income from the sale of ammu- nition alone amounting to more than £53. The expenditure totalled £lO5 18s. 7d.; which, with .R 5 owing for ammunition, left a surplus of £l3 4s.

div.head: "A FEW EXPLANATIONS."
div.p: "A FEW EXPLANATIONS."

The Treasurer said a few explanations were necessary with regard to the balance sheet. To some extent the surplus given was illusory, as repairs which might very well have been done had been deferred. In the balance statement the sum of £8 Os. 6d, put down for depreciation might seem a very liberal allowance, but they, would probably agree that it was not an exces- sive estimate in view of the increased wear and tear of their service rifles during the past season. Owing to the absence of members with the Forces, and for various other reasons, continued Mr. Grocott, thirteen subscriptions remained unpaid, but a few of these might come in later. The largely-increased membership should aug- ment the subscription list for 1915, but again there would be an almost certain want of £2O from the 4th Battalion South Lancashire Regi- ment, and £5 from the Nittional Service League—which they had been accustomed to re- ceive regularly for some years, and the absence of which would represent the loss of a hundred members as long as the war lasted. The accounts were passed unanimously, there being no discussion.

div.head: SECRETARY'S REPORT.
div.p: SECRETARY'S REPORT.

Mr. A. Shepherd was unable to be present, but the following report from him was read : "It must be admitted that the past year has been a very eventful one, and has kept the offi- cials of the club busy right to the end. "The outdoor season was officially opened by the President on May 2nd, there being a good attendance of members and friends. One of the earlier competitions was that taken up with the 'Military in the form of postal matches, and quite a keen interest was taken in them. Some good scores were recorded, but the matches came abruptly to a close in consequence of the outbreak of the war. The Secretary was pre- sented with the 'Military Mail' medal for the best average made for our team. The other competitions completed were for the ' Bell ' medal and the 'Daily Mail' certificate. These were won by Mr. j. Hartley. The xpress' medal was taken by Mr. C. P. Day, the S.M.R.C.', medal by Mr. P. Harrison, and the 'Daily Telegraph certificate by the Secretary. The ' Donegal ' badge was not competed for. Upon the outbreak of war all competitions and matches were cancelled or postponed, and the competition for the beautiful silver cup pre- sented to the club by the,President was one of them. Only four matches have taken place, the •club winning three and losing one.

div.head: Declaration of War.
div.p: Declaration of War.

"After the declaration of war there was quite a rush of men wishing to join the club, and up to the year end seventy-four new members had been elected. This kept the officials busy, as most of the men had not previously handled a rifle.' The club can claim to have justified its existence, and fulfilled the object for which it was formed, as fifteen old members and nine new members are now serving in the Army, and instruction in musketry has been given to mem- bers, • including those forming units of Volun- teer Training Corps; three of such organisations have used our range.

"Further results of the war arc the forma- tion of. many new clubs in the town, and the inauguration of a ,municipal range. It has often been remarked that the old club—which Can now be looked upon as the parent—would find it difficult to put a good team in the field if all the club members represented their " own " club. But I think if the test came we could about prove the winners. " Rumour is quite well to the fore that the Government will eventually take rifle clubs under its wing. Should this take place, it is
Continued in preceding column.

div.head: Cost of Teaching Our Children Goes Up £3,000.
div.p: Cost of Teaching Our Children Goes Up £3,000.
HOW THE WAR HAS HIT THE SCHOOLS.

Monday was Budget Day with the Warring- ton Education Committee, the estimates of receipts and expenditure during the coming twelve months being laid before a well-attended meeting, presided over by Councillor Henry Roberts. The -estimates were approved after they had been lucidly explained by Mr. A. J. Jolley, who is the chairman of the Finance Sub-committee. They included a number of anticipated increases in expenditure, some of them directly due to the war, and others to the natural expansion in local educational effort consequent upon the development of the town, and the progressive attitude which is nowadays taken up by Education Authorities throughout the country with regard to the.importance of givjng all the children of the land a sound and useful education. The directions in which in- creases were budgetted for is plainly shown in the following list, each total given representing the amount over and above that estimated for the same purpose last year :
Elementary Teachers' Salaries 1,500 Loan Charges Rent Rates and Taxes l4O Fuel
School Keepers' Wages Evening Schooli,Expenditure Books and Apparatus School Attendance Officers' Salaries 55 Medical Inspection Work, l2O Repairs

the lives of its sons and of its material re- sources. They, as members of the Education Committee, were engaged in a war that was less exciting, but, in his opinion, was even more important. The true progress of the country depended mainly upon the efficiency of its edu- cational system—more upon that, he thought, than upon any other single thing—and tjle com- mittee would be doing their duty, locally, if Any passed those estimates in a cheerful spirit. The speaker then formally moved the passing of the estimates and the adoption of a resolution requesting the Corporation to provide ,R 29,000 from the borough rate for the purposes of edu- cation.
Mr. E. PLINSTON seconded. EDUCATION AND WAR.

Alderman 13ENNETT, after congratulating Mr. Jolley upon his extremely lucid statement, said that whilst none of them liked to hear that heavier charges were to be imposed, but, having listened to Mr. Jolley's full and frank state- ment, they would all more or less agree that to advance the call upon the rates was the only course open to them. It was not due to any fault of the Education Committee, but to the inevitable growth of their work and the expan- sion of their requirements. He entirely agreed with Mr. Jolley that no money they spent in the work of the town brought better results than the expenditure upon education. He would almost go sip far as to say that it brought ranch better results than the enormous expen- diture they were pouring out in bloodshed on the fields of Europe at the present time. He had a strong suspicion that if they were really educated—he was not 'thinking of that bogus education commonly spelt with a "k "—(laugh- ter)—and if they could get other countries edu- cated to the same standard, such a sacrifice of life and money might be avoided. Anything that tended to prevent the repetition of a dis- aster so horrible was cheap, even if it cost a considerable sum to pave the way to it. Sound Teaching Necessary to Social Reform. He was extremely keen on social reform, and he thought one of the preliminary steps to such reform was that. they should get the whole of the population educated on right and sound lines. As far .as his observation went, he was happy to think that they were, more and more, getting on right lines. The men of all classes that one met—" the man in the street "—showed obvious signs of the good that had resulted from past expenditure on education. The "man in the street" showed it in his demeanour, his conversation, his habits, and in his general out- look on life. As education grew and developed, he thought they would not only produce better and happier citizens, but they would also devise some more sensible means of settling interna- tional differences than those at present in vogue —means that would be more worthy of civilised nations. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, -Alder- man Bennett said that he was strongly in favour of a readjustment of national and local burdens in this matter of education, and hoped that that would be one of the first questions to be tackled when the war was over.

div.head: BIG LOCAL BUDGET FIGURES.
div.p: BIG LOCAL BUDGET FIGURES.

The estimates further showed that the total required for elementary* education was £52,194 155., as compared with -X49,159 estimated for the financial year now drawing to a close. The largest item was one of £36,266, 10s. for elemen- tary teachers' salaries. The receipts were put at £27,235 9s. 2d., as against £26,820 for, the present year. The aid grant is estimated to produce.X6,loo (as against £6,200 this year), the annual grant £13,330 (X 13,325 and the fee grant £6,150 (X 6,200 The cost of higher edu- cation during the ensuing twelve months is put at £9,738, .as against £9,349 in the present year. The new estimates involve a call upon the borough rate; during the coming year, of £29,000, as against £26,000 for the financial year 1914-15,

div.head: CAUSES OF THE INCREASES.
div.p: THE CAUSES OF THE INCREASES.

In moving the adoption of the estimates, Mr. JOLLEY said that before going into them in de- tail he might, perhaps, be allowed to repeat a general observation he had made many times, and which he thought it desirable to emphasise. That observation had to do with the difficulty of presenting satisfactory estimates at that time of the year, owing to the doubt that necessarily existed as to how the actual income and expendi- ture would compare with the estimated income and expenditure. There were still-six weeks of the financial year to run and, though, as a rule, their estimates had come out in a most satis- factory manner, they had occasionally been very considerably out, and for reasons over which the committee had no control, partly owing to the fact that the Government's methods of assessing and paying grants were sometimes changed in the middle of the year and partly owing to measures taken by the local authority in one or two directions. Owing to these causes the committee's working balance at the end of March, 1914, was £l,OOO less than they expected. He. was hoping that that would not occur again this year; indeed, So far as they could judge at the moment it was probable that the figures would come out pretty near the estimate; but there was an element of uncertainty about it which justified them in adhering to the policy hitherto followed of submitting their estimates on conservative and, as he thought, sound finan- cial lines, in not over-estimating their income and not under-estimating their expenditure, and, if they erred at all, erring rather on the side of over-estimating their, expenditure and under-estimating their income. (Hear, hear.)

Seeking a Grant as a Necessitous Authority. It would be seen from the estimates dealing with elementary education. that they were look- ing for a grant of £5OO as a necessitous author- ity. That was a grant which was promised by the Chancellor of the Exchequer when the com- mittee's expenditure exceeded the equivalent of is. 6d. in the X, and if it were continued year by year it would be a larger amount. They anticipated a somewhat lower grant for health work and also that salaries would cost more, the increase being in part due to the fact that the new Oakwood-avenue School would be open during about seven months of the coming finan- cial year. An increase of about £4OO was esti- mated in the cost of books and apparatus, that being in part due to the 10 per cent. rise in prices, and also, of course, to the fact that the new Oakwood-avenue School would have to be equipped. For similar reasons, the item, "fuel, lighting and cleaning, £3,226,'! showed an in- crease. The item for loan charges was also up, but that was an item which he, for one, would be glad to see grow more rapidly; for he thought it was high time that the children of the people were entirely educated in schools owned and controlled by the people through the people's representatives. or course, that was a matter over which there was a difference of opinion, but the bill was there and had got to be paid.

div.head: Medical .Inspection to Cost Slightly More.
div.p: Medical .Inspection to Cost Slightly More.

The work of medical inspection was expected to cost .2136 more, partly owing to the appoint- ment of an additional officer and partly to the development of the work of that department. On the receipts side of the account, they anti- cipated a small increase of grant. It was a source of great pleasure to him to see that their evening school work was steadily growing and increasing in volume, and, he believed, in effi- ciency. Altogether, there was an increase in the education estimates of .23,400, off-set by a few minor reductions and a few minor increases of grant and by the special grant to necessitous bodies of 02500, leaving, it was .estinlated, a net increase of £2,786. Part of the increase in the cost of elementary school teachers' salaries was due to the fa qt that a number of the men had gone to the Front—(applause)-----and that, in accord with the atrallement made .by the Cor- poration, any difference between their salaries and their military pay was being made up to them, whilst other peolile had been engaged temporarily to fill their places. The increase of .22,786 in the expenditure was approximately 6 per cent., and of that about four-fifths fell on the ratepayers and one-fifth on the taxpayers, as distinct from the ratepayers. That meant that the taxpayers' contribution would increase 1 per cent., whilst that of the ratepayers would increase 10 per Cent. To some of them that did not seem to be by any means fair and equitable, and he had no doubt that, had it not been for the war, they would have seen some readjust- ment of the burden as between the ratepayers and the taxpayers. The Chancellor of ,the Ex- chequer promised definitely that that matter should be taken in hand with a view to making a more equitable adjustment, but the war had, for the time being, forced that matter on one side, and in place of that rioadjustment, they had to put up with a makeshift in the shape of the £5OO, which they expected to receive as a grant as a necessitous authority, to which_ he had referred. •
Thinks the Ratepayer Gets Value for His Money.

It was not very pleasant to have to advocate additional calls on the rates, and the ratepayer was entitled to ask whether he was getting value for his money. -Personally, he thought that the ratepayer was, though he did not sup - Pose that that view would be accepted with absolute unanimity either in that room or in the town. Some people entertained what cer- tain of the members of that committee regarded aS obsolete ideas about social responsibility, but he thought the majority there would recog- nise their -responsibilities in this matter of the education of the young and would accept the estimates, knowing that in so doing they were, providing part of the munitions of ivar for the campaign of social reform in which .they were willing to take their part. The nation was at the present time giving most ungrudgingly of

div.head: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND "FACING
div.p: COUNCILLOR PEMBERTON AND "FACING
THE MUSIC."

Councillor PEMBERTON contended that the com- mittee were not really "facing the music." The total deficiency was £29,735, but apparently .2735 was being taken from the working balance, which they assumed years ago ought not to stand at a. farthing less than it amount at that time. Yet they had already taken .t 2,000 out of the balance on two occasions, and it would appear that they would require another £l,OOO to adjust matters for the year just ending. It would be far better for the committee to levy a proper rate, which would really meet the expenditure, because .there was no doubt that things would not go cheaper during the coming year. The burden imposed on the ratepayers was heavy enough already, and it would be heavier still if they were to follow the Chairman of the Finance Committee in his desire to see them go in for more and yet more schools, and for more expenditure on thbse that they already had. lie did not know where the education rate was going to end. The champions of education, when the Education Bill of 1,902 was before-The House of Commons, said the rate would never exceed 3d. in the .2. It only showed what those prophets were and how. people forgot these things. (Laughter.) He never could agree with Alderman Bennett, because that gentleman had no idea of business spending at all. If a thing looked nice, money was no object with him; it didn't matter at all! (Laughter.) Getting a Very Serious Matter.

The education rate was Offing a very serious matter, and they ought to be careful of every additional pound which they spent. There was bound to come a time when there would be it re-action, for there were many people who did not believe that the public were getting value for their money in this matter of education, and the number of those people was growing. There ought to be more economy on the part of education committees, and they ought to join in pressing. the Government to take its proper share of the burden of educational expenditure. The first year or two the Government found the greater part of the money, but now, as Mr. Jolley had told them, it came to this: that the people of Warrington—and they were not so very different from the people in other towns in this respect—had to find tour-fifths of the cost of education out of the rates, whilst the tax- payers only found one-fifth—a position of affairs that, surely, was wrong. Surely, if education was of national benefit, the nation ought to supply the money, or, at least, the major por- tion of it. When the Governlment were raising their taxes for domestic purposes he did not see why they should not deal with this question of education as well as the other matters. " Kultur" Not Worth Twopence.

"Alderman Bennett," he said, "amused me in his remarks as to the effect of education. Lots of men who have as much education as Alderman Bennett would wish them to have would go in for war. You will always have war. ('No.') The nations who are not prepared for it will go under. The only way in which you will ever keep yourselves from having war is by being strong enough to defeat your opponent, and then he would not dare to go to war with you. Germany has been held up for years as the finest educated nation in the world. They were the people we were told to copy. But look what these finely educated people have done. Look at the value of their education and liultur.g"The word is not worth twopenee." (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN: There is rather a difference between education and " kultur."
Councillor PEMBERTON : Well, I suppose there is, only I am not used to these fine distinctions. I believe that what we ought to give is a good, sound education.

Mr. JOLLEY : • Hear, hear! Councillor PEMBERTON : Yes, but I don't agree with your kind of education—(laughter)—be- cause my experience is that if the ability is in a boy or girl" it will Come out, and that if it is not you cannot Create it, however much money you may spend.
Money Cannot Create Geniuses.

If a boy is a genius you can cultivate his talents,, but you do not want to go spending millions of money all over the country in a haphazard attempt to make geniuses. If the genius is there it will come out of itself. The education rate, Councillor Pemberton con- cluded, had reached such a pitch that it was time to call a halt. If they did not be was afraid the public would try to compel them seriously to consider the matter. According to the present estimates, the real increase in the education Tate should be fourpence. If they did not face the music now they would have to face it next year. ' The estimates were then approved.
