div.head: TENDING THE WOUNDED.
div.p: TENDING THE WOUNDED.
The Splendid Work at Raddon Court Hospital.
MRS. CROSFIELD PRESENTS
CERTIFICATES.

There Was a most interesting gathering at Haddon Court Temporary Red Cross Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, when Mrs. Arthur Cros- field formally presented a number of certificates for proficiency in first aid and nursing work to local ladies who, since the opening of the hos- pital for the reception of sick and wounded soldiers, have been busy putting into practice the knowledge that they had gained in "the piping times of peace" through the medium of the local Voluntary Aid Detachments; know- ledge which, as it was intended to do, has proved of invaluable service—as many a poor hurt and maimed warrior can testify—in the present awful European cataclysm. The presentation. ceremony was witnessed by several of the men temporarily laid hors de combat, and the whole- heartedly, boyishly-enthusiastic manner in which they applauded every recipient of the coveted pieces of cardboard spoke volumes con- cerning their appreciation of the services which the ladies, thanks to their application to the study of. the first principles of surgery, had been able to render them.

div.head: TRAINING IN PEACE TO QUALIFY FOR
div.p: TRAINING IN PEACE TO QUALIFY FOR
WAR TIMES.

Miss SYLVIA BROADBENT, vice-president of the Daresbury Division of the Voluntary Aid De- tachment movement,-most graciously presided over the presentation proceedings, and prefaced Mrs. Crosfield's congenial task with a few ex- planatory words. It was not necessary, she said —to an accompaniment of applause from the numerous company assembled-4o introduce Mrs. Crosfield in Warrington, where she was so well known in connection with any good work. (Hear, hear.) They were delighted to welcome Mrs. Crosfield in their Red Cross Itospital, and were honoured thht she should have consented to present the certificates gained in the recent examinations. The aim of the British Red Cross Society, under whose Eegis the Hospital was being run, was to train men and women in peace times to qualify to tend the wounded in time of war. During the past few years they had been trying to form Voluntary Aid De- tachments in that district, and had completed two—Cheshire, No. 22 (Commandant, Miss M. Broadbent), and Cheshire, No. 48 (Command- ant, Miss Monks).

div.head: "Did AU the Work of the House."
div.p: "Did AU the Work of the House."

Those two detachments now provided the per- sonnel at Raddon Court, who, under several trained nurses, did all the work of the house, in addition to the nursing. They, now wanted to form new detachments, and for that purpose lec- tures had been given in several of thd town- ships of the Daresbury Division. She was very glad to notice the number of certificates to be presented that day, and she hoped that all those who had taken the nursing course would take the first aid course also, and so qualify, as soon as possible, for joining a detachment. She would like to take that -opportunity of person- ally thanking most heartily the doctors and nurses who had so generously given their time in lecturing and examining, and for all the trouble they had taken. (Hear, hear.) She was sure that the candidates, too, would join with her in that expression of sincere thanks. (Applause.) The object of the British Red Cross Society was a noble one, and she trusted that they might all do their best to live up to its high aspirations.

div.head: MRS. CROSFIELD AND THE WOMAN'S PART.
div.p: MRS. CROSFIELD AND THE WOMAN'S PART.

Airs. CROSFIELD then distributed the awards, remarking that she would like to congratulate all the lucky candidates, not only upon their success, hut also upon their having the oppor- tunity of working under such able leaders as Miss Sylvia Broadbent, the commandant, and Miss A. Broadbent. (Applause.) It oughtsto be a matter of pride to those two ladies that things were being done so *ell in the Daresbury Divi- sign. When she (the speaker) visited Raddon Court some months ago, before it was quite ready, she was surprised to see the prepara- tions which were going on and to learn that it was all being done by what she hoped she might call, without being considered disrespectful, amateurs.

Same Spirit Animates Both Sexes. The women of the nation had shown the same spirit as that which animated the men. (Ap- plause.) A few prime movers—such as the • I leaders among them that day—had taken the matter in hand long before the war broke out, and were prepared, but the majority of women in England were not prepared for the work which they were now undertaking, and under- taking so well. She was sure that none of the ladies attached to Raddon Court had been ani- mated by the spirit which was shown by an otherwise very nice young lady of her acquaint- ance, who talked to her about nursing and had formed great plans and projects about going to the Front.
An Example Not To Be Emulated.

"Oh, yes !" said she (Mrs. Crosfield) to the young lady. "Of course, you have passed all your examinations and have medals and badges and everything else necessary?" "Oh, no !" the young lady answered, "we have not done that yet, but we went out shopping this morn- ing and we tried on the caps—some of them were most becoming." (Loud laughter.) But that 'was- not: the spirit which animated the majority of the women of Bngland, for in large, and ever increasing numbers, they were devoting themselves and their energies to what was, per- haps, the highest of all tasks. She did not know whether her hearers had read the recent articles by Hilaire Belloc in which he enunci- ated the proposition that the greatest help in the achievement of victory was the morale of a nation. If not, she would advise them to do so. The women of England would be able to claim a share in the victory, because they had in these trying times evinced a morale which was full of courage and energy and devotion. (Applause.)

div.head: CERTIFICATE WINNERS.
div.p: THE CERTIFICATE WINNERS.

Before presenting the certificates, Mrs. Cros- field, on behalf of the nurses who had been at- tending that lady's course of lectures handed to Nurse Davy a pretty wristlet-watch. She then handed certificates to the followinit the names of the recipients being., called out by Mrs. Wheeler, the Divisional Secretary : Stockton Heath.—First certificates: Mrs. Bradshaw, and the Misses M. Allen, Mary Bainbridge, M. Caldwell, M. Dolan, M. Gornall, Ethel Glover, 11. Nicholson, 0. Payne, P. Wood- cock. Advanced: Misses Ridgway and Pember- ton. Proficiency: Misses Monks, Ronald, Stone and Venn.

Latchford:--First certificate for Nursing: Miss M. G. Corney (seventeen members of the class had already received their certificates). Pro- ficiency medals Areviously gained: Miss S. Broadbent (for first aid) and the Misses Horra- bin and Monks (for nursing). First aid cer- tificates: Misses .Edith Bradshaw, May Cullis, Dorothy Deane, 'Nellie Kirkham, Nora Rumney, Katherine Robb, Lucy Skinner, Lily Skelland (proficiency) and Edila Taylor. Warrington.—Nursing certificates: Mrs. E. Baker, and the ;Misses E. Barker, J. Browne, Margaret Baron, Marjorie Bennett, Edith Bradshaw, Elizabeth Cooke, Jane Cooper, Sarah Dainteth, Ethel Dearden, A. Ewart, Frances A. Eddowes, Betsy Forshaw, Lucilla M. Hill, Nellie Hirst, Ella K. Hazlett, Constance Hitchins, Eleanor M. C. Joyson, Ruth Mitchell, Dorothea Mitchell, Elsie P. Mason, Olive Payne, Cecilia Joan Reynolds, Lilian Wright, Pattie Wood- cock; Ruby M. Witts.

div.head: MERE MALE "FIRST-AIDERS."
div.p: MERE MALE "FIRST-AIDERS."

There has also been a men's class in first aid, and Miss Sylvia Broadbent announced that she was very glad indeed to report that seventeen went in for the examination, and that almost all of them passed. They hoped, therefore, soon to be able to form a complete Men's Voluntary Aid Detachment. Before the visitors left, Mrs. Crosfield was accorded a hearty vote of thanks for SD kindly distributing the certificates. Mrs. Crosfield then played a number of piano- forte solos for the entertainment of the wounded warriors quartered in the hospital, the fact that her kindness was keenly appreciated by the gallant fellows being evidenced by the heartidr ness of their apPlause.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915.

div.head: SPLENDIDLY KEEN!
div.p: SPLENDIDLY KEEN!

We have the permission of the War Office to announce that our local Terri- torials are now in France, but we are asked to refrain from stating when or how they got there. It is sufficient to know that they are there, with the additional iptimation, conveyed to the readers of "The Examiner" by Mr. ARTHUR CROSFIELD, speaking at the Liberal Women's social for Latchford Ward, that the Men are "splendidly keen." These are the words used by MAJOR CROSFIELD in a letter to his brother, and display the prevalent. spirit that will prove that Britain still has the will, and also the power, to up- hold the cause of justice in Europe. Mr. CROSFIELD, who has taken the keen- est interest in the Territorials, pre- sented them with a sufficient number of periscopes to enable each platoon to see the enemy from the cover of their trenches. We all wish our men the best of luck, coupled with a chance to show the enemy how a way can be packed through to Berlin, if the opera- tion towards Paris has been found impossible.

div.head: RIDICULOUS POSITION.
div.p: A RIDICULOUS POSITION.

There will be a unanimous feeling in Warrington that Mr. HoLmAN KINGDON must not be allowed to carry out his threat—courteously conveyed—of re- signing from the chairmanship of the Medical InsPettion Sub-comMittee of the Education 'Committee. Parliament. in its wisdom—undoubted wisdOm in this case—has charged Education Authorities with the highly important duties Of looking to the bodily as well as the mental .welfare of children of school age. The reason is apparent, for physical defectives cannot be men- tally sound, and it is a waste of public money, as well. as. gross cruelty, to attempt to link,. up the two according to a common standard. • Our legislators moved- with , caution. First they allowed for the medical inspection, and then the medical treatment of children, and many are the eyes that ',caused headaches, tonsils that caused deafness and stupidity, and bad teeth that fouled the stomach and .caused indiges- tion with all their debilitating effects upon immature constitutions, that have been mended, to the betterment of the young sufferers and the ultimate ad- vantage of the State. How pressing was the need for this official oversight may be judged by the fact that three out of every four of the thousands of' children in our elementary schools, were suffering from decayed teeth.
The need for this remedial work being unquestioned, there remains the consideration of the method by which it should be done. The work was deliberately imposed upon Education
Authorities, who had already effective

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915.

charge of the children. It is admittedly right that the health affairs of a town should be under one and the same head, but that .does not mean that the Health Committee are in all matters to keep the Medical Inspection Sub-committee in leading strings for ever, and at all points ; but difficult as it is to believe, Mr. KINGDON and his committee have been subjected to the indignity of hav- ing had a permanent dental officer appointed by tile Health Committee without having been consulted or in- formed of the appointment. Mr. KING- DON, in effect, says the Health Com- mittee/may make the appointments, but they must, if they do so, ,see that those they appoint do the work. That is fair. There is another way out. The Council must see that the Health Com- mittee are more sympathetic towards ' the good work that the Medical Inspec- tion, Committee are doing in the interests of the children.

Mr. KINGDON and his colleagues are doing splendid service. to the town, and it would be a.pity to see it checked by such incidents as the one against which this startling protest is made. What reason is there why appointments should not lie made by • the two committees in conference?

at some battle in the ring; if this was a sort of stand-up prizefight between Britain and Ger- many, every Englishman would deem it un- sportsmanlike to wish to see the intervention of anybody else. But it was not a prize-fight.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S FINE BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S FINE BRIDGE.
First Tramcar Crosses the Newest Portion.
COUNCILLOR AS MOTORMAN.

The first tramcar to cross over the newest por- tion of Warrington Bridge—now metamorphosed into a fine, artistic structure of splendid width —did so on Monclay afternoon in the presence of three or four thousand spectators. The car took the now permanent route to Latchford, and, in the unavoidable and regrettable absence of the Chairman of the Electricity and Tram- wais Committee (Councillor Joseph, deputy mayor), it was driven by the Deputy Chairman of the committee (Councillor John Wilkinson); who took his place at the driver's handle exactly as the neighbouring clocks struck three, and, fuming on the current, got the car over the bridge in fine style, amid cheers"from the inter- ested onlookers. As his passengers Councillor Wilkinson had a number of prominent mem- bers of the Corporation—including the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock)—aboard, and' after he had !driven them as far as York-street, Knutsford-road, and back again to the bridge; he 'and most of his "fares "—the Mayor being amongst the exceptions—repaired to the Old Academy, where many other well-known people assembled, and where a few brief speeches were made.
MANY PUBLIC PERSONAGES PRESENT.

The car in its passage over the bridge was followed by a motor car containing the Mayoress (Mrs. Peacock) and lady friends. Among those who witnessed the starting of the car, and many of whom subsequently adjourned to the Old Academy, were Alderman Smethurst (chairman of the Bridges Committee) and Mrs. and Miss Smethurst; Aldermen Pierpoint and Bennett, the driver of the car (who was heartily con- gratulated by-his brother members of the Cor- poration on the skill he had displayed in a new role), Councillors Chrimes, Skelland and Halli- well, Mr. Alfred Thorne (of the firm of Messrs. Alfred Thorne and Sons, the contractors), Mr. G. H. Hodgson (resident engineer), Mr. Paine (Mr. Thorne's manager), Dr. Peacocke, Hall (a member of the Board of Guardians), Mrs. Gough, Mrs. Roden, Mr. John Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Mr. A. M. Ker (borough engineer and surveyor), Mr. M. A. Piercy (deputy engineer), Mr. F. V. L. Mathias (engi- neer of the Electricity Department), Mr. .T. Telfer (manager of the Tramways Department), and Messrs. James Whitley (a member of the Stockton Heath Parish Council), W. Furness, G. Venn, J. C. Coppock. W. Bibby, W. J. Edlesten, T. H. Ashcroft, J. Critchley, T. Weir and John Gandy. •

div.head: AN INTERESTING DAY IN LOCAL HISTORY.
div.p: AN INTERESTING DAY IN LOCAL HISTORY.

The car-ride over, and the numerous company duly assembled in the Old Academy, Alderman Bennett, in felicitous terms, proposed the healths of the Mayor (in his absence), the Chairman of the Bridges Committee, the Chair- man and Deputy-Chairman of the Electricity and Tramways Committee, and of the contrac-, tor and the contractor's foreman (Mr. Paine). That day, said the worthy Alderman, was an interesting one in the -history of Warrington, marking as it did the running of the first tram- car Over the newest portion of the splendid town bridge. It was a matter of great regret to them all that Mr. Webster, the eminent engineer, who had designed the new bridge, had not been spared to see the completion of the work of his brain—the completion of a fine bridge for this, his native town. Still, the structure would always' serve to keep his memory green and fra- grant in the borough of his birth. (Hear, hear.) The erection of the structure had been in ex- cellent hands; indeed more reliable work could not have been done, and they were all proud of their new bridge, which was, indeed, a credit to the town.

div.head: NO SERIOUS ACCIDENT DURING RE-BUILDING.
div.p: NO SERIOUS ACCIDENT DURING RE-BUILDING.

Alderman Smethurst, in returning thanks. mentioned the fact that during the work of constructing the bridge, which had extended over three years, Igo -serious accident had occirred, a fact whin., he thought, spoke well for the care which had been exercised by the contractor and hit foreman, and no less by the workmen themselves. (Hear, hear.) The toast of -" The memory of the Engineer, the late Mr. Webster," having been honoured in silence,
Councillor Wilkinson regretted the absence of the Deputy Mayor, and said how much he ap- preciated having had the honour of driving the first tramcar over the newest portion of the bridge.

div.head: CONTRACTOR'S THREE SONS IN THE ARMY.
div.p: CONTRACTOR'S THREE SONS IN THE ARMY.

Mr. Thorne, replying for his firm, mentioned the fact that during the time the bridge had been undergoing re-building there had been a little friction between his firm (the contractors)' and the Corporation from time to time, but it had not been of such a character as to give cause for either alarm or regret. (Hear, hear.) He also mentioned the fact that the work of direct- ing the re-building had in the main been in the hands of his three sons, who had now, however, joined the colours. (Applause.) He concluded by paying a tribute to the memory of the late Mr. Webster, with whom, he said, he had been associated between thirty and forty years-. The company then dispersed.

div.head: Little Unemploment.
div.p: Little Unemploment.

Inquiries undertaken during the last few days by the Town Clerk's department show that the amount of real' poverty in Warrington at the present time is, despite the war, little, if any, more than the normal, and that the state of the local employment market is healthy, the diffi- culty in some trades being to .find sufficient suitable men. A few peoule of both sexes had been thrown out of work owing to a temporary check in the fustian trade, but it is understood that the factories engaged in this class of work will resume business next week.

div.head: TERRITORIALS IN FRANCE.
div.p: TERRITORIALS IN FRANCE.
Last of Liberal Ward Socials for Soldiers' Comforts.
LATCHFORD'S BIG RALLY.

The last of the highly successful and thor- oughly enjoyable series of ward socials pro- moted under the auspices of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association for the purpose of raising funds out of which to buy materials to work into comforts for our soldiers, was held in the Crosfield Memorial Hall on Monday night. Primarily intended for the Liberals of Latchford, it not only drew a large crowd from that quarter of the town, but also many from other parts, anxious to seize the last opportunity of attending one of t .3 series, the fame of *hich has penetrated to all quarters of the town. The result was, of course, that the Latchford social was one of the most successful of the many suc- cesses; the numerous whist and domino tables being all occupied, whilst when the games over, and the prizes won therein duly presented —the dancing came on, the spacious floor was fully taken up by the throng of merry devotees of the goddess Terpsichore. Those present in- cluded the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock), and Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Crosfield, the prospec- tive Liberal candidate' and his wife being accorded a hearty ovation upon entering the hall.

THE WORKERS AND THE ENTERTAINERS The arrangements for the social were admir- ably carried out by Mrs. Locker (the ward captain), assisted by the following ladies:— Mesdames Knowles, Berry, White, Newall, Wright, O'Brien and Davies. After the games light refreshments were served and in between the dances the following well-known, local artistes amused the company: The Misses Winstanley, Walker, and Minnie Poden, and Messri. H. J. Nurse and W. Rigby, and the Excelsior Quartet Party, whose contri- butions were extremely popular, as was also the humorous "turn," written and devised by Mr. H. Nurse and presented in most successful fashion by the author and his brother. Mr. Louis Hale was the pianist for the evening, and Mr. E. A. Sanders, as usual, made a most effi- cient M.C.

The prizes won in the whist drive and domino tournament were presented during an interval called after the first dance, Mrs. Crosfield per- forming the ceremony of presentation and being rewarded for her trouble with a round of ap- plause, which she smilingly acknowledged. Mr. Crosfield then briefly addressed thecom- pany, his remarks being frequently punclrated with loud applause.

div.head: NEVER AGAIN!
div.p: NEVER AGAIN!
Mr. Crosfield and the Lesson That
Europe Will Learn.

Mr. CZ:WIELD began by saying that his only regret was that Mrs. Crosfield, sen., was not with them that evening, for it would have de- lighted her heart to see what an excellent use they were making of the beautiful hall which she had given them. (Hear, hear.) They had had a really fine series of delightful and most enjoyable social evenings, which_ he thought a very happy way of inaugurating the hall, and that evening he had the good for- tune of being able to congratulate Mrs. Toni Locker and the ladies from Latchford, who were associated with her, upon the fact that the social for which they were mainly responsible, had broken the record. (Applause.) The won- derful success which had attended the social gatherings in that hall augured most promis- ingly as to the excellent purposes to which it would be put in the future. (Hear, hear.) There' was one topic which, he thought, ought not to be passed over in silence; indeed, he was sure that everyone present would wish him to make some reference to it; viz., that the Warrington Battalion had gone to France. (Cheers.) His brother, Major Crosfield—(more cheers)—wrote: "The men are splendidly keen." (Loud cheers.) Splendidly keen! Yes, that was ,the spirit which one found all over the country, and it was that spirit which was going, once and for all, to put an end to the ascend- ancy of Prussian militarism. He thought it would not be unfitting if, through the columns of "The Examiner," they sent a message of good cheer to their friends, the Warringtoniana who were now at the war; a message wishing them every success in their great and ever-to-be- remembered undertaking—an assurance that everybody in the old town would watch their doings with anxious and admiring solicitude— (cheers)—filled as they were with great pride and with high hopes that their fellow-townsmen would do great deeds, and that having achieved their mighty task it would not be long before they were joyously welcoming them back again in Warrington. (Loud applause.)

THE GREATEST CAUSE IN HISTORY. He had heard it said that the authorities in- tended that every patriotic son of Britain, who had COlllO forward in the hour of need, should receive something in the nature of a permanent reminder of the services volunteered and ren- dered to the country. He had no definite infor- mation on the question, but he felt most strongly that something of this kind ought to be done, and would be done, and he had seen no better suggestion than the one put forward the other day that a medal, should be given bearing the simple inscription "I was there!" (Cheers.) In the course of her "wonderful island story," this country had passed through many great and momentous periods, but there had never been a time when her men were called upon to fight in quite so great a cause; never before were the Army and Navy set the task of achieving such vast ob- jects. They were told by a famous historian that too great a reverence for antiquity was not exactly evidence of any special vigour and capacity in a nation. Reverence for antiquity within moderation was a very good thing, but it could bp overdone, and he for one would not by any means like to see it carried as far as it was carried by the Chinese, who worshipped their ancestors. Still at the same time the people of this country were all proud of the history of their race—(hear, hear)—and of all the great deeds their ancestors had performed. And what a wonderful thought it was, that, when the story of these mighty events and stirring times came to be written it would be
an even greater and more inspiring chapter than anything written hitherto in the whole of our history. •

div.head: MESSAGE FOR THE WARRINGTON
div.p: A MESSAGE FOR THE WARRINGTON
"TERRIERS."

With that thought in their minds, they might join that night not, only in expressing admiration for the gallant lads who had gone from Warringtou to serve their country, but might also send them a message of whole- hearted and mo§t. sincere Congratulation upon the very fact that it was their priceless privi- lege to be able to strike a blow in so great a cause for England; a cause which so vitally affected the well-being of the whole of the Empire with its •four hundred millions of people; a cause of supreme moment and value to the entire civilised world. (Cheers.) When these plucky Warrington lads got into the field, they and the scores of thous- ands of others from all parts of the country who had volunteered their services to their country would, he trusted; strike a blow so powerful that it would suffice to turn the scale in the struggle which was still ahead. (Ap- plause.) There were peoples in Europe— weaker peoples than the .protagonists, in the great struggle—who at the moment were wait- ing to see what was going to be 'the tendency of that scale. When they saw what England was doing, and the still greater things that she was going to do, he hoped the effect was going to be to turn the balance, so far as those smal- ler nations ,were concerned, in favour of the (Hear, liearj If they wup :co on

div.head: WAR A SHAMEFUL CRIME.
div.p: THE WAR A SHAMEFUL CRIME.

No, it was a crime, the depths and shameful- ness of which looked blacker with every page that was revealed. It was a crime which was made blacker still by the abominable manner in which the nation responsible for it had con- ducted their military and nautical operations. (Hear, hear.) They had put themselves beyond the pale—(hear, hear)—and it was in the inter- ests of the whole civilised world that the people of this country should not only see the great undertaking in which they had embarked brought to a successful issue, but should also see to it that that Satisfactory conclusion was reached i,n the shortest possible time. (Hear, hear.) That was why he was not ashamed to say that he looked forward with eagerness to the time when certain other nationalities—for instance, some of the Balkan States— would throw their weight into the right scale and help this country and • her , Allies to bring this dread war to a triumphant con- clusion. There were people—they had all heard them—who said, "Oh, yes! but you won't be at the end of the business then !" He ventured to think differently. He was not going that night to preach what he had never yet preached in Warrington; he was not going to pretend that he was optimistic. enough to think that when that war was over they would have reached any

div.head: TOO TERRIBLE TO BE REPEATED.
div.p: TOO TERRIBLE TO BE REPEATED.

The colour problems of the world were too difficult to enable them to hope for that, but he would tell them, frankly, that he was not one of those who 'believed that it would be possible, within the confines of Europe, to ever see a repetition of what they were seeing now. The thing was too terrible. It was said that history repeated itself; but it did not always do so. The United States of America had their North and South war! They would never have another. It was such a lesson to the nation as they would never forget, and frightful as were the sacrifices and terrible the sufferings in such a war as that, there was, at least, this silver lining to the cloud: that such a war taught a nation that that kind of thing could not be repeated. Humanity did make its progress, and the Allies were going to make their progress in Europe, too, and see to it that at the end of the present war there was one motto that went round the Continent, and that motto would be "Never again!" (Applause.)

In conclusion Mr. Crosfield said that they were all looking forward to the happy day when they would be able to say that "Never again !" nnd to welcome their 'brave lads hack to old War- rington. (Cheers.).

div.head: WAR ITEMS.
div.p: WAR ITEMS.
TRADE UNIONISTS IN THE RANKS. __ . _
The actual number of members of the -Gas Workers' and General Labourers' Union who have enlisted at Warrington is 1,226, says the January Warrington "Labour Gazette."

div.head: DOUBLE TRAGEDY.
div.p: A DOUBLE TRAGEDY.
News has this week been received that Pte. Hill, of 30, Brooklands-m reet -3-frother to the young man recently killed by a circular saw— has lost his left at th.l Front.

div.head: MENTIONED IN DESPATCHES.
div.p: MENTIONED IN DESPATCHES.

div.head: ANOTHER TEACHER FOR THE WAR.
div.p: ANOTHER TEACHER FOR THE WAR.

The Education Committee has given leave of absence to Mr. Aaron Peaker, a certified assist- ant master in the Boys' Department of the Hamilton-street School, during the period of his military service, and have undertaken to make his Government pay up to an amount equal to his salary.
"JOINED UP"-IN THE ARMY OR THE NATIONAL RESERVE.

About twenty men have this week enlisted in various regimpents at the Drill Hall, also a num- ber of men are, being signed on daily for the National Reserve. Already one company of the Reserve has been formed, and a second one started.

LADY GREENALL -OFF TO THE FRONT. We learn that Lady Greenall is to leave in a week for France, where she will have charge of a refreshment buffet, to be run on Y.M.C.A. lines, at one of the big base camps. iter lady- ship will be accompanied by a staff of assist- ants, who, under her direction, - will supply "Tommy "with tea, coffee, cocoa, Oxo, Bovril, biscuits, tobacco, cigarettes and such like creature comforts.

div.head: ESPERANTISTS' MOTOR AMBULANCE.
div.p: ESPERANTISTS' MOTOR AMBULANCE.

We have been favoured with a picture post- card depicting the first field motor ambulance presented to the Belgian Red Cross Society by members of the British Esperanto Association. Towards the cost of providing this ambulance the various Esperantist organisations of the country have contributed, the Warrington Esperanto Society being among the subscribers. The Association hope to send out another am- bulance very shortly.

div.head: WOUNDED WARRIORS IN THE INFIRMARY.
div.p: WOUNDED WARRIORS IN THE INFIRMARY.
There are at present 21 wounded soldiers under treatment in the special ward at War- rington Infirmary, seven of them being Bel- gians.

On Sunday afternoon a concert was arranged for the enjoyment of the men by Mr. W. B. Randall, the well-known local organist and choirmaster, the following artistes giving their services: The Misses Tanner and C. Rigby, and Messrs. Hannan, A. Pearce and Humphries. Mr. Tanner and Master Hannan acted as accom- panists.

A second concert got up by the same gentle- man was given on Thursday evening, Mr. Ran- dall himself singing and playing the piano, and the following artistes also assisting: Madame Armstrong, Miss Delaney, and Messrs. J. H. Hannan and Pearce.
ONE OF THE "LION'S" MEN. Overstays His Leave and Is Arrested.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, William Cooke, a Naval stoker, was charged with having been an absentee from his ship, H.M.S. Lion, since February 4th. The evidence showed that when prisoner was arrested on Friday, in Warrington, he said that he was going back to his ship on the morrow, and produced a pass, the returning date on which had been altered from the 4th to the 14th.

Cooke told the Court that he had got "so attached to the little town of Warrington" that he had stayed longer than he should have done. lie was quite willing to go back. The Chief Constable said, the man was in the recent North Sea fight, when the Germans ran away as fast as they could. Ile suggested that the Bench should mark the charge-sheet "Sent back to his ship," when the matter would be struck off the records altogether and the man would not be dealt with as an absentee by the Naval Authorities. .
The Bench adopted the Chief Constable's sug- gestion.

div.head: WAR AND WAGES.
div.p: WAR AND WAGES.
Increases for L. & N.-W. Employes.
2,500 AFFECTED LOCALLY.

The managers of the L. and N.-W. Railway Company met the representatives of the National Union of Railwaymen and the Amal- gamated Society of Engineers and Firemen in London, and, after a week's deliberation, have agreed to give a war bonus of 3s. a week to their men whose rate of wages is under 305., and one of 2s. to those whose rate of wages is over 30s. This, subject to review in three months' time, will continue as long as the war lasts. It does not affect overtime pay. Naturally, a resolution of this character will greatly affect the Warrington district!. We understand it will benefit about 1,000 men in the local goods district alone, in addition to over 1,500 in the locomotive and traffic depart- ments.
This is the only occasion upon which a settle- ment of such magnitude has ever been made so amicably in any trade.

div.head: WORKERS' EDUCATIONAL ASSOCIATION LEG tURE.
div.p: WORKERS' EDUCATIONAL ASSOCIATION LEG tURE.
TROUBLE IN STORE.

The recovery from precedents created will be difficult. The employer says: "Take half- pay or leave!" The precedent of that half- pay which the worker makes during the war is going to prove an evil at the end of it. The conditions under which it was imposed are somehow forgotten. The adjustment is going to be difficult—and particularly difficult for the temporary worker. Many of the people whose places have been taken, for various reasons, by temporary workers will not come hack. Now, if their places have been so filled and you are going to sift out some here and there to become permanent workers and yet say to others: " You must go:" y0...1 are going to have a jumble straight away,

These striking words were spoken—in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening—by Mr. A. N. Shimmin (of Manchester University, the tutor of the local W.-EA. Tutorial Class), who delivered an instructive lecture upon "The War and Wages," under the auspices of the Workers' Educational -ASsocia- tion. Alderman Bennett presided over a fair attendance, which included Mr. J. A. Ransome, Mr. W. 11. Sherburn (chairman) and Mr. F. Rennie (,honorary secretary). _

The Honorary -Secretary read letters of apology for inability to attend and messages of encour- agement and good wishcs from: The Rev. W. Temple (president of thb W.E.A.), Mr. Albert Mansbridge (general secretary), the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson (president Warrington branch), Mr. M. IL Marshall (a vice-president), and Mr. J. Upson..

div.head: WARRINGTON WORKERS' FAULT.
div.p: WARRINGTON WORKERS' FAULT.

The Chairman said it was desirable that the ramifications of that association should be more generally known. The movement comprised 2,555 organisations, and had over 12,000 mem- bers in this country alone—besides huge num- bers in Australia, South Africa and New Zea- land. In its earlivr -stages the movement had met with many &acuities, but it was now soundly established, and he ventured to suggest that there was a great future before it. The subject they had met to discuss was one of enormous interest and importance and they had to look beyond the horrors and desolation of the war to the time when it would be over. If people were sensible—as he hoped they would be—they would think these problems out, be- (wise nothing could be more lamentable when peace was restored to have anything in the shape of industrial strife. .He hoped that know- ledge on these subjects would be scattered to avoid disputes. He regretted to say that the people of Warrington did not show that interest in the causes on foot for their own betterment which they might be expected to show. But never mind! "It was a long way to Tipperary," and it was a long way to the realisation of their aims. But if they studied those questions more soundly and amply, believing in the principles of co-operation rather than of competition, they would be better altogether. (Applause.)

div.head: PRESENT AND FUTURE INDUSTRY.
div.p: PRESENT AND FUTURE INDUSTRY.

The Lecturer said that the question of wages was not now what it had been at the beginning of the war. The prospect then was that trade was going to be stopped and industries dislo- cated. It was thought that the question of enlistment would seriously affect the labour market, but instead of that there was an actual shortage of labour. But our industries were now humming with a very regrettable form of activ- ity; and if, after the war was over, the people of this country could be occupied to the same degree of activity, what a splendid thing it would be! But that industrial humming would not continue, for the simple reason that in times of peace they could not get the same efforts at now productive labour that times of peace called forth. They might say it was the human desire for return. But he asked them this: Was it anything short of a disgrace for them that only a war called forth capital at the rate of ten millions a week? And all the present industrial activity was in unproductive work— khaki, munitions of war, and the like. Yet what mattered v'ras not the war, or tlie nation, or anything like that, but the standard of life of a single human being—(hear, hear)—who was the unit of everything. So far economy "was the basis of everything.

A Costly Process." Industrial readjustment was, at the best of times, a costly process. It was easy enough to walk down a hill, but it was difficult to .come up again. All the workers' wages were now being earned on non-productive work, and when the men came back from the war there would be no shortage of labour. There would be terri- fic congestion in the labour market, and by then there would also have grown up quite a new relationship between organised and unorganised labour. Organised labour was finding itself in reality little organised, for the trade union funds were already largely, used, and nothing else could replace the solid fact of a fighting fund. Organised and unorganised labour had been interchanged far more than anyone had expected. The Government had even Oproached the unions to 'relax their regulations so as to enable the shortage of labour to be made up. Then the old battle for a minimum wage would come up—but the question of the living wage was of greater importance! (Applause-) Several questions were asked by gentlemen in the audience, and to these the lecturer replied.
A vote of thanks was afterwards passed io the Lecturer and Chairman, on the motion of Mr. W. H. Sherburn, seconded by Mr. J. Jarman.

div.head: NATIONAL PROVINCIAL BANK.
div.p: NATIONAL PROVINCIAL BANK.
Lord Ineheape and Business in War
'Conditions.

Lord Inchcape, presiding at the annual meet- ing of the National Provincial Bank of England, said that when credit got the shock which it did at the outbreak of the war the position was promptly tackled by the Government and by the banks, with the result that within three months the moratorium which had been pro- claimed was brought to an end and the ordinary conditions of business were to a great extent resumed. The loans to the Stock Exchange against securities were still under what might be termed a limited moratorium and could not be called up until the conclusion of the war, but interest on these was being regularly paid, and to some extent the loans were being dis- charged. 'The position of the National Provin- cial Bank in regard to these loans was f)erfectly easy; the amount outstanding against the secu- rities which they held was very moderate, and they had no reason to anticipate that they would incur any eventual loss. Notwithstand- ing the financial troubles of the past five months the bank's net earnings amounted to .t 680,000. This would have enabled the directors to distri- bute a dividend of 18 per cent., but they had considered it prudent in the present condition of affairs to set aside ‘400,000 for the contingen- cies and to reduce the dividend for the year from 18 per cent. to 16 per cent. The bank held something like .U 4,000,000 of gilt-edged securi- ties, and though these had been valued at or under list prices there was a possibility that the provision which had been made in previous years for depreciation might have to be aug- mented. The bank's customers had increased by nearly 50 per cent. in the last ten years, and their turnover had increased in the same pro- portion. The report was unanimously adopted.'

div.head: RAILWAY CLERKS. War Changes Make a Doubtful Future. COMPETITION REDUCED; FEWER MEN.
div.p: RAILWAY CLERKS. War Changes Make a Doubtful Future. COMPETITION REDUCED; FEWER MEN.

To the Editor of "The Examiner." Sir,—As a representative of the Railway Clerks' Association, I should be obliged if you would kindly grant me §pace in which to appeal to all railway clerical workers who are unorgan- ised.

The war brought about a change in the con- trol of the railway industry, and in consequence the future position of railway clerical workers is exceedingly doubtful. When we now men- tion amalgamation or nationalisation we cannot be accused, as in the past, of "dreaming of pos- sibilities," for it is generally agreed that it is unlikely that the old state of affairs will be re- established, even if the Government should re- linquish its control of the railways. Many railway clerical workers whose work was only necessary because there was competi- tion between the railway companies have already been , seriously disturbed. The staff of the Railway Clearing House is now less by one- third than it was last July. Railway agencies have been closed. Canvassers have been called in, and many of them are doing work which is lower in grade than that which they did before the war. Most canvassers have had their ex- penses stopped, and some townsmen have had their expenses reduced, if not stopped entirely. All over the country clerks are having to cover without assistance the work of men who have enlisted, and overtime (often unpaid) and speeding-up are prevalent. The places of some of the men with the colours are being filled with girls, whose rates of pay are much lower than those of the absentees. All this'simply shows what could be done, and done in a greater de- gree, in the event of complete amalgamation or nationalisation of our railways, and it would seem that clerks in' head and district offices, in audit and rates offices, and others whose work is more or less dependent upon .the separate and competitive management of our railways, are in a very precarious position.

Vie- Uncertainty of our future makes it im- perative that all unorganised workers should de- liberately and dispassionately ask themselves whether their objections to the Railway Clerks' Association are legitimate and well grounded. We have frequently met opposition which could not stand before any real thinking. Might I suggest a popsible comparison to any objectors? When the National Telephone Company was taken over by the State, did the employes re- ceive the treatment they expected? Were they • satisfied with the altered conditions? The answer in each case is indisputably in the nega- tive. But the telephone eniployes were unor- ganised, and in this respect railway clerical workers compare much more favourably. Already the general secretary of the Railway Clerks' Association has discussed our future with Government officials, and the present posi- tion of all railway clerical workers is better to- day than it would have been had there been no such association. Years ago our association se- cured from a Departmental Committee which inquired into railway amalgamations and work- ing agreements a number of important recom- mendations, but these must be backed by a bigger membership if they are to be of the greatest possible value.

Everything possible has been done by the Railway Clerks' Association, and will be done, to safeguard the interests of all clerks, includ- ing those with the colours, but it will at least be conceded that if our organisation contained more units it would be stronger and more effective, and every man who enrolled would know that he had shouldered his sharp of the burden. We who are members feel that, to put it bluntly, we are each carrying on our back two passive objectors, who, of course, share in the conces- sions which our Association secures, and because these objectors hinder our progress, and, in- deed, are a danger, we are anxious to have them side by side with us in the ranks of our Associa- tion, which is the only safeguard of railway clerical workers.

Warrington District Annual Meeting.

The annual meeting of Warrington District No. 4 Independent Order of Rechabites was held in the Independent Methodist Schoolroom, Pemberton, Wigan, last Saturday. Bro. J. R. Barker, D.C.R., was supported by the District Officers and 28 tent representatives, and Sisters Ratcliffe, Simcock, Taylor and Ashurst, repre- senting the female tents. A vote of condolence was passed, on the motion of Bro. E. Walkden, to be sent to the family of the late Bro. W. Baxendaje, adult district guardian, treasurer for the Juvenile District funds, and tent secretary for the "Hope of Brynn " Tent for over 25 years. The D.S. presented the report of the execu- tive. The district has 29 branches, with a mem- bership: Voluntary section, 1,755, a gain of 25 on the. year; State section, 1,797 men and 840 women.
The district funds at the year end were: Sick .24,032 Gs. 9d., -funeral .0,854 18s. 5d., juvenile funeral .2500, special til4 25., management .L 23 us. 10d., "total funds .28,424 19s. 2d.

div.head: JUVENILE TENTS.
div.p: JUVENILE TENTS.

Bro. Peter Howard, D.S.J.T., presented his report on the work successfully carried out in the juvenile tents. A good year has been re- corded and valuable instruction has been given to the children. Large increases of members have been made in several tents. The most successful is that of " Sunbeam " Tent. The membership of the Juvenile district is 1,662, a gain of 59, after transferring 70 mem- bers to the adult tent.

OFFICERS. a The election of officers resulted Bro. J. Gaskell, D.C.R.; Bro. B. T. Parkes, D.D.R.; Bro. P. Howard, Levite; Bro. R. Pasquill, guardian; Bro. J. R. Barker, D.P.C.R.; Bro. T. Winstaniey, D.S.; Bro. J. Hill, A.S.; Bro. S. Fernley, D. State Secretary; Bro. T. Massey, D.T.; auditors, Bros. T. Arrowsmith and J. Gee; trustees, Bros. Jas. Shaw, E. Walkden, and W. Wright. Conference representatives at Bradford next August: Bros. J. Gaskell, P. Howard and S. Fernley.

div.head: " SUNBEAM " TENT.
div.p: " SUNBEAM " TENT.

The members of this Juvenile Tent, having been successful during the past year in gain- ing the largest increased membership of any Rechabite Tent in the district, were provided with an excellent tea in the Thewlis-street Schoolroom on Thursday evening. Over 100 sat down to tea, which had been prepared by Mes- dames Barrett, Lowe, Werrall and Gleave. After tea an entertainment was held, presided over by Bro. A. Tilling, the fiudienee being augmented by a good number of adults'. Songs were rendered bj• Miss Eva Tanner (Temperance Queen), and Miss O. Dale; two choruset.by a number of the juveniles; a humorous recitation by Miss L. Rigby; and a dialogue entitled "Founding a Colony" by a number of boys. Mr. T. Tanner acted as accompanist. During the evening Bro. Briscoe, District Superintendent of Juvenile Tents, presented the " Gavil and Block'" won by the "Sunbeala" Tent for the largest percentage of increased membership, Bro. Albert Lowe, the Tent Super- intendent, receiving the articles on behalf of the, tent. The Retiring District Superintend- ent, Bro. P. Howard, presented the Challenge Shield, also won by the tent for the greatest aggregate increased membership, the Shield being received by Bro. W. Worrall, Tent Secre- tary. About 30 prizes (books, badges and brooches) were distributed to various members for regular attendance at the meetings, and three special prizes were given by Bro. T. Massey (District Secretary) for introducing new members. A framed Legion of Honour was handed to one of the juveniles (Frank Edwards) for having secured the largest number of entrants.
The proceedings throughout were exceedingly interesting and enjoyable.
Last Week Colder Still.

The week ended February 13th was the coldest this year, the mean temperature recorded being 37 degrees, or five degrees lower than in the preceding seven days. The highest and lowest temperatures recorded during the period under review occurred on the same day—the 11th inst. —when the glass, after having touched 47 de- grees. dropped to 27. The rainfall was very slight for the time of the year, only 27in. being recorded'.

• Pending County Court At.lion. in the matter of Messrs. S. and P. Acton, painters and decorators, v. the Warrington Cnion, Mr. Knowles, solicitor for the plaintiffs, made application to his Honour Judge Gilmer, .at the Warrington County Court on Thursday, to have the hearing adjourned until the next Court on March 18th.—Mr. Knowles explained that the reason why he desired the adjournment was that a material and necessary witness, one Arthur Jerams, was at present lying in the Infirmary suffering from a compound fracture of the thigh, and was, of course, quite unable .to attend the Court. He had, in fact, been lying there ever since the day of the accident, Which gave rise to the case, and it was pro- bable that before very long he would have to go under a very serious operation,. viz. the ampu- tation of one of his legs. Of course, there was risk that if that operation was performed it might prove fatal, and, 'in any case, it was not likely that the man would be in a tit state to be •discharged from the Infirmary for quite another Nix months. He (Mr. Knowles) therefore asked for a month's adjournment, and for permission to take the man's evidence on eomm:ssion in the, meantime.—His Honour granted the ad- journment, and said that the Itegistrar (Mr. :Ridgway) would take the man's evidence. He also ordered that the costs of that application and of. the taking of the evidence shall follow the event.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A.

The address at Sunday's -Pleasant Afternoon At Wycliffe was given by the President (the :Rev. T. T. James), who began by thanking the Members of the P.S.A. Brotherhood for the. 'many kind things which had been said by them .toncerning The two years' service lie had been .onabled to render the Church. Be was glad to feel that his *ork had won the ap;,roval of the P.S.A. members, and, also, glad to note the happy feeling which pervaded all their gather- Ings. Mr. James went on to refer to the fact 'that they would soon be celebrating their 22nd Anniversary/ a fact which would recall happy Memories to the minds of • many. At such a 'stage in their existence the question naturally 'occurred to them: "What can we chi to further interest in our work?" A few answers to the question readily flashed across the mind. For The thing they had to bear up under the great difficulties of the present troublous times; for Another, they must see to it that their present turge numbers were made even more. The larger the number the more encouragement and help would they get from the Brotherhood, and by pressing on with the work of the organisa- tion they would be doing much more good than, Perhaps, they would ever know. Down at the root of their faith as Christians should be the desire for personal service, and that desire could find expression in work such as that suggested .by the Brotherhood movement. Let them con- secrate their lives by doing all in their power to help others to improve, in the highest sense of the word, their conditions in life.--The Bible lesion was given by Mr. Payton, who also 'played an organ solo. A vote of sympathy was accorded to Councillor Miller, of Widnes, whose wife passed away recently.---The 22nd anniver- -sail' gathering is fixed for March 7th.

div.p: New Ambulance Class.

Wheat Prices "Slightly Easier." Wheat sold a little• easier in Warrington Market on •Wednesday, the price running be- tween Bs. 2d. and Bs. 3d. per 701 b. The easement was no doubt ,due to the prospect of .foreign supplies coming in at no distant date. Oats sold firmly at 4s. 6d. to 4s. 71d. per 45113., and there was a better sale for wheat and oat Straw at prices ranging from 325. 6d. to 345. per ton. Clover hay fetched £4 to. £4 10s. per ton, and meadow hay found ready buyers at £.3 15s. to .1:4 Flour prices remained firm, XX varieties selling at 475. 6d. per 2801 b. Best bran sold at is. 6d. per 201 b.

div.head: Railway Staff at Whist
div.p: Railway Staff at Whist

At the offices of the London and North-Wes- tern Railway DiStrict Goods Manager, Arpley, on Monday evening, ninety members and friends of the staff held a pleasant whist drive—the proceeds being devoted to the Raiilway Temper- ance Union. This happy function had been sug- gested by Messrs. C. Eccles and A. W. Allman. The M.C.'s were Messrs. A. W. Allman, F. Atkinson, G. Holland, W. G. Limb and A. B. Starkey. Refreshments were served during the evening. Handsome prizes for whist were car- ried off by Miss Sally Eccles and Mrs. Sutton, Messrs. Fred Holland and A. J. Greenhalgh ; whilst the competition prizes were won by Miss Amy Hall and Mr. Fred Gibson.

div.head: "The Examiner 4' Has A Chance With
div.p: "The Examiner 4' Has A Chance With
Them All.
Lance-Corporal W. Crawford, 6th Battalion Border Regiment, stationed in East Anglia, writes :

'lt is with pleasure I see the old paper keep- ing up its reputation. It is really fine to get to know how things are going on in the old town of Warrington and how the boys are going on at the Front. When the roll is called I know the good old town will be well repre- sented. Good luck to all the boys who have had the pluck to see to its reputation. I receive 'The Examiner' every Sunday morning and all the boys in my hut are eager to have a look at it. We get all sorts Of papers here from all over England, but the old ' Examiner ' has a chance with them all."

div.head: Shprthand Writers.
div.p: Shprthand Writers.

A whist drive and dance in connection with the Warrington Shorthand Writers' Association was held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Monday evening. There was a large gathering, some 80 membeA and friends being present. Shortly before the distribution of the whist prizes the Secretary (Mr. T. Lowe) said he hoped that the outcome of this social evening would be a rally of the shorthand writers of the district to help to further the work of the association. Follow; ing the whist drive a long programme of dances was gone through, the music being played by Mr. J. Fairclough. Songs were rendered by Miss L. Fleming, Miss Kershaw, and Mr. H. Nurse. The M.C.'s for the evening were the Secretary, Mr. W. Durant, and Mr. H. B. Bell. Credit is due to the Secretary and his committee for the great success of the evening. Lent at the Parish Church.

The annual series of special Lenten services at the Parish Church commenced on Wednes- day, when the scholars of the Fairfield, Paro- chial and Smith-street Schools attended early morning service and were addressed by the Rev. W. H. Hendy-Cock (vice-principal of the Train- ing College). At a special service in the evening the Rector (the Rev. Canon addressed a large congregation, and on Friday afternoon the Rey. Canon Morley Stevenson (principal of the Training College) preached at a largely attended service for women only, remarking that since the outbreak of war many people had learned to pray as they had never prayed before, to give more 'generously, and to practice more self- denial. When the time of peace came it might be that the country would be found to have learned precious lessons through the horrors of war—that her people would have Warned to be more earnest in prayer, more generous in social service, and more temperate and self-controlled in their lives. The Canon preached again in the evening. Next Friday's sermons will he preached by the Rev. F. Lindon Varkyn, vicar of Holy Trinity; Southport, at 3 and 8.

Looking Ahead! The School Management Sub-committee re- ported to the Education Committee on Monday that they had met the Chairman of the Street Improvement Committee (Alderman Bennett), the Mayor, Councillor Pemberton and the Town Clerk with reference to certain land in Museum- street, and resolved that the Sites and Buildings Committee be recommended to, accept the transfer of the, piece of land on the south side of Museum-street, containing 2,428 square yards, purchased by the Corporation, subject to the Board of Education's approval of the site for the purpose of the future development of the Secondary School and Technical Institute.—The Sites and Buildings Sub-committee, in turn, reported having considered the foregoing reso- lution, and they recommended that the recom- mendation of the School Management Sub-com- mittee be approved, and that the necessary plan of the site referred to be prepared and for-warded to the Board of Education for their approval. —The minutes were approved. •

div.head: Death of Mr. Edward Howard.
div.p: Death of Mr. Edward Howard.

The death occurred, at his residence, Thorn- yule, Knutsford-road, Latchford ,Without, on Thursday morning, of Mr. Edward Howard, who was well known and respected throughout the village, as well as in business circle's in War- rington. He was 43 years of age, and during the whole of his business life he was employed by Messrs. R. A. Naylor, holding an important post on that firm's office staff at the time of his death. He was prominently connected with the, Grappenhall Independent Methodist Church, and, as secretary of theChurchl Trustees, worked strenuously. .for the erection of the new church. Before removing to • Latchford Without, Mr. ! Howard was the secretary and superintendent of the Brick-street Independent Methodist Sunday School, Warrington. He leaves a widow (sister, to Councillor Robert Henshall's ' wife) and wie son to mourn their loss. The interment takes Place this afternoon at 'Warrington Cemetery,: at 3.15, following a memorial service Which will be conduced in the Independent Methodist ! Chapel, Grappenhall, at 1.30 by Alderman Jas. ! Evans (of Warrington) and Mr. Worthington (of ' Wigan).

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 20, 1915.
WAR STORIES.
"BILL'S" BIIMIDAY. Big Guns Shower " Presents " On The Kaiser.

In a letter to his brother—Mr. J. Wright, of 93, Cartwright-street, Warrington—Driver Stan- ley Wright, of the Army Service Corps, who is serving with the Expeditionary Force, writes expressing deep thanks for the ...too of "The Examiner" which is posted to him each week, and remarks: "You cannot think what a wel- 'come thing the paper is and how much I like to read the news of the old town."

"I am still hard at it," he adds, " going -op to the trenches with my ambulance wagon and horses and bringing back the sick and wounded. I am glad to tell you that just lately the wounded have not been so numerous and that most of the chaps. I have had to drive 1-ack have been only sick. From this you will gather that things are a bit quieter just now. On the Kaiser's birthday our big guns were busy all day sending him birthday souveniis. We did give him 'em hot and strong, I can tell ypu!"

div.head: nEcßurs CALL FOR RECRUITS.
div.p: nEcßurs CALL FOR RECRUITS.
Letter From A %%Tarringlonian Who "Joined Up."

Bombardier P. Broadhurst, "A" Battery, R.F.A. (69th Brigade), wiites us—from the place in the South where he has .been undergoing training—what he describes as "a .few lines to the boys of Warrington who have not yet ans- wered their country's call," hoping that mcs're of them will come and join in with the "men here, who are going through strenuous work day after day in preparation for the fight for liberty and a just cause." He adds that he und his comrades are having plenty of work, and, to his delight, every man is doing his best to bring himself up to the level of a fully-trained soldier.

" Now's your time, young men of Warring- ton 1" he concludes. " Rally round and show that you want to do something for your counay, and do not say Oh, there will be plenty of time to-morrow!' for every minute is precious in this strenuous struo-gle. . . . . Wake up, men of Warrington! 'Don't be afraid. Come boldly forward to help in the fight for Liberty and Right!"

div.head: " SIIOPPING " UNDER DIFFICULTIES
div.p: " SIIOPPING " UNDER DIFFICULTIES
" Tommies "_Shelled As They Go To
Draw Ration.

Mr. H. Boyle, of the Dancing Academy, Legh- street, has just received a letter from his son, Lance-Corporal Fred poyle, who is serVing at the Front with the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Welsh Fusiliers. In his letter the gallant Lance-Corporal says : " The ground here is very sloppy, and we are up to the knees in mud. Although it is cool during the day; it often freezes keenly at night. We experience many exciting adventures. On Sunday we were 'drawing rations,' when the iiermans, by the aid of their search-light, spotted us. They kept the light upon us for about five minutes, and all at once fired a Trench Mortar at us. The missile fell about 150 yards from us; and we were covered with mud. We are billeted in a small farmhouse when off duty, from which place I am just re- turning to take another turn in the trenches." The writer conclude with a playful allusion to his father's profession :—" There is no chance of a dance here," he writes, "unless a shrapnel bursts near at hand, and then you dance, I can tell you!" As a boy, the Lance-Corporal attended the Hamilton-street School, and up to the time he enlisted le was in the employ of Messrs. Flet- cher, Russell and Co. He has now been in the Army about ten Months.

div.head: SAVED. BY 1111511 RANGERS.
div.p: SAVED. BY 1111511 RANGERS.
Gay Gordon's Tribute To Their Reck- less Valour In Night Attack.

Writing to his father at 541, Great Eastern- road, Parkhead, Glasgow, Private Robert McGregor, of the Gordon Highlanders, gives the following thrilling account of a night en- gagement with the Germans : "I am leaving the trenches, where we have been for about ten days, and we are now enjoy- ing a well-earned rest at . You may have heard of tie severe fighting by this time. It was awful, and I am sorry to say many of our poor fellows will never come home again.

div.head: Searchlights From The Sky.
div.p: Searchlights From The Sky.

"On the night Of 26th December we were in- formed that the Germans would make an attack on our trenches, so not an eye was closed that night. About four o'clock we thought it was a false alarm, and we settled to enjoy forty winks, when their artillery opened fire on us. Our trenches for two miles were of a V-shape, and the ' Huns ' seemed to direct all their guns on this part, but, thanks to their marksman- ship, our immediate neighbourhood didn't get much attention at first. We were near what I think you ,call the apex of the V. and the howling- and screaming shells passed well over us, until we heard the throbbing of an aero- plane. Then a searchlight played on us, fol- lowed by the dropping of bright balls, which brilliantly lit up the whole place, and in a few minutes the shell got us. and were coming plump into us. One shell came right into our position and knocked over twelve of our fel- lows. They were practically torn asunder, and the whole side of the trench was torn up. "Our guns. were blazing away, and, I think, found the fellows who were annoying us, as their fire got slacker, and finally ceased. This sort of thing was kept up till day dawned, and we lost (remainder of this sentence censored). Then we saw the Huns advancing as uncon- cerned as if on parade. On they came in close formation, and there must have been ten to one against us. We fired as hard as we could, but they seemed to come out of nowhere, and never halted. When they were getting too close we charged. It was our only chance. When they saw us leave the trenches they halted for a moment, but afterwards came on to meet us. I don't remember much of what took place then. It was stab and hack, hack and stab. You could hear the smash of gun against gun— the thud, thud.

div.head: "An Uncanny Silence."
div.p: "An Uncanny Silence."

"But beyond this there was an uncanny silence, broken sometimes by an oath and a groan. How long this went on I hardly know (but it seemed years to me). We drove them back about a hundred yards. Our officers saw the Germans reinforced, and sounded the re- treat, but owing to a few machine guns we ccr-ildn't get back to our trenches. The Ger- mans, now greatly increased, came on again, and our fellows, only about 170 left, got ready to meet what seemed certain death.

div.head: "God Save Ireland!"
div.p: "God Save Ireland!"

"But just at that moment we heard the sound of singing, and the song was God Save Ire- land.' It was the Connaught Rangers coming to our relief. I have seen some reckless Irish- men in my time, but nothing to match the recklessness and daring of those gallant Irish- men. They took the Germans on the left flank.

"The Germans now would probably number about 2,000 against about 500 Connaughts and 170 of us; but had there been 50,000 Germans I don't believe in my soul they could have stood before the Irish. They simply were irresistible; and all the time kept singing 'God Save Ire- land.'

"One huge red-haired son of Erin having broken his rifle got possession of a German offi- cer's sword, and everything that came in the way •of this giant went down. I thought of Wallace. Four hundred and seventy huns were killed and woundO, and we took 70 prisoners. Had it not been for the Irish. I wouldn't be writing this, and when it comes to a hand-to- hand job there is nothing in the whole British Army to approach them. God save Ireland and Irishmen!"
Bishop Vaughan at Emmanuel Church.

To-morrow the Right Rev. Frank Vaughan. assistant Bishop in the Reformed Episcopal Church will preach morning and evening at the Emmanuel Church, Bold-street, whilst in the afternoon he will address the Incumbent's Bible Class in the Knutsford-road Institute.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM LONG.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. WILLIAM LONG.
Worthy Citizen Passes Away Full of Years

div.head: and Honour.
div.p: and Honour.
AN ACTIVE AND USEFUL LIFE.

Mr. William Long, who for a period, covering more than one generation of Warringtonians had played a leading part in the political., social, educational, insiustrial ant religious- affairs of the town, passed away early on Saturday morn- ing at the ripe age of eighty, leaving a memory as full of honour as his life had been of years. A successful man of business, Mr. Long's ample means had allowed him to set np a second- home in the unrivalled English Lake District,, but it was fitting that the end should come at Mel- wall Heys, Grappenhall, near the scenes, by which he had been surrounded during the strenuous days of his active career. Up. to quite recently Mr. Long had been in the best of. health, and he continued to-take a keen interest in all local doings, though he could not tale the part in them be would have liked; but eighteen: months ago he began perceptibly to. decline. Three weeks ago his condition became critical.," and. two hours before sunrise on Saturday he passed peacefully away.

' general and Cairo-street Unitarian. Church in particular, will suffer a grievous loos. He was the last of three outstanding benefactors, of Cairo-street, the other two being the late Mr. W. D. Houghton and the late Mr. F. Monks. , Each gave to the funds libeially, an& all will , be much missed,. though we are glad to know that this famous place of worship; which stands for a definite cause, and has continuous his- tory for 260 years—the Rev. Robert Yates, the minister ejected from the Parish Church in 1662, being the first on its list of pastors—is in a very good financial position. Mr. Long was the old- est member of the congregation, for although his. membership of the chapel committee had ceased; his connection with the place was unbroken, and he was a subscriber to the end. He had. been, in conjunMion with the gentlemen we have named and others, a generous giver to thel funds for the building of the schools and other work, and largely contributed to placing the church in the satisfactory position in which it now is.
There will be a memorial service in the chapel on Sunday conducted by die Rev. W. H. Drum- niond (London), a former minister at Cairo- street.

He took an active part in Unitarian affairs. Among other offices he held were those of presi- dent of the British and Foreign Unitarian Association (1894), and of the Suste4tation Fund. He was one of the managers or trustees of the Sustentation Fund almost from its start. For a great number of years lie was on the Committee of Management of the Manchester College, Oxford, which was an outgrowth of the old 'Warrington Academy.

div.head: TYPICAL GENTLEMAN.
div.p: A TYPICAL GENTLEMAN.

The story of the late Mr. Long's life is the story of a career of a typical English gentleman and,a successful man of business. A kindly for, tune favourM him at birth. Not only were his parents in a position to give him a g3od start in the race he was to run, but he was endowed" with, all those elements of character that go ta the making df a kindly; generous, self-reliant, yet conscientious man—the kind of man that retains the confidence and the regard' of the world in face of that success w:lich sometimes brings about other 'results. A.s he was favoured at the beginning, so he was in marked measure fortunate to the end, for lie had the somewhat rare experience of celebrating his golden wed- ding nearly two years ago. Those intervening fifty 'years were crowded with many happenings, domestic and public, and Mrs. Long had con- tributed her full wifely share. towards the building up of the all-round reputation her hus- band achieved.
Mr. Long was born in Manchester, November sth, 1834, the son of Mr. William Long, who was the founder of the firm of tanners, Nressrs. W.

Long and Son, Grappeuhall. He began his school days at Knutsford, and subsequently con- tinued his studies at Boroughbridge, Yorkshire. His father evidently believed in the theory which has many practical advocates now, that the beginning of a business training, given a good foundation, should not be unduly deferred, and Master Long was set to face the realities of the tan yard at fifteen years of age. Later he or.c:.pied the position his father had occupied before him at the head of the firm. Finally-- about eight years ago—the tannery at Thelwall and that at Grappenhall were passed over o Mr. Long's nephews, Messrs. James and Charles H. Tinsley, the present proprietors. _ - _

It was On the 28th July, 1863, that Mr. Long warried Miss Emily Jane Milner, second daugh- ttr of the late Mr. W. E. Milner, Springfield, Warrington, and sister of Mr. Walter Milner, secretary of the Whitecross Company, Ltd. The happy couple \ lived in the village and some time after the marriage removed to Thelwall Heys, which was built for them and remained their home to the last. They had one son and one daughter. The death in early life of the former was a keen and lasting sorrow; the daughter became the wife of a well-known Manchester solicitor, Mr. Walter M. Shipman, and resides at Altrincham. DEVOTION TO THE PUBLIC WEAL.

Mr. Long was not, in one sense, a public man, though he devoted much of his ability and re- sources to the public weal. He did not aspire to serve on such bodies as the Town Council, although he was, for a period, a Parish Coun- cillor for Grappenhall. He. had, however, other ways of working for the general good. There is no better method of serving this end than by promoting the education of the people and encouraging thrift among them. Mr. Long's period of full usefulness educationally lay in the days that preceded the latest Education Act, but the passing of the greater Act of 1870 pro- vided him with opportunities at the entrance to the most active portion of his career. • He was prominently and officially connected pith People's College, which has held such an hon- ourable place among the elementary schools of the town under a succession of headmasters; and with the Boteler Grammar School, of whioh he was a Governor. He was also on the, manage- ment of the Grappenhall School. His concern for thrift found suitable expres- sion during a long and successful connection with the Warrington Savings Bank, at which institution he was successively trustee (1879), vice-chairman (1880), and chairman (1896). Dir.- ing this chairmanship, which was only ended by death, the bank grew in usefulness, extended its branches, and increased its members in un- precedented fashion, the yearly transactions in- creasing in the eighteen years from 19,716 to 38,747, or, roughly speaking, by 100 per cent. As a magistrate for the county of Chester he was a regular attendant on the Bench at the Paresbury Petty Sessions.

div.head: GENEROUS AND DISCRIMINATING.
div.p: GENEROUS AND DISCRIMINATING.

The Infirmary, of which he was a vice- president, found in Mr. Long a true friend. So early as 1894 we find him supple- menting gifts, which had already made him a life Governor, by giving to a building fund that was then opened £llO 10s.; and in 1906, when the larger extension was undertaken, he gave as large a donation as anyone else, viz., £l,OOO. Gentlemen who knew him intimately and were acquainted with his methods, say that he was a generous giver, but that he gave with discrimination. He had to be satisfied that the cause was a good one, and he liked to know that others were doing their duty. Given tbesa conditions, his kindness was unbounded. Quite naturally, Mr. Long ranged himself on the side of those who refuse to allow industrial- ism unchallenged to sweep away old landmarks or to encourage apathy on the subject of main- taining the libks between the present and the hitoric past. He was the president of the Warrington Society, whose chief object it is to see that posterity does not suffer in this respect by default of the present generation. Mr. Long was thoroughly convinced of the usefulness of the Guild of Help, and supported it most generously. On more than one occasion he gave ,large donations to the administrative funds in order to maintain it on a satisfactbry footing, and one of the last things he did before his death was to send a cheque to the treasurer when he found that the Guild's financial year had ended with a deficit. He was ready at all times to act as a stand-by for individual cases of distress recommended for assistance by the Guild.
A PROMINENT UNITARIAN. By the cicat-L of Mr. Jong, TJnitarianisin in

div.head: AS POLITICIAN.
div.p: AS POLITICIAN.

Mr. Long was an ardent politician, and he in- tended his only son, who unfortunately died at the age of twelve or thirteen, for a political career. He was a strong Liberal, and we be- lieve that when Mr. Joseph Chamberlain in the height of his Radical days visited Warrington, prior to the 1885 election, the great man from the Midlands stayed with Mr. Long, the two being old friends. Mr. Long is reported to have prophesied at the end of the meeting, in the presence of Mr. F. Monks and lir. that Mr. Chamberlain had lost them the elec- tion. He had been asked not to speak on education, a question, which at that time, was a very delicate one. He persisted in doing so, estranged the Catholic vote, and, as Mr. Long foretold, lost the election for the Liberal party. When Mr. Chamberlain turned Unionist, Mr. Long followed him, but he returned to his old faith when Mr. Chamberlain deserted Free Trade; and Mr. A. J. King, who won the Knuts- ford Division for Liberalism in the great anti- Protection revolt of 1906, recalled the fact dur- ing the funeral on Tuesday, that "Wm. Long took the chair at my first meeting in the Knuts- ford Division, ten years ago, on his 70th birth- day."

div.head: HIS WINDERMERE RESIDENCE.
div.p: HIS WINDERMERE RESIDENCE.

Mr. Long had had a house at Windermere for thirty .years. In the first instance he rented a house, and about twenty years ago* he built Cleabarrow, which was surrounded by an estate, of at least 2,000 acres of fells and agri- cultural land in the valleys. He took the interes. t of a country gentleman and endeared himself to the people among whom he moved. He was a director of the Windermere and Dis- trict Electricity Supply Company, Ltd.

div.head: GOLDEN WEDDING.
div.p: GOLDEN WEDDING.

The fiftieth anniversary of the marriage of Mr. and Mrs. Long was celebrated quietly at Thelwall Heys on July 28th, 1913, the wedding having taken place at St. Oswald's Church, Grasmere, where Wordsworth and his wife are buried, on July the - 28th, 1863. The clergyman, ,the Rev. E. Jeffreys, • had passed away.- but Mrs. Thornely (Mr. Long'S sister) and Miss Milner (Mrs. Long's sister), bridesmaids, were at the happy gathering of relatives and friends, and were able to give and receive congratulations upon that unique occasion. Fifty-three past and present servants gave a carriage clock and combined in congra- tulations and wishes for a long continuance of health and happiness. Mr. Joseph Chamber- lain (who died just a year later) sent a telegram of congratulation, and Miss Chamberlain sent a gold cup.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral took place at Grappenhall Church on Tuesday, in the presence of a large number of representative men and women, workpeople and villagers. There was no ostentatious show, but there was every indication of the high esteem in which the deceased had been held by every section of the community. The .coffin was borne to the church on one of the waggonettes belonging to Thelwall Heys and was covered with the wreaths sent by members of the family and consisting of chaste and beautiful flowers, among which the early spring varieties, snow- drops, narcissi and lilies of the valley appearea with tulips and small red roses. The body was carried into the church by eight of the deceased gentleman's employes at Cliffe-lane .Tannery, Grappenhall, and Windermere. Other employes attended and lined the sides of the approach to the church gates for the chief mourners to pass between. They were met at the church gates by the Rev. H. V. Pigot (rector) and the Rev. E. H. Cock (Windermere), who officiated. As the large congregation filled up the commodious country church, Mr. W. Asquith Wood, who was at the organ, played "0 rest in the Lord." The 90th Psalm and "Now. the labourer's task is o'er" were sung, and as the party were leaving the church for the graveside, preceded by the choir (who chanted the responses), the Dead March in " Saul " was effectively and sympathetically rendered by Mr. Wood. The grave was lined with purple cloth and ever- greens, mixed with flowers similar to those that had been placed upon the coffin.

div.head: WREATHS.
