div.head: PUBLIC REFERENCES..
div.p: PUBLIC REFERENCES..

At the Lymm Petty Sessions on Wednesday morning, the Chairman (Mr. W. PeteritYlands) said that before the Court sat he thought it was the duty of the Bench to refer ta the sad loss it had sustained in the death of: their old friend, Mr. William Long. He believed Mr. Long was practically the senior magistrate in the division, having served not far short of fifty years. Although in later years his failing health had prevented him from attending so regularly as previously, the county owed him much for the services he had rendered during a very busy life, and his loss would be deeply felt. At a meeting held—in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Tuesday evening—under the auspices of the Warrington Branch of the Workers' Educational Association, Alderman Bennett (who occupied the chair) said lie felt that he ought .to say a word at that meeting with reference to the great loss Warrington had sustained by the death of their old friend, Mr. William Long, at the ripe old age of 80. His life had been a long and honourable one, devoted to the furtherance of all good causes—particu- larly to the cause of education, in earlier years; he was one of the principal supporters of the Manchester College, Oxford. Although in re- cent years he had not been able to take his former active part in the public affairs of War- rington and the neighbourhood, he manifested considerable interest in them almost up to the last. He (the speaker) was sure that all the members of the meeting would join with him in that expression of great regret.

div.head: WARRINGTON ARTILLERY UNIT? Town's Chance to Remove "A Very Serious Blot."
div.p: A WARRINGTON ARTILLERY UNIT? Town's Chance to Remove "A Very Serious Blot."

Lord Derby is raising a Royal Field Artillery Brigade in Lancashire, and Lieut.-Colonel C. Lyon, of Appleton, is to command one of the four batteries—a howitzer battery. This week those responsible have started to recruit for it, and in three weeks' time it is hoped to have horses and everything else complete in a useful army section. The men now joining go into billets at Lytham for preliminary training, and it is hoped that as many Warrinaton men as possible will join—in fact, Lieut.-Colonel Lyon told the members of the Appleton Rifle Club at their annual general meeting on Monday night that he would like a whole Warrington battery! lie would, he promised, see that the local men were kept together. Warrington was very closely connected with the South Lancashire Regiment, but it had no artillery unit—and, in his opinion, it was a very serious blot on their Territorials.

div.head: LORD DERBY TO ADDRESS A RECRUITING
div.p: LORD DERBY TO ADDRESS A RECRUITING
MEETING.

With the object of stimulating recruiting for this new section of the Army, Lord Derby will address a public meeting in the Parr Hall at eight o'clock on Wednesday evening next, when the Mayor (Alderman Peter Peacock) will pre- side, and Crosfield's Band will play a number of selections.

The Mayor desires, through our columns, to appeal to the men of Warrington to do their utmost to help him to assist Lord Derby in the raising of a Ararrington unit in the new bri- gade, "so that the name of Warrington may be permanently associated with the great work England has now in hand." Lieutenant-Colonel Mocatta will be glad to re- cruit applicants at his office in the Police Sta- tion. Upon enlistment men will be drafted to Lytham and St. Anne's for training.

div.head: RELEASED PRISONER-OF-WAR.
div.p: A RELEASED PRISONER-OF-WAR.
Warringtonlan Amongst the Batch of
Disabled "Exchanges."

Among the disabled soldiers who have been for some months prisoners of war in the hands of the Germans, and who have now been ex- changed for an equal number of their own men in a like pass, is Bombardier George. Brough, of the Royal Field Artillery, whose mother resides in Wakefield-street, Warrington. On Wednesday his mother was surprised and delighted to receive from him a telegram, stat- ing that he was sailing for England, and that he hopea to be home shortly, the wire being followed by another message, which set forth that when he does return it will be minus a leg. He had already?' written—whilst a prisoner —that he had been wounded in the knee during the fierce fighting at Mons, in the early part of the war, and it was during the retirement from that place that he fell into the hands of the enemy.

His- return so soon had not been expected, for only a few days earlier his mother had received a letter from Mme. de Parvilley, an ambulan- tiere, attached to the Red Cross, in which that lady said: "When I left the military hospital at Mons on the last Tuesday your nice boy, George, was in the best of healths (sic). He sends you his best love I am very fond of George; he is, indeed, a general fav- ourite."

Bombardier Brough is quite a young man; indeed, he is little more than a youth, and the fact that he had been raised to non-commis- sioned rank at so early an age gave promise of a successful career in the Army, had it not, unfortunately, been cut short. We learn that the firm with whom he was employed prior to enlisting have generously come fotward with an offer to give him his old job back.

div.head: Teachers At The Parish Church.
div.p: Teachers At The Parish Church.

On Saturday afternoon a party of members of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association and friends paid a visit of inspec- tion to the Parish Church. They were received by the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), who gave a very interesting and lucid account of the historical associations of the church. The Rector's explanatory remarks covered the period extending from St. Elphin to the present day. The chapels were objects of great attention to the visitors, but the chancel, the oldst portion of the church, with its crypt vestry, which VHS visited, were decidedly interesting from an his- torical point of view. The registers were open for inspection, and the valuable plate Was also shown and examined. The more energetic mem- bers, who came within the necessary measure- ments, climbed the winding staircase up the tower to above the bells, from where a splendid view of the surrounding country was obtained. On behalf of the association, the Secretary (Mr. George Newborn) has forwarded a letter to the Rectorl thankhig kini tor bin kindness.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
HILARIOUS FRENCH FARCE AT THE ROYAL COURT.

Those who advocate laughter on B,CCOlat of its hygienic and other values could not mom.' mend any better resort for the exercise of that faculty—in these days not easily provoked— than the Royal Court Theatre. At this popular institution large audiences have been delight- fully entertained throughout the week by. that. sparkling French farce, "Oh! I Say !"—which, as is well knowa, proved the success of the 113 and 1914 seasons at the Criterion Theatre, Lon— don. Founded on Henri liesoul and Albert Barre's " Une Nuit des NocPs," it has been- cleverly adapted by Sidney Blow wad Douglats, Hoare.

There is not a dull moment in the whole piece. Nay, there is not a moment which does not pro- voke general hilarity, and as the unique plot develops the whole audience rocks with laugh- ter. At the outset of the farce one cannot but be struck by the apparent simplicity of its scheme. Yet complication follows complica- tion with such amazing—and yet quite natural —rapidity, that, in less time than it takes to tell, everything is in an indescribable tangle, and the bewildered bridegroom (who, on his wedding day, has encountered an old love, and is happy in her company) starts upon such a course of "explaining away" as would put Baron M-unchausen in the shade. Happily, the general confusion is not added to by a host of characters. Indeed, those involved are sur- prisingly few when one takes into account the remarkable variety of incident, action and ex- pression which contribute to the successful

; effect. The London Criterion Farce Company present this undoubtedly brilliant farce. They have been chosen wisely. Finesse and "polish" stand a poor chance in farcical comedy as a rule, but this talented company introduce both with apparent ease; and thus the "delicacy " of the piece is saved. It would be impossible to do justice to the particular art Of each individual participant, but a special tribute must be paid to the delightful interpretation of the role of Marcel—the bridegroom. This was given by Mr. Arthur Stanley, over whose very talented por- trayal of the principal character in "When Knights Were Bold" we still enthuse.. Miss Ida Stratham was a fascinating Sidonie de Matisse—the actress whose innocent appearance upon the scene of the honeymoon wrought such havoc with the detailed arrangements and the hearts of the three gentlemen who had made them. Of the three hundred nights during which "Oh! I Say !" was played at the elite- rion, Miss Stratham appeared no less than a third in this role, and we appreciate the privi- lege of enjoying her portrayal of it. The genial Monsieur Duportal could hardly be presented more realistically than by Mr. Charles Ross, who is the essence of freshness. Miss Glory Shannon creditably impersonates the bride, Suzette; and Mr. Cedric Percival as Henri, the best man, enters well into the spirit of the piece. Miss Violet Yorke impersonates Claudine, Sidonie's maid, in quiet and convinc- ing style.- Miss Nellie Marler makes an excel- lent Madame Pigache, the housekeeper; whilst Mr. Henry Wallace plays the part of the waiter, Joseph, in characteristic matter-of-fact style. Mr. Herbert Madden is most amusing in both his roles—the impecunious tragedian, Sorbier, and the Commissionaire of Police, Jacques Laverdet, who is so dumbfounded to discover his fiancee's duplicity and real identity. The tearful and impulsive Madame Duportal is quite suitably portrayed by Mrs. J. W. Braith- waite.
Ladies will be interested to know that the dresses are from the leading London and Paris eostumieries.
Another Panto. Next Week.
Twice nightly next week, and at matiees on Monday and Saturday, patrons of this popular theatre are to have the opportunity of 86eing a rollicking, 'bang-up-to-date version of "Little 80-peep."

div.head: MIRTH AND IVIUSIC AT THE
div.p: MIRTH AND IVIUSIC AT THE
lIIPPODRONIE.

The bill of fare at the Hippodrome this week fully maintains that high standard for which this popular place of amusement is so deser- vedly and favourably known throughout War- rington and district. Premier place in the pro- gramme is given to an uproariously funny sketch, entitled "The Demon Photographer," and played in a most frolicsome spirit by Mr. Charlie Bell and his company, who cram so many laughs into so few minutes that the audi- ences are left with aching sides. Mr. Bell, him- self, has charge of the principal part, and he invests it with the very essence of brted comedy, whilst his little company play up to him excellently and do everything in their , power to justify the claim, made for this fultny 'farcelet, that it is the biggest laughter-maker in contemporary vaudeville. A dozen youthful vocalists and dancers--Charburn's Young Stars —provide a delightful scena, entitled "A Picnic ,up the River," the patriotic selections with with which their -clever turn is studded proving especially popular, whilst the closing. rminber, "Comrades in Arms," in the parlance of the , profession "fairly knocks the house silly !" lErnie Ream tells a host of good stories and sings excellently, his "yodelling" song being especi- ally popular. Mdlle. Cameo appears in a series of artistic poses, and Gus W. Blake and Maud Granby submit a bright duologue—" A Hus- band's System "—in merry and bright fashion. Tom B. Davis knows how to sing a comic song, and Hymar and Metford get through some clever ' work on 'the light fantastic"; indeed, they are a particularly talented pair of dancers. The war pictures on the bioscope give a splendid ' idea of the complexity and importance of the , work carried on at the seat of war by our hos- pital and commissariat departments.

Big Musical Novelty Next Week. At big expense the management have secured for next week the novel musical production, " Violet and Pink," which recently scored a big hit at the London Pavilion, and which is bound to prove a big draw in Warrington.

div.head: HAPPILY BLENDED PROGRAMMES
div.p: HAPPILY BLENDED PROGRAMMES
AT STAR KINEMA.

Drama and comedy, happily blended, have proved an irresistible attration to Warrington picture-lovers this week, and they have been flocking in hundreds to that favourite resort, the Star Kinerna—where, as they know, every provision is made for their comfort.

- For the first half of the week the management secured a very fine programme. This included: "Happy-Go-Lucky," which, though giving a. pathetic story, was cleverly relieved at intervals with touches of genuine humour. The result was a happy one. An excellent issue of Pathe's Animated Gazette" gave a clear pictorial description of the training of our Colonial Armies—in addition to other war news, of course. "The House of Temperley " was one of those carefully-prepared films which one, having seen, -would like to see again. Based upon that famous story. of the boxing-ring given in Conan Doyle's "Rodney Stone," it makes in turn its appeal to many emotions—admiration, lothijig; gallantry, treachery; love and hate. "Laugh- ing Gas" was too funny for words. Concluding this evening, a capital bill of fare has occupied the second half of the week. In it the place of honour is given to "The Scales of Justice," an attention-rivetting drama of love, duty and the law.

div.head: Six Fine Films Next Week.
div.p: Six Fine Films Next Week.
The "star" film, at this cosy aipjure-house will be changed each .evening next week, six specially attractive " top-liners " having been booked for this interesting experiment.

div.head: Man's First State After Death.
div.p: Man's First State After Death.

Continuing the series of Free Church lectures, the Rev. Lewis Slight,. of Oldham, spoke at the Masonic Hall on Tuesday, on " Where men. meet after death." There was a fair audience. Mr. Slight dwelt on the teaching of the parable of the rich man and Lazarus as picturing the awakening of man into conscious life in the spiritual world immediately after bodily c:e- cease, and portraying the persistence of personal existence. The life into which man awakens, the reverend gentleman said, was a different state from life as they at present enjoyed it, and it might be defined as a state of real rela- tionships. The first need of that life, as indeed the first need of man in every fresh state, was _ _ _
the need of instruction. Thus, according to the disclosures in the writings of Emmanuel Sweden- borg, the first state of man after deatk was a state o 4 instruction.

div.head: JOITINGS BY AN OLD
div.p: JOITINGS BY AN OLD
The,Robert Peelers.

lathe course of evidence at,one of the sittings -at Warrington Borough Court last week, an old clender accused of drunkenness was stated to Ilave said in his haste that lie did not care for tweaty "Bobbies." I wonder the members of the force do not strongly resent the increasing use and more extended application of the too 'Familiar if not positively offensive term just quoted. Once I heard a severe admonition delivered frora the Bench to a witness who had referred to a police constable as "that Bobby." After sharply administering direct reproof, the dignified J.P. added a few words of warning to all and sundry concerning the habit repre- Ilended. Yet in the very next case, involving a complaint as to not sending a child regularly to i‘chool, the defendant described the attendance vfficer to the Education Committee as " t'skooil Bobby." Hard Cases.

The reckless and defiant prisoner alluded to in the preceding ,paragraph seems latterly to lave averaged some half-dozen appearances in the dock per annum. In every town in, which I have lived there has been at least one wretched aspirant to the like bad eminence, and when le was in his cups—and, as a matter of course on the warpath—a quartet of "Bobbies" generally had to tackle him. I have known only two of this class to change their habits. The Salvation Army got hold of one of these " toughs," and I found his street lectured to 'Spoor sinners" like myself pretty edifying until he became a backslider, and the "sow that was washed" returned to "her wallowing in the mire." The other fellow did ever so much better than that. He asked the magis- trates to send him to an Inebriates' Home, and as the effect of three years' treatment there, he vut off the old man with his deeds, and turned out quite a reformed character. For many years before thati he had been what in some circles is significantly termed "a -'holy terror once, when a constable endeavoured to arrest him single-handed, he promptly fractured that presumptuous officer's left leg. "Good Old Times."

Methinks those. Daresbury publicans do pro- test too much, and ,they may possibly derive k:ome little consolation from the assurance that An the olden days the community was often sub- jected to much more rigorous compulsion than anything experienced in this our own day and generation. In the former part of the sixteenth century, for instance, complaints were made that many of the workers spent their time in ale-houses, " playnge at the cardes and tables" (draughts) "and spende all that they can gett lArudigally upon theym selfes to the highe dis- pleasure of God and theyre owne ympovershyngt whereas, if it were spente at home in theyre own houses theyre wiffes and childerne shulde have part thereof.": By way of response to this •appeal, with its self-evident proposition, the authorities at once took the bull by the horns. The petition was made in 1548 to the Corpora- tion of Coventry, and. the latter decreed that any "labourer, journeyman, or apprentice" whoiso much as eptered an ale-house on a work- day should be imprisoned for a day and night. My word! Fancy. anyone trying that sort of thing on nowadays, eh? However, that reason- able experiment in the Daresbury district is •in quite a different category, and neighbouring places might copy it with advantage.

Betting and Gambling. , Those sixteenth century wastrels and ne'er- do-wells wasted their substance in intemper- ance and " playnge-at the ctrdes and tables"; ana we between three and four hundred years later (vide last week's "Examiner" report of the Church of England Men's Society meeting at Sankey) are still discussing the ethics of gambling. Turning from that aspect and look- ing at the thing from the standpoint of the average "sport," it does indeed seem to be impossible to convince a. certain class of mind that the odds are always in favour of the book- maker, just as the chances are always in favour of the tables at Monte Carlo, and that although "plungers" may often win, and -sometimes "the bank," whether it takes the form of a bookmaker or a trente-et-quarante table, is hound to gain in the end.
More About Names.

The examples given in the "Children's Corner" last week brought to my mind the case a a family whom I knew 50 years ago at Queensbury, on the heights between Bradford and Halifax. The boys were numerous, and they were given such names as Captain, Major, Colonel, Admiral, Lord, Squire, O. The late Bishop Gallier, once asked to baptise a negro baby boy "Hallud," hesitated, and remarked to 'the mother that it was a strange name. " Scripter name," rejoined the happy mother, with a confident grin. "I never saw it in the "Why, Bishop, how kin yuh atan' up dar kiddin' a ole ignorant niggah laik I is? Yuh says dat name whenevah yuh says de Lawd's prayer-- Hallud be Thy name!" . famous Hymns.

Dr. Bennett's lecture in the Latchford Wes- leyan School brought to my mind a few .facts which some who were of that gentleman's large audience may perhaps like me to set down here. Keeping in mind what Dr. Bennett said of Charles Wesley as hymn-writer, I note that, the Rev. F. L. Wiseman has a highly intereating study of the same subject. We are reminded that John said of his brother that "his least praise was his talent for poetry." His emo- tional nature, however, unsuited him for the sterner and more practical work for which John was so supremely fitted. Charles, says Mr. Wiseman, was almost as prolific of hymns as was Soloman of proverbs, and • his discourse covered nearly as wide a field. Dr. Bennett credited him. with over 700 poetical composi- tions; I had previously understood that the precise number was 6,700, about half of them consisting of evangelical paraphrases or meditations on select passages of Scripture. By way of illustration, our present authority cites "Come, 0 Thou Traveller unknown," so highly Praised by Dr. Watts, James Montgomery, and the Tate Dean Stanley; and the solemn "A charge to keep I have," which has been called the Afarseillaise of Methodism. To be '"'re, a great many of the hymns are too severely doctrinal or otherwise out of (late. The obser- vation recalls the bitter controversy which arose between Toplady and John Wesley over a doc- trinal point, and led to the former's penning his immortal hymn, "Rock of Ages." Coming

div.head: Irtters to the Obit=
div.p: Irtters to the Obit=
APPOINTMENT OF WHOLE-TIME DENTIST.
Sir,—At the meeting on Monday night the Chairman of the Health Committee said that they had not done anything -which their regula- tions did not entitle them to do.

That is not the point. The point is, whether the time has not come for the existing regula- tions to be altered. If they are not altered you will not get business men to serve on a- com- mittee, for the work of which They are respon- sible, but in the appointment of the officials of which they have no voice or influence. • If the Health Committee had wished to alter the present. regulations, which do not suit the present circumstances, they could have made recommendations to the Town Council, and it is hardly likely that the Town Council would have disapproved of any recommendations that had the support of both the Health and Medical In- spection Committees. These two committees must work together closer and closer as time goes on if the best results are to be achieved and under the /same head, viz., the Medical Officer of Health, as the latter is also the principal. School Medical Officer. If this is done there will be no over- lapping, but as the medical insßection of school children-- is a duty imposed by Statute on the local Education Authority, the Medical Inspec- tion Committee must always be a sub-committee of that authority and not of the Health Com- mittee.

Another point to which I desire to draw at- tention is that while the Medical Inspection Committee have no representation on the Health Committee, members of the Health Committee can, and do, through the local Education Authority, become also members of the Medical Th'spection Committee. They have always been: welcome, and, in fact, have been invited to join in Order to secure a closer co-operation between the two committees, but it is in this way, and in this way only, that the Health Committee should be able to influence appointments made to do the work for which the local Education Authority are responsible.
noL NI A N KINGDON Bank Quay, February 19.

div.head: WOMEN'S UNITED SERVICE CLUBS.
div.p: WOMEN'S UNITED SERVICE CLUBS.
Appeal by Lady Jell Woe and Lady French.

Sir,—Are are conscious that the war has already produced many leagues and societies, but may ,we beg a few lines of space in order to plead for one more, on behalf of the women of our sailors and soldiers now on active ser- vice?
Already many centres for rest and recreation have been formed by . various organisations, such as the "Tipperary Clubs" founde.l by Mrs. Juson Kerr and her friends.

We earnestly suggest that all such clubs should, if possible, be co-ordinated, and the work of forming them be. extended by a per- manent organisation. It is quite clear that the need of such centres will increase as the New Army is recruited and called up; the present need is only a tithe of what it wll be. and it is above everything desirable that efforts for the good of the women of the services should not be wasted by overlapping or duplication. The League of Women's United Service CI tiNs has accordingly been founded with t!be object ed furthering the work already begun in different directions and in different ways, and we cordially invite all who are interested, espe- cially the wives and relations of officers of both services, to communicate with the Honorary Secretaries of this League. Advice as to the formation of clubs and social centres will gladly be given, and We hope that those who have al- ready opened such clubs will co-operate with us. This is not an organisation for relief, but for the extension of human sympathy and neighbourliness to all those who need it; to give counsel in time of personal trouble; to organise employment; ,to visit the homes and to take interest in the children of the absent husbands, sons and fathers; to provide suitable entertain- ment at the clubs or centres; to furnish news- papers and to provide opportunity for letter- writing. The League is non-sectarian and non-,political. Where the neighbourhood is too poor to undertake the financial responsibility of opening-a. Women's United Service Club, an approved scheme will be assisted by a grant from the League. -

Let us make quite clear triat these clubs are not merely for social intercourse or amusement, but that their object is also educational. We wish to help women in all their daily difficulties, accentuated as these will be by the absence of the man of the house; not to take the women out of their home-life, but to send them back to their daily routine strengthened and re- freshed by the gentle companionship and en- couragement which a little social intercourse affords.

We appeal hopefully for funds for the pur- poses of this League to all who have the wel- fare of the women of the services at heart. It is estimated that a sum of .4220,000 may ulti- mately be needed to impleme'nt the movement and make it a really national one, by opening women's clubs in sufficient numbers, and to ensure permanence to them.

Donations and annual subscriptions may be addressed to the Honorary Treasurer of the League, Sir Henry Kimber, Bart., at the Capital and Counties Bank, Victoria-street Branch, S.W.; or to either of the Honorary Sevetaries, by whom the same will be acknow- ledged.
GWENDOLINE JELLICOE, ELEANORA FRENCH, Presidents. The League of Women's United Service Clubs, Westminster Palace Hotel, 5.W.., January 20th, 1915,

The officers of the League of Women's United Service Clubs are the following :—Joint presidents. Lady Jellicoe and Lady French; vice-presidents, Mrs. Winston Churchill, Mrs. Parker, the Countess of Limerick, Lady Henry Somerset. and Muriel Countess Helmsley; finance chairman, Mrs. M. A. Cloudesley Brere- ton ; honorary secretaries, Admiral Sir James Goodrich, K.C.V.0., and Mr. F. J. Higginbottom.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
MISS-PENT SICK LEAVE.
Soldier Back Fronythe Front Finds His Way Into the Dock.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, before Messrs. R. T. Faiiclough, A. J. Jolley, D. Tinnion and T. Iremberton, , John Williams, a private, of the Depot Bat- talion of the South Lancashire Regiment, sta- tioned at Orford Barracks, Was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Bewsey- street the previous day.—When asked to plead, he said, "I know nothing about it," whereupon the Magistrates' Clerk observed, "You must be guilty then !" The evidence was to the effect that a police constable was called to Mr. Bottomley's office in Bewsey-street, and there found the prisoner, who was very drunk, jumping about like a madman.

Prisoner said that he had only recently arrived from the Front on sick furlough, and lie had a drop of whisky, and it took hohl of him. He had been all through the campaign, and not being strong again yet, the drink took hold'of him.

The Chief • Constable: He's quite right. It had taken hold of him with a vengeance. (Laughter.) If he has been in anything like the fighting form in which he was last night, it is a pity that he did not get hold of a few of the Germans. He would }Hive pulverised them. (Laughter.) No doubt he's a man of plenty. of pluck, and I think if the Bench will 'fell him that he Must not repel& his conduct of yester- day that will be about all that the police desire. It appeared, continued the Chief, that he went into a public-house in Bewsey-street with two other men. Ohe of the men called for three drinks, and without her seeing the prisoner, the barmaid fetched the liquor in. As soon as she saw the state the prisoner was in, how- ever, she at once took hold of the whisky which had been ordered for him, whereupon a struggle took place, and her hand was -injured. The prisoner was certainly maii drunk. Prisoner said lie was .sorry; he had never before "been up" in all his life. Ile was ordered to be hariaed.- over to in escort, after the Chairman had admonished him concerning the folly of over-indulgence.

div.head: BOROUGH POLICE COURT
div.p: BOROUGH POLICE COURT
MONDAY.
Before Mr. S. Wright in the chair), Aldermen Bolton arid Smethurst, Councillor Joseph, and

_ . Messrs. W. Furness, Pilling and T. Locker. Parleyed with Poker.—Thomas Roberts, black- smith's striker, of 17, Elizabeth-street, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in that street on Sunday afternoon, and/ also with assaulting his stepdaughter (Margaret Forbes) and a police officer (P.C. Ballard).— Prisoner admitted the first two offences, but denied assaulting the police.—P.C. Ballard stated that at a quarter to one on the previous afternoon Emma Roberts, wife of the prisoner, came and said that her husband had locked her three daughters and herself out of the house, threatening them with a poker. He went to the house, and prisoner came into the street. He was very drunk, and used very bad language. He also brandished the poker, and threatened to "do hill} (witness) in." He then struck wit- ness on the shoulder, and witness took the poker from 'him.—Margaret Forbes (18), said her step- father threatened her mother with the poker. She (witness) got between them. He then swore at her, seized her by the throat and threw her on the table, causing 'her mouth to bleed. She had to remain in a neighbour's house till halt- past pine, and he used filthy language when she went back.—Prisoner said when he went to bed on Sunday afternoon his wife went out. He came downstairs and asked where she was, and his stepdaughter replied that .she was in the yard. That VMS how the bother started. Later in the evening his wife brought some neighbours in. He wanted to kick them out, as he had as much right in the house as they had. Then the trouble arose. The door was not locked against his wife and stepdaughter, and when he went to the door he was pulled into the street. He only had the poker to protect him- self from the other people coming into the house. He did not strike anyone.—The Chair- man (Mr. S. Wright) told Roberts that his was a very serious offence, and the police might have charged him with an even graver one in view of the weapon he had had.—A fine of 20s. and costs (Bs. 6d.)—with the alternative of a month's imprisonment—was imposed. Magistrate's Pertinent Query. Dominick Chrimes, of Red House Farm, Preston Brook, was summoned for having been drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on Saturday.—He said he had only had three drinks, and they were the first he had had since Christmas.—Dr. Joseph: What sort of drinks were they? (Laugh- ter.)—Chrimes : Tbree glasses of rum and a pint !—The Chief Constable: Well, that would knock any ordinary man up. (Laughter.)—The offender was fined Bs. 6d., including costs. "Best Swimmer in Warrington !"—James Henessy, a middle-aged man, was charged with drunken and disorderly behaviour at Warring- ton Bridge on Sunday.—lt was stated that he took off his boots and made as if to jump into the river, shouting that he was the best swimmer in Warrington! He had appeared in Court four times previously for fighting, and being drunk and disorderly.—The Chief Con- stable: It will appeal to all if the Bridge has anything to do with it. (Laughter.)-11enessy was fined five shillings, including -costs.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.
Before Councillor 11. Roberts (in • the chair), Messrs. James Hepherd, C. Jackson Holmes,
T. Locker and J. Rymer Young.

Warrington or Berlin?—Thomas Hinde, lab- ourer, of no settled abode, was summoned for having been drunk and disorderly in Butter- market-street on Monday.—P.C. Bennett 'proved the case.—Defendant said that if the Bench gave him a chance lie intended to join the Army.— The Chief Constable: "He will have to be in the German Army; he is no use in ours. His language when brought to the Police Station was most disgusting. He is a stranger out of work, and was selling penny packets of laven- der. He ought to sell them in Berlin, not here." —Defendant was fined 56. and costs.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.
Before Messrs. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), H. Thornton, C. Jackson Holmes and W. T.
Williams

A NightOut.—Beatrice Bratt and May Gregory, two young women, were charged with wandering abroad in Wilderspool-road without visible means of support.—P.C. Lievesley said that at 5.5 that morning he saw the ..young women in Knutsford-road, and keeping observa- tion on them, watched them go into a timber yard in Wilderspool-road. He questioned them and found that they were absolutely destitute. —The Chief Constable (Mr. Martin Nicholls) said that the girls had been detained in order that, if possible, something might be done for them, with a view to reclaiming them from a certain course of life, which they had undoubt- edly been following for some time. It appeared that one night last week the girls slept in the guardroom at Orford Barracks, and that the night before their arrest, according to their own story, they were taken by a man in a motor car to a house in Latchford Without. It was after leaving that house that they were arrested.— The girls promised to enter a home, and were remanded for a week in order that one may be found for them.

div.head: FRIDAY.
div.p: FRIDAY.
Before Mr. S. Wright (in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst and James Evans, Coun- cillor Wilkinson and Messrs. W. Furness and

A. J. Jolley. A Young Couple Parted.—Sarah Lizzie Donoghue, a young married woman, who car- ried a baby in her arms, *as granted a separa- tion from her husband, George Donoghue, a labourer, of 48, Howard-street, on the ground of desertion, and was awarded 14s. a week alimony. —She told the Court that she had two children, and that her husband could earn 30s. a week. Last Saturday week be came home the worse for drink, and, after demanding his tea, pushed her and struck her in the eye. He then went out of the house and had not returned since. Six weeks ago he enlisted and was drafted to Pres- ton, but he was discharged.—The husband alleged that his wife had been drawing the Government pay since he was discharged.—The
Continued in next Column.

div.head: ii ISTRICT MEWS
div.p: ii ISTRICT MEWS
STeeKTON HEATH.
Diphtheria in the Township.—lt was reported to the Parochial Committee that disinfection had recently been carried out in houses in which had occurred five cases of diphtheria.

Street Lighting May Cost More.—A letter from the Warringtoti Corporation Gas Department read at the monthly meeting of the Parochial Committee, on Tuesday night, stated: "We find that some of the lamps in your district are not yielding any profit, and, as fuel has risen in price, we shall probab'y require some readjust- ment in the charges L_..de."

Present at the Parochial Committee.—At a meeting of the Parochial Committee held in the Council School on Tuesday night there were present: Messrs. G. Pilling (in the chair), H. J. Westbrook, J. H. Clarke, F. Pearson, W. Mc- Intyre, John Hallows, J. McDermid, and A. Bottoinley ; with Messrs. W. E. Hough (deputy- clerk), S. Wright (survNyor) and E. Bradshaw (clerk to the Parish Council).

Knocking Sornething Off the Gas let- ter was read from the Gas Department of the Warrington Corporation at Tuesday night's Meeting of the Parochial COmmittee stating that a credit of .t 3 7s. 4d. was to be allowed in re- spect of the period in September when the street lamps were not lighted—that period, it will be recalled, when great shortage of gas pressure was experienced owing to •a, scarcity of labour at the Gas Works consequent upon so many. of the men having gone to the war.

Warning Signs for Motorists.—A letter was read at Tuesday night's meeting- of the Paro- chial Committee from the Automobile Associa- tion offering to supply five warning signs bear- ing the words "Swing Bridge," provided the committee would undertake the cost of finding posts on which to erect them along the ap- Proaches to the bridge crossing the canal. It was decided that the committee could do noth- ing in flip matter, the road over the bridge in question coming under the jurisdiction of the sCounty Council.

Funeral of the Oldest Inhabitant. —The mortal remains of the late 31r. James Lawton, of Duke's Cottages, Walton-road—who passed away, as re- corded in our last issue, at the patriarchal age of 91, and who was Stockton Heath's oldest in- habitant—were interred in St. Thomas' Church- yard on Saturday afternoon in the presence of a large number of people. The principal mourn- ers were Messrs. Richard and James Lawton ksons), Luke Caldwell, William Cook and Wil- liam Isherwood (sons-in-law), William Coon, jun., James and George Isherwood, Harry Cald- well and J. Cartwright (grandsons), and Isaac Lawton (nephew). The following friends of the deceased bore the coffin to the grave: Messrs. J. Isherwood, J. Dumbell, Whitlow, C. Pittam and W. Spencer. Mi. John Hallows attended as representing the St. Thomas' Men's Bible Class (of which the deceased was a member), and the Aged People's Treat Committee ‘(who had twice " crowned " him "king" and at whose annual festival he was always a specially welcome guest): Among many floral tributes was one from the Aged People's Treat Com- mittee.
terms they could for the last monopoly left them to confer.

Mr. Bottomley said that, whilst quite agreeing with Mr. Westbrook that the people of Stockton Heath ought to get all they could, he thought that it was up to them to find out how many people would be likely to , take the current if the mains were extended beyond the Square, so that when the Corporation were applying for their Order the parish could be ready with their case for an early extension. He thought Mr. Westbrook was labouring under a misapprehen- sion that the members of the Warrington Cot- poration were simply tumbling over -each other to • get their electricity into Stockton Heath. Mr. Westbrook: I don't give them the credit of being so far-seeing.

div.head: ELECTRIC LIGHT QUESTION. Should the Corporation Be Pressed for a Bigger Scheme?
div.p: THE ELECTRIC LIGHT QUESTION. Should the Corporation Be Pressed for a Bigger Scheme?
OR IS "HALF A LOAF BETTER THAN NO BREAD?"

The Warrington Corporation's .proposal to extend their electricity service to Stockton Heath formed the subject of a somewhat lengthy discussion at a meeting of the Parochial Com- mittee, held, under the chairmanship of Mr. G. Pilling; in the Council School on Tuesday even- ing. _ _

The matter arose on a resolution forwarded by Mr. E. Stanley Taylor, the secretary of the Stockton Heath Tradesmen's Association, set- ting forth that the members of the association heartily supported the Corporation's proposed scheme of extension, provided always that the charges for current to Stockton Heath consum- ers shall be the same as those levied in War- rington.
The Deputy-Clerk (Mr. W. E., Hough) said that the matter was one for the Rural District Council now, and not for that committee.
A Popular, But Erroneous Idea.

Mr. H. J. Westbrook said there seemedito be a popular idea in the parish that if Warrington got power to bring electricity to Stockton Heath it would be laid on generally in the dis- trict, but that was not the case. The present proposal was that Warrington should come so far, and no further, titan would justify them in having .the statutory order granted. If the proposal were to introduce electricity into., the parish generally, the people of Stockton Heath would not object, ,but they did object to the Corporation merely just qualifying to hold powers to supply in the parish, and then, per- haps, keeping the place waiting another ten or a dozen years before taking the light along the main roads.

Mr. John Hallows: Do they propose to stop at Victoria-square, then? Mr. H. J. Westbrook explained that a stipula- tion in the order asked for would be that the Corporation must bring the electric light to the Square within two years, and that they would only carry the light :further than the Square upon it being shown that there would be a suffi- cient demand for the current in other parts of the .parish to .repay them for their outlay. The Corporation required that guarantee, so it might be years before people living beyond the Square would get the electric light.

div.head: Canvass for Possible Customers.
div.p: A Canvass for Possible Customers.

Mr. A. Bottomley. ,thought that committee ought to do all they could to spur the matter forward. It was only natural that they who lived in Stockton Heath should want to get as many of' the amenities of modern life as they Possibly could, but they could scarcely expect the Corporation to lay mains all round the township straightaway, for the simple reason that the cost would undoubtedly be tremendous. By 'way of inducing the Corporation to extend the supply beyond the Square he thought it was up to the people of Stockton Heath to get to know, something like definitely, how many householders would be prepared to take the electricity. If they could show the Corporation that there was a prospect of their getting a fair return on their outlay, he thought they would find that body only too pleased to put the cur rent anywhere where it was neede I.

The Last of Stockton Heath's Monopolies. Mr. Westbrook thought it was for the Cor- poration to obtain that information and not for the Parochial Committee or the Parish .Council. There were two sides to the question'. A man, when he put up a cotton mill, did not expect to get:a full return the first year. lie thought the Corporation should look at this question of lighting Stockton Heath with elec- tricity in the same way, for he was convinced that, though they couid not expect it in the first two or three years, they woro.l ultimately get a very good return for flteir outlay. he possibilities open to the Corpov:ition eid not end at Stockton .Heath, for there were the par- ishes beyond, so that Warrington would be get- ting a very valuable monopoly and one that they could very well afford to, pay for. The people of Stockton Heath ought to get the best

div.head: IN THE COURTS—Continued.
div.p: IN THE COURTS—Continued.

Magistrates' Clerk (to the wire): Have you?— The. wife: Yes, sir !—And he not in the Army? —No, sir. He told Me that be was not going to work While he could get Lloyd George's money. —he had been "on the club "—and said "You must get money from the Government." Damaged a Door.—Mary Burrows, of 32, Bat- tersby-lane, was ordered to pay 10s. for wilfully damaging a door at 14, Gandy-street, and also ss. court costs.—The evidence was that the de- fendant went to the house of a, woman named Sullivan, and after challenging the woman, with whom, she had been quarrelling, to come out and "'have some more," kicked the panels in ith Ler clogs.

div.head: Other Side of the Question.
div.p: The Other Side of the Question.

Mr. Bottomley : No credit would attach to them if they went to the tremendous expense that would be involved in lighting the whole of our parish, if they could see no return for the money thus laid out. ' Mr. Westbrook said it was only a question of the Corporation feeling the pulse of the parish, so to speak. Mr. Bottothley : But they have no need to feel the pulse of a district into which they don't intend to come yet! Mr. J: H. Clarke said that if the Corporation did not propose to go further with the electric light than Victoria-square he was strongly opposed to their having an Order, but if it was their intention to, some time in the reasonable future, extend their supply to other parts of the parish, he was in favour of their coming into the parish. • Mr. Bottomley : Exactly, and I think every other man in the room is in the same position. Mr. Clarke, continuing, said that the resolu- tion from the Tradesmen's Association was a selfish one. They were only asking for the elec- tricity for themselves—for the centre of the township. ("No, no.") Their 'position would have lieen stronger if they had gone a bit further and said that they not only asked for the current for their shops, but for the private residences as well. It was his emphatic opinion that if the Corporation would not give an under- taking to carry the light further than Victoria- square, it was the duty of everybody in Stock- ton Heath to oppose the Order.

Electric Light Badly Wanted. Mr. Bottomley : Electricity is something we badly want here, and we must do everything that lies in our power to try and get it into the district. That is my main- point. Mr. J. McDermid .failed to see why the Paro- chial Committee should obtain information as to the probable number of users if the current were carried into all parts of the parish. Surely that was part of the duty of the Corporation! A question having arisen as to the price likely to be charged if the Order were enlarged to take in the whole of Stockton Heath, Mr. Bottomley said that in effect the Order that was being applied for was simply an ex- tension of the Corporation's present Order, therefore Stockton Heath would come under the same Order as Warrington, and whatever price ruled in Warrington would rule in Stockton Heath.
The Chairman having pointed out that the Corporation had promised to extend their scheme if they found out that it would pay them to do so, the discussion dropped.

div.head: PEN K ETH.
div.p: PEN K ETH.

C.W.S. Cinema-Lecture.--An interesting lec- ture, illustrated by cinematographic pictures,was given in the Wesleyan School on Friday last on "What the Co-operative Wholesale Society has done for the Workers," by Mr. Armstrong, of the C.W.S., the lecture being held under the auspices of the local Co-operative Society. Mr. George Faulkner presided over a-large audience, and at the close moved 'a vote of thanks to the lecturer. During the evening part-songs were sung by a choir of about forty girls.

div.head: GREAT SANKEY.
div.p: GREAT SANKEY.

Helping the Local War Fund.—A whist drive and dance in aid of the Great Sankey War Fund was held in the Sunday school, which was kindly lent by the Vicar for the occasion, on Friday evening of last week. Over 170 people attended and a thoroughly enjoyable event it proved to be. The proceedings commenced shortly after 8 o'clock, and continued until half-past one. The whist party numbered 100, and 24 hands were played. The ladies' first prize (a handbag pre- sented by Mr. John Randall) was won by Mrs. James Ray, whose score was 180. The second prize (a silver and cut-glass scent-bottle, pre- sented by Mr. W. A. Clatworthy) went to Mrs. Jos. Smith, with a score of 179. The gentleman's first prize (a copper kettle, presented by Mr. W. H. Hughes, of Messrs. Caldwell's, Ltd.) was captured by Mr. F. Dendy, whose score was 176, whilst the second prize (a pair of silver serviette rings, presented by Mr. Arthur Fur- ness) was won by Mr. L. Davies with 171 points. There were two hidden number prizes (a lady's necklace, presented by Mrs. John Dodds, and a pipe and case, presented by Miss Beswick, through Mr. James Knowles), the winners being Miss E. Craske and Mr. Wm. Webb. The dance programme contained 21 items. The Ray Brothers provided the music in a way that was much appreciated. Mr. James/Woodward had tastefully decorated the room. The proceeds amounted to upwards of .215, which includes 'll sum. of £4 6s. realised by the sale of refresh- ments, supplied, as a gift, by the Chairman (Mr. William Furness), who, during the even- ing, expressed the thanks of the committee to all those who had so kindly assisted in making the entertainment such a great success.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

Preparatory Training Corps.—An interesting handicap rifle competition was held in connec- tion with the Padgate and. District Preparatory Training Corps on Monday evening, 22 members of the corps entering and some fair shooting being witnessed. Mr. Jos. Smith won first prize with a score of 77 out of a possible 80, Mr. E. Andrews coming second With 76, and Mr. Frank Oaks third with 67. The prizes were the gifts of local gentlemen.

Wesleyan Church.—Sunday last was the day set apart for the annual home missionary ser- vices, and eloquent sermons were preached in the morning and evening by the Rev. W. Ash- ton, of Castleford.—Owing to being called away suddenly, Mr. Ashton was unable to deliver his promised lecture on "France before the War" on Monday evening, but an excellent substitute was found in the Rev. A. J. Morton, who gave a very interesting account of his ministerial experiences in Ireland. Ile explained the diffi- culties of preaching Nonconformity in the open- air in the Green Isle, and how on several occa- sions he had been compelled to seek the assist- ance of the police to protect him from the threatening mob. The reverend gentleman also recalled many pleasant reminiscences of the farmhouse services which were held in the different villages.—Mr. Sanderson, of Warring- ton, presided, and at the outset gave a descrip- tion of his journeys with the Century Roll in the Ilkley district of Yorkshire.

div.head: Different Reasons.
div.p: Different Reasons.

Geordie and Bill, who have enlisted in the Northumberland Hussars, were deep in conver- sation, when Geordie said to Bill: "Aa say, whaat made thoo list?" ." Wey," said Bill, "Aa had ne wife or bairns—nobody but mysell •to think aboot ; an, besides, Aa likes waar." After a short silence, Bill remarked: "Wey, Geordie, whaat set thoo te join th' Army?" "Wey, thoo sees," replied Geordie, "Aa hey a wife, an' Aa joined th' army becaase Aa likes peace !"

div.head: LYM M.
div.p: LYM M.

On the Bench.—At the Petty Sessions held on Wednesday morning the following magistrates were on the Bench: Mr. W. Peter Rylands (in the chair), Vice-Chancellor D. Stewart-Smith, and Messrs. A. W. Callender and John Coxon.

To Aid Nurses' Fund.—A whist drive in ,aid of the Lymm and District Nurses' Fund was held on Tuesday evening in the Warburton Schools. It was organised by the ladies of the Sewing Class, and the financial result has proved very satisfactory.

Oughtrington Social.—A very enjoyable and successful social was held in the Ougtrington Church Schoolroom on Wednesday evening. Re- freshments having been partaken, the Vicar (the Rev. Tudor Evans) presided over an enter- tainment. For this there was a programme of interesting musical items, and Mrs. E. Ridgway 'also recited in excellent style.

Missionary Services.—Missionary services were held in the Primitive Methodist Church on Sunday. The preacher was the Rev. Wm. Paw, of Altrincham. In the afternoon a special ser- vice for young people was held, when Mr. Paw gave an instructive address. A public meeting took place on Monday evening, at which Mr. G. L. Welford presided, and the speakers were the Revs. R. W. Ferguson and W. Paw.

Football Match in .the Mud.—Defeat awaited the Lymm footballers, when on Wednesday afternoon, they visited Stockport to play a match in the Manchester Wednesday League. The whole display was very unexciting, the wetness of the weather being only exceeded by the muddiness of the ground. H. Holt scored Lymm's solitary goal rather well, but the home team got three.

Broadheath Minister's Appointment.—The annual meetings of the A Itrincham and District Free Church, Council were held on Wednesday. The Rev. W. D. Thomas, minister of the Con- gregational Church at Broadheath, wilt) has acted as hon. secretary to the Council for the last seven years, was appointed president, and he is succeeded in the secretarial office by the Rev. W. Lamsdell,. of Partington. Mr. George Rhodes, K.C., was re-appointed treasurer.

The Wick That Wouldn't !—At Wednes- day's Sessions, -Bertie Bradburn, tanner, of 1, Cherry-lane, Lymm, appeared for riding a bicycle along the highway on Sunday,'January 17th,, without a dauld said he had been on Penny Hill when he noticed Bradburn riding a bicycle without-a light, and pointed it out to him.. Bradburn replied that the lamp must have gone out at the corner; it had been lighted all the way from Altrincham. He then lighted it, but it went out. There was plenty of oil in the lamp, but the wick would not turn up.—A fine of 2s. 6d., including costs, was im- posed.—" See that your lamp is in better order next time!" was the Chairman's advice to de- fendant.

The Horse That Walked Away.—Ernest VoHands, butcher's assistant, of Heatley Heath, Lymm, appeared at the Petty Sessions on Wed- nesday morning for having, on Tuesday, Febru- ary 9th, been in charge of a horse and trap on the highway without having control of the horse.—P.C. Atherton stated that, at about a quarter to one on the day referred to he was in Broomedge and saw the horse, which was un- attended, drawing the trap along the side of the road towards him. He stopped .it. In a short time Vollands came running from a house. —Defendant said the horse had only gone six or seven yards, and it must have heard his foot- steps as he was coming back to it—he was de- livering m-at. He' had often left it like that, and it had never walked away before. He had a chain, but did not think it worth while to put it on.—ln fining defendant 2s. 6d., including costs, the Chairman said it was serious—a great danger—to leave the trap so that the horse could move. .

Choir Visits Broomedge.—The members of the Broomedge Chapel had the pleasure of a visit from the Dunham Woodhouse choir on Wednes- day evening, when an excellent audience gath- ered to enjoy a concert given in aid of the chapel fund. Mr. J. Perrin occupied the chair, and briefly and suitably addressed- the gather- ing. The Misses Knight gave a pianoforte duet. The soloists were: Miss N. Holt (who sang "The Sweet Old Melody" and "Your Eyes have told me so "), Miss M. Astall (whose contributions were "Angus McDonald," and,, by special re- quest," Your King and Country want you "), _ _

and Miss D. Pennington (who gave "1,;. Mar- seillaise" in French). Miss Pennington also re- cited "The Road to Heaven." Four young ladies gave an amusing dialogue, "The Jumble Sale," and six took part in an action song, "Six Lancashire L4ssies." A comic trio, "Shut the Door," was contributed by a lady and two gen- tlemen, and "Branagan's Band/1 proved a great attraction.

div.head: "NOT UNDER CONTROL."
div.p: "NOT UNDER CONTROL."
Carter In Trouble For Leming Horse
Unattended.

John Leather, a carter for the Bridgewater Colleries, of High Legh, was summoned at Wed- nesday's Petty Sessions for being in charge of a cart on the highway at Lymm on Thursday, January 28th, without having control of the horse drawing the cart. —Tie pleaded guilty to having been without control "-for about half a minute !"

Sergeant Davies said that at the time in question he saw a horse attached to a light coal- cart standing opposite to the Fleece Hotel. He went in and inquired where the driver was. Presently he saw Leather and told him he would have to report the matter. About ten minutes before he had seen Leather coming out of another hotel. There was no chain on the cart, and it was getting dusk. Defendant explained that he met a, friend, who had just come over for a few days. They went inside the Spread Eagle and his friend bought him a drink. • When they got to the Fleece Hotel, he took his friend in to pay for a drink for him, in return, but he. had not got

a yard inside the place when the sergeiZnt walked in. ire (defendant) was not even at the bar, and did not have his drink at all. The sergeant pointed out to him the cart across the road. He had often passed himself when other carts were standing outside in the same way, and there was nothing to stop a cart getting past them. The Chairman (Mr. W. P. Rylands) said that the leaving of a horse and cart was a very dan- gerous practice—particularly on the bridge, which was very steep. Defendant would be fined 55., including costs.

div.head: MORE WOUNDED ARRIVE
div.p: MORE WOUNDED ARRIVE
At The Lymin Red Cross Hospital.

On Thursday four more " Tommies " arrived at "Brookfield," the Lymm Red Cross Hospi- tal. They are Drummer H. O'Brien (2nd South Staffordshires), Private Peter Cowan (2nd South Lancashires), Private Spencer Elliott (2nd East Lancashires) and Private Thomas Ingham (Ist Northumberland Fusiliers). At the same time as these arrived, two others left for home. Thus there are now eighteen patients at the hospital, as formerly.

Of the four warriors who hav4 arrived, one is suffering from frost-bite; another fell sixteen feet and slightly damaged his spine; a third has bronchitis; whilst the last is "rather pep- pered with shot." They are all progressing very favourably, and are delighted with the Carefully-made arrangements for their comfort at "Brookfield."

Private Elliott, who is under the care of Dr. De Jong and belongs to Nelson, was, three weeks ago, in the trenches at , where he had been a fOrtnight—after spending an equal period in other parts of France. In that part of the war-zone the fighting was rather desul- tory. There were four stretcher-bearers in his trench, for the shells were a source of danger; but fbrtunately only a few of his comrades were wounded. The private had to leave the firing- line suffering from frost-bite.

div.head: Forthcoming Concert for Red Cross.
div.p: Forthcoming Concert for Red Cross.

On Wednesday next, in the Drill Hall, a con- cert is to be given in aid of the. Lymm Red Cross Hospital. It is promoted by the Work- ing Men's Committee. The Warrington Male Voice Choir and Crosfield's Band will attcne
and among other entertainers one of the wounded soldiers from "Brookfield "—who in peace times was principal violinist in a leading, London orchestra—will play selections.

div.head: AFFILIATED!
div.p: AFFILIATED!
Home Defence Corps Joins ‘A lilt Volunteer Training Corps.

In its affiliation with the Central Association Volunteer Training Corps, the Lymm Home Defence Corps have taken an important and wise step. This was decided upon, 'after due discussion, at a well-attended meeting held on Thursday evening, with Mr. Alfred Watkin in the chair.

It had been arranged that the Lymm Corps should follow the coarse if it could get a total membership of not less than fifty. At the meet- ing a goad number were enrolled, and the mem- bership now stands at thirty-five. The com- mittee has hopes of good recruiting in the Oughirington district, and it is highly probable that even more than the desired number will be enrolled in the near future. Meanwhile, the secretary will be glad to receive the names of all wishing to join. Official recognition! That is the reason for the affiliation. This very desirable—even neces- sary—distinction could not be obtained in !Any other way, and the application, which the com- mittee forwarded a few weeks ago to the Volun- teer Corps, was, they knew, quite representative of the general feeling. To-day preliminary training begins, and it will continue to-morrow, afternoon—though, of course, the Tuesday evening drills at the Drill Hall fill make the real start. From that time onward the Corps will work in earnest. , •

div.head: "ON HILL FACING SEA."
div.p: "ON HILL FACING SEA."
First Detachment of Lymm Soldiers
Arrive In France.

The gallant lads of Lymm who elected to serve their King and country are now in France. Many letters have been received during the week by the parents and other relatives of these " Tommies " who have now set foot on Con- tinental soil. These show that the men are in excellent spirits. But although there is plenty of information in the letters—the departure from England; hurried arrangements, the " lovely " sail across the water, Ste., &c.,—not a hint is given as to the whereabouts of the men, or their destination. Every communication has passed the eagle eye of the Censor, arid the nearest approach to information on the subject is that they are at present "on a hill facing the sea."

Mrs. Joseph Clare, of Booth's frill, haa iwo sons and a nephew in this batch. Another of her sons was unable to go with them owing to sickness, but he writes quite cheerily that "lie hopes to see them in Berlin !"

div.head: STUDY OF .THE HEAVENS.
div.p: STUDY OF .THE HEAVENS.
Lecturette at Sankey Bridges Adult
School.

A- lecturette on astronomy, which proved to be full of interest, was given on Sunday morn- ing at the Sankey Bridges Adult School by Mr." T. Thornley. From the earliest times, said the lecturer, the heavenly bodies had attracted the thoughts and attention of scientific men. One got an idea of the immensity of the solar system when he recalled the fact that it would take a train travelling sixty miles per hour, day and night, no fewer than 5,280 years to accomplish the journey from the earth to Neptune, the outer- most of the planets known to mankind. If the same train, travelling at the same rate. attempted the journey of the worlds orbit, it would take it a thousand years; yet the earth accomplished the tremendous journey in 365 days. But the distances between the earth and the planets were nothing as compared to the distances between the earth and the stars—dis- tances that were not to be recorded in figures, but in terms of what the. 'astronomer called "light years." Light from the nearest star, travelling at the rate of over 180,000 miles a second, took four years to reach the earth. The man with a telescope found endless variety to occupy him in a study of the stvs. Whether any of the other planets, beside our own, were inhabited was a point about which scientists differed, but it was pretty certain that life could not exist Upon them in any form such as we were familiar with. An evening spent with the eye, at the end of a powerful telescope broad- ened one's views Of life considerably, and gave one a far more understanding conception of Nature in her greatest forms, just as the micro- scope helped to an appreciatioll of her wonders in the realm of the infinitely small.

div.head: AFTER A WOMAN IS 30.
div.p: AFTER A WOMAN IS 30.

At thirty a woman may reasonably expect to enjoy good health, having then overcome the troubles of early womanhood, yet being free of the later trials of middle-age; but various causes tend to undermine the strength of many women of thirty. 'Foremost among these causes are the cares of motherhood and household worries, which have a depressing effect on a woman's regular health and nervous system; then again women at work or in business will often be similarly afflicted, for overwork, business anxieties, hurried meals, too little rest and lack of sufficient out-door recreation thin the blood and give rise to much suffering. div.head: EXAMINER, S kTURDAY,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, S kTURDAY,
OUTSTAYED AND OUTPLAYED.
Warrington's Good Beginning Makes a Bad Ending.

div.head: BROUGHTON'S 16 UNANSWERED POINTS.
div.p: BROUGHTON'S 16 UNANSWERED POINTS.
Notes by "Centre."

Broughton continued their successful career on Saturday—this time at the expense of War- rington, who returned home from The Cliff Pointless and with a score of 16 on. the wrong side,to ruminate over. The game was not alto- gether so one-sided as the score would suggest; indeed;in the earlier stages Warrington looked like having more than a sporting chance of winning. But they were gradually worn down and the superior staying powers of the Brough- ton men told their tale. Had Warrington only been able to sustain the bright form which they displayed at the commencement the score-board might have worn an altogether different ap- pearance at the close of the game. But, for one reason or another, they could not do so; and instead, after making an initial splash, they appeared to wilt, so to speak, and for the major portion of the match contented themselves with defensive tactics, appearing unaccountably deficient in( initiative.
play appeared to be quite purposeless, and Broughton experienced little difficulty in taking the sting out of all .their too-few attacks.
TRANTER TRIES A TRY-BUT FAILS.

The first few minutes promised a spirited game, but, like many another promise, this one was not fulfilled. Early on Tranter raised high the hopes of his side, but they were soon dashed to the ground—and so was Tranter; just as he was within a stride or two of the line.. So near yet 'so far! Shortly afterwards" Baker had -a cut at scoring, but Ruddick forced him into touch, and then Warrington's best and almost their last real effort went amiss. Laws, for once in a while, found the ball coming from the heels of his men in the scrummage, and he passed it across to Tranter, who, with Bradshaw at his elbow, raced down the field. When close to the goal-line, Tranter found himself hard pressed and parted to Bradshaw, and the latter endeavoured to kick over Danson's head, but the leather skidded low to the dead-ball line. •After this venture the visitors rarely got really dangerous, and spent most of their time ward- ing off as many as they could of the hostile rushes of the Broughton forwards, who, in more senses than one, were a slippery lot.

div.head: FORWARDS' GAME.
div.p: A FORWARDS' GAME.

The playing pitch was in anything but an ideal condition, heavy rains in the forenoon and on the previous day having transformed it into something like a quagmire. Some of the worst patches had been liberally sanded, but even the lavish use of the product of the sea- shore did not prevent the players sinking ankle deep in the mud, the result being—as will readily be imagined—that the finer points of the game could not be developed, and that work was, more or less, of a slip-and-slide, rough- and-tumble character. The bulk of the play devolved upon the forwards, and, of the two packs, Broughton's were decidedly the more enterprising, whilst they also had the advan- tage of weight—an advantage of which, by the way, they made the best possible use. Nine times out of ten they beat their opponents when it came to a tussle for the possession of the ball, and they appeared to find the mud less of an inconvenience than did their opponents. There- was plenty of fly-kicking—so much of it, in fact, that the game was largely deprived of its interest—but on the whole it could be excused, seeing that the ball was so greasy that it Was only little short of impossible to handle it with any degree of accuracy.

div.head: BROUGHTON'S BETTER FOOTWORK
div.p: BROUGHTON'S BETTER FOOTWORK

Yes, on the whole, feet were as useful as hands, and Broughton undoubtedly enjoyed the advantage* of superior skill in footwork. Time and again did they out-distance Warrington in the matter of driving. In the first half in particular many chances fell to the Wilderspool boys, but they allowed them to slip by un- seized, seteral penalty kicks being poorly taken and more excellent openings wasted. It was Positively exasperating to notice- the number of opportunities that were allowed to go a-begging, and one was forced to the conclusion that Saturday was, decidedly, one of Warring- ton's off-days. Except during the opening stages, they displayed a lamentable lack of u!aison—a disregard for the principles of com- bination that could not but result in disaster. True, they made spasmodic efforts at pulling hemselves together, but, on the whole, their

div.head: HOW THE POINTS CAME.
div.p: HOW THE POINTS CAME.

The first score came per Tighe, who nipped round the scrummage and crossed over the line near the corner-flag. Davidson essayed to put on the goal points, but failed hopelessly. A minute or so later Harris grazed the goal-post with a fine , penalty shot, taken from an awk- ward angle. Another score was not long delayed, for, after a nice dribble by the forwards, Howarth got over. Harris failed to improve, but just before the interval Davidson landed a beautiful goal from the centre line. Crossing over eight points to the bad, Warrington ap- peared disheartened, and Harris soon piled on three more points against them, the goal-kick once again proving a failure. Towards the close J. L. Clampitt put on another try and this time Harris made no mistake with the goal- kick—a beautiful drive that fetched loud ap- plause from the crowd. When the final Whistle sounded the score board read: Rangers, .2 goals 4 tries (16 points); Warrington. nil—a result which just about represented the respective merits of the teams, judged on the day's play, for there could be no doubt that Broughton were far and away the better side.

div.head: JOLLEY'S DOGGED GAME.
div.p: JOLLEY'S DOGGED GAME.

Had it not been for Jolley's doggedness— maintained right up to the bitter end—the score against Warrington must have been heavier than was the case. He worked desperately hard, and, on the whole, very well, but one man by himself, be he never so industrious, cannot avert defeat. Bradshaw and Txanter played well in the early stages of the game, but they "browned off" all too soon, and, during the second half, were hardly ever in the picture. Laws played a most serviceable game at half-back, quite eclipsing his partner, Dainteth, who appeared to be quite off colour. The play of the forwards was scrappy; lacking method, and, as a result, lacking also effective- ness. Of a mediocre bunch, perhaps, the Brothers Cunliffe and Fearnley were the best. The home forwards worked together as one man and therein had a big advantage over their rivals. The Broughton threequarters also dis- played effective combination, and the halves— Tighe and Manley—were a reliable and most useful pair; whilst Danson, at full-back, never made a mistake. Out of their seven .last matches Broughton have recorded six wins.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
Warrington 'eVorking Men's
Association.
N.A. CENTRE.

A few members paid Mickle Trafford a visit on. Sunday, but results were nil. Again they failed to catch the stream in anything like condition. The water was some 12in. to 15in. lower than the week previous, but was not fined down, the result being that the drainings off the meadows turned this clear running stream into a stream of water that is not adapted to the angler and fish life. However, members will still continue to go on the off chance of catch- ing it in condition, as we have only four more week-ends left before the close season comes in.

div.head: VALUE OF ADVERTISING.
div.p: VALUE OF ADVERTISING.
Great Firm That Has Benefited By Others' Timidity.
NEWSPAPERS SUPREME.

Bovril, Ltd., had record transactions and pro- fits last year, notwithstanding the war. Mr. George Lawson Johnson, in seconding the motion for the adoption of the report, said: I do not think you were surprised to hear that the sales were up, as you have become accustomed to expect that, but to learn that the advertising expenditure was down at a time when Bovril is more prominent than ever is somewhat satis- factory. The fact is that we have used the Press more and the other media less of late, and as there are fewer adwertisements in the papers, you cannot very well avoid Bovril catching your eye, especially as at
present you probably -read -More, Papers than usual. The Examiner" is the best advertising medium this neighbourhood.

div.head: EX-WARRINGTON PLAYER'S PLUCN
div.p: EX-WARRINGTON PLAYER'S PLUCN
Creevey Saves A Woman From
Drowning.

Matthew Creevey, the well-known half-back of the St. Helens Rugby , Football Club, and formerly of the Warrington Club—with whom he played three seasons ago—was complimented by the magistrates at St. Helens on Tuesday for a particularly gallant rescue of a drowning woman.

On Monday night, about eleven o'clock, Creevey saw Mrs. Bridget Corcoran throw her- self into the canal at Pocket Nook. Though the night was•bitterly cold Creevco, plunged in with all his clothes on and got the ,woman, who was big and heavy, out of the water. Inspector Dunn said Creevey's conduct was most heroic, and it merited recognition. As he wanted the woman to be remanded for a week, perhaps Creevey's conduct would be recognised in the meantime.

div.head: TRAIL OF FEATHERS.
div.p: THE TRAIL OF FEATHERS.
How A Fowl-Thief Was Captured.

At the County Petty Sessions, held in •War- rington.on Wednesday, before Messrs. W. Peter' Rylands (in the chair), Roger C. Parr, Joshua Ball and Jos. Bailey, Henry Chorley, a marine store dealer, of Long- ford, Warrington, was charged with stealing a fowl, valued at 3s. 6d., the property of Robert Walker, at Myddleton, on February 15th. Inspector Clark said that Mr. Walker, who was an attendant at Winwick. Asylum, havinc, missed the fowl, gave information to P.C. Duffers, who at once recalled haVing seen the prisoner and his dog in the 'vicinity of the hen roost at about 3.30 in the afternoon.. A search showed a trail of feathers leading from near the roost to a place some two hundred yards away, where the iirisoner siablec; his horse and cart. An examination of the cart showed feathers also on the bottom of that. On calling at prisoner's house the constable noticed similar feathers on the. floor. Prisoner was lying asleep on the sofa, so the officer searched the house, and under the staircase fobild the missing hen. He awoke the prisoner and asked him about the bird and he replied, "I have no hen here !" He then jumped up suddenly aa 'rutted the con- stable in Ile mouth, causing it to 'bleed. A. struggle ensued and eventually the officer over- powered his assailant and got him to the Pad- gate Police Station. Prisoner told the Bench that he was driving along the road when the hen got in the way and his horse trod upon it. His dog picked it up and brought it to him, and he put it in his cart, thinking . that he would pay the Owner for it.. .

div.head: HOLLINS GREEN BEAT THE CENTRAL.
div.p: HOLLINS GREEN BEAT THE CENTRAL.

A. sub-committee of the Warrington and Dis- trict League met at the Lion Hotel, Bridge- street, on Tuesday, Mr. H. Range, presiding. The matter of the registration of players with the Grappenhall and the Fairfield United Clubs in their " Starkey " Cup-tie was discussed and settled, and the re-played tie between the clubs was ordered to be played on the Elmwood Con- gregationalists' ground, in Manchester-road, to-day.

A protest arising out, Of the match on Sat- day between Hollins Green and Warrington Central was discussed, and after a lengthy and careful consideration of the points at issue, the protest was upheld- and the match was ordered to be replayed to-day on the Paddington United ground. It was decided to play the second round of the " Starkey " Cup Competition on Saturday, March 6th.

conditions prevailed and the teams decided to play on the Elmwood ground, which is only a few •minutes' walk further away.
