div.head: STARKEY CUP COMPETITION.
div.p: STARKEY CUP COMPETITION.
Re-played Tie.
WARRINGTON CENTRAL v. HOLLINS
GREEN.
Owing to the above teams having played a drawn game in the above competition a• week ago at Hollins Green, they had to meet again on Saturday in Victoria Park. The following players lined out :

Central: Ashcroft; Ashcroft and Glover; Brown, Gilbert and Williams; Mason, Hands, Sankey, Farrell and Williams. Hollins Green-: J. Blundell; H. Johnson and Buckley; Mellor, Cleworth and Atkinson; Har- rison, Gibbons, Blundell and Etchells. Referee, B. Howell.

There was a good' number of spectators pres- ent when the visitors won the toss, and the Central kicked off against a strong wind. Sankey sent the ball out 'to Mason, and the latter raced towards the visitors' goal, but his colleagues failed to accept his centre. From the goal kick Mellor received and by good play beat the oppos- ing half-backs, and passed on to Gibbons, and the latter transferred to Harrison, who sent in a splendid shot, which completely beat Ashcroft, and the visitors took the lead after five min- utes' play. From the centre-ldek the Central for- wards again looked dangerous, but the Visitors' half-backs proved foo good for them. Then Williams got away on the wing, but off-side spoiled the opening. The situation was made more difficult for the home team respecting the off-side rule, as the visitors' were playing with only ten players and resorted to the one-back game. Mason and. Hands combined well to- gether, but Johnson at full-back proved very safe and cleared, and Mellor was again in the thick of it. He passed. out to Etchells, the latter sending in a shot which Ashcroft fisted away. At this juncture the Central forwards resorted to individual play, and., their- efforts were erratic, but Sankey, working his way through the opposition, was brought down in the' penalty area by Cleworth. The kick was ,entrusted to Brown and Blundell brought off a very good save. After this the visitors again attacked the home goal, and from Atkinson's centre Etchells scored the second goal. Half- time: Hollins Green, 2 goals; Warrington Cen- tral, nil.

The second half opened with a rush by the homq forwards towards the visitors' goal. Hands shot in, but Blundell saved, and then a long kick by Gilbert again placed the visitors' goal in danger, When Off-side against Sankey relieved the situation. The home team continued to have most of the game, and a shot by Mason was partially saved by Blundell, and the home forwards following up, Hands sent through the goal. During this half Mellor and Sankey were having some rare tussles, the visitors' centre- half often coming off best. The visitors began to have more of the play. Good movements be- tween Johnson and Buckley led to the ball being passed out to Gibbons. The latter was chal- lenged by Glover and the home back lost pos- session, and Gibbons raced away and shot for goal. The ball hit the inside of the upright and went over the line. Glover kicked out, but the referee awarded the point. This decision was received with ,some dissension amongst the Cen- tral players. The home lot played very keenly, and from a breakaway Sankey scored their second goal. After this the home team appeared to become very excited, and were erratic in their play. With the call of time the result was: Hollins Green, three goals; 'Warrington Central, two goals.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT LEAGUE.
EARLESTOWN Y.M.C.A. v. EARLESTOWN
ST. JOHN'S MISSION.

This attractive fixture was played on the Y.M.C.A. ground, but owing to the inclement weather there were not many spectators pres- ent. The following players turned out : Y.M.C.A.: Owen.; J. Riley and Mort; Berry, Goulden and S. Buckley; Wilson, Gilman, C. Buckley, Hughes and P. Riley. Mission: H. Wallas; Winders and A. Eaton; Bennison, F. Eaton and Sherlock; W. Wallas, Collins, Rothwell, Rodgers and J. Plumpton. Referee, J. Smith. The home team won the toss and played with .a strong wind at their backs. The opening ex- changes in midfield were even and were fol- lowed by an advance by the Y.M.C.A., the final shot going wide. The home team, with the aid of the wind, had the best of the play, which was confined chiefly to the visitors' half, and Riley, on the home left, was the chief source of danger to the . visitors' defence. The latter kicked very ell and Wallas in goal was promi- nent by making several smart saves. Several. efforts by the visitors were well checked by J. Riley and Mort. A. splendid shot from Goulden hit the crossbar and rebounded into play, and Gilman receiving sent in a grand shot which was well saved by Wallas. The visitors broke away and Owen was called upon to clear. Play was quickly in the visitors' half, the home for- wards having good control over the ball.- After forcing several fruitless, corner kick's, Hughes was successful in opening the score for the Y.M.C.A. The visitors played more keenly and made several raids to the home end, and after these had been repulsed the visitors again made an attack on the home goal and Wallas equal- ised. The interval was called, the scores being one goal each. On resuming, the visitors; having the wind in their favour, were expected to take the lead. but J. Riley, Mort and Owen defended so well that they succeeded in frustrating the oppos- ing attacks, and, despite a number of corner- kicks taken by the Mission, they failed-to im- prove upon them. The Y.M.C.A. forwards very rarely became dangerous, owing to good play by Winders, but on one occasion P. Riley broke away and looked • a certain scorer, when he passed the .ball instead of shooting. The visi- tors' backs; intervened and cleared their lines. Directly after a splendid long shot from 'mid- field by Winders was tipped over the bar by Owen. From the ensuing corner J. Riley, and Mort defended well and cleared, and it was only in the closing stages of the game that. Rodgers managed to gain the lead after Owen had first cleared. Result :—Earlestown Mission, 2 goals; Earlestown Y.M.C.A., 1 goal. _

For the Y.M.C.A., J. Riley, -Mort, Owen, Hughes and P. Riley were the pick, and. the visitors were best served by IT. Wallas. Winders, W. ;Wallas and Plimpton. In the second por- tion the visitors did not have the same com- mand over the ball as their opponents and their shooting was very erratic. -

div.p: TIONALISTS.

This match was postponed owing to the visi- tors being unable to raise a team due to sick- ness. This hardly appears to be a satisfactory excuse for a club failing to play its away matches, as no doubt they will have from 20 to 30 players registered. This kind of sportsman- ship has a lot to do With killing the enthusiasm of a Club Secretary, for, the position of. this "Official at the best of times is one not to be envied. GRAPPENHALL v. ST. BARNABAS'.

The above teams met on Saturday on the ground of the, formerclub, off Knutsford-road. Owing to the 'inclement weather there were only a few spectators present when the visitors, win- ning the toss and playing with the wind at their backs, kicked off, and straightaway advanced to the home goal. They were driven back by a strong clearance by T. Ford. From a throw-in, the visitors again advanced. Long was tripped up just outside the penalty area, and from the free-kick Vernon opened the visitors' score with a rasping shot, the home goalkeeper being com- pletely beaten. From the centre-kick the visi- tors again attacked, but the home defence played very well under heavy pressure. J. Ford, train- ing possession, made a splendid individual effort and, after beating several opponents, passed out to Thomas. The latter raced away and equalised the score with a splendid shot. After this the game was for a while very evenly contested, but, as the interval was drawing near, the visitors made strenuous efforts to take the lead, and, owing to a mistake by the home baeks, they were enabled to score a second goal in simple fashion. The half-time 'score read :—St. Bar- 'nabas', 2 goals; Grappenhall, 1 goal. On the resumption, the home team had the wind in their • favour and attacked very strongly and. before many minutes had elapsed J. Ford scored the equalising goal. The home team con- tinued to have most of the game, but, in their eagerness, they missed many good opportunities of gaining the lead, and the game ended in a draw of 2 goals each.

div.head: D %RICER STREETS AT NIGHT.
div.p: D %RICER STREETS AT NIGHT.
Order for Cheshire Towns.

Following the action which has beenAtakeli with resnect to some of the larger towns, the Military Authorities have decided to place cer- tain restrictions upon lighting in Che Shire,. in- cluding Runcorn and other towns in the county. An important order on the subject, dated on Monday, has just been issued, and is signed by Colonel W. C. Neville, commanding the 22nd recruiting area, Chester. It is pointed out that the order is only a measure of precaution against possible attacks by an enemy, and need sause!no alarm among .Cheshire folk-. It is Made pursuant to regulation 12 of the Order in Council of November 24th, 1914, under the De- fence of the Realm (Consolidation) Act, 1914. The following reduction is ordered, to be made on the lighting of the county.of.Chester, inelud- int, the boroughs, except the portion' comprising the Mersey Coast Defence. In all the brightly lighted streets, especially in the centre of the towns and boroughs, the lights must either be lowered or made invisible from above by shad- ing them or by painting over the tops of §ind upper portions of the globes. The use of illu- minated sky'signs, illuminated fronts or letter- ing. illuminated clocks on prominent buildings, and powerful lights of all descriptions for out- side advertising or for the illumination of shop fronts, picturedromes, &c., must, uptil further orders, be discontinued. All large lighted roof areas must .be covered over or the lighting re- duced to a minimum. Powerful head-lights on motor cars are prohibited.,

div.head: VALUE OF HUMOUR
div.p: THE VALUE OF HUMOUR
IN THE GREAT WAR.
Br ERIC YOUNG. (Author of " Robert Bridges, the Poet Laureate.")

Whoever it was that once defined laughter as the most democratic thing in the world was say- ing, I am inclined to think, something rather deeper than he was aware. It has been left to us, who see democracy militant for its existence, to realise just how true that saying was. He laughs twist, of course, who laughs last. But possibly one of the things the war is going to show us, and not the least significant, will be that he who laughs last can do so precisely because he was able to laugh best. It it no easy acquirement, this sort of laughter. It is an edi- fice that demands a pretty solid basis of civilisa- tion. It is not by accident that the French are called the wittiest race in Europe,vand the Eng- lish the most humorous. 'Europe, and Westerh Europe in particular, has grown civilised to the accompaniment of laughter, and it is to an undertone of this "eternal mystic mirth," as Mr. Machen calls it, that democracy marches into battle. Laughter goes hand in hand with companionship, and the joyous effort of com- munities to realise their aspirations. And, per- haps, if we contrast the laughter of militarism we shall estimate the balance of power more nearly than by counting up figures of men and guns. In a battle of armaments we might con- ceivably lose; in a battle of laughter we shall inevitably win.

div.head: German Humour-Squadrons.
div.p: German Humour-Squadrons.

All of which fantastic considerations are sug- gested to me by no less familiar an object than the current issue Of "Punch." I have always held, as an orthodox Englishman, that "Punch" is as distinctly a national institution as the British Navy. But I had never before been so 'forcibly struck with the fancy that the two institutions have more than a little in common. I wrote just now about a battle of laughter, and suggested that in its way it might be almost as significant as a skirmish in the North Sea. If that be so we have at any rate the satisfaction of knowing that our principal laughing unit has been engaging the enemy with great success since the outbreak of hostilities. I can write this with the more confidence because I have already had a glimpse of the German humour- squadrons—sundry copies of " Simplicissmus," which came to me by way of Amsterdam. Now they contain some distinctly good things—here and there even dangerously good things, aimed unerringly at what are held to be the more vul- nerable points of our armament. But making all allowance for difference in temperament and point of view, I do not think there can be a shadow of doubt that they are completely out- classed by the native product.

div.head: " Punch " v. Prussianism.
div.p: " Punch " v. Prussianism.

It " Punch " were not so consistently good it might be another matter. I have deliberately chosen the best exponent of English humour to oppose the heavy batteries of " Simplicissmus." But, after all, it is the English public—l mean the real public, as opposed to the dilettante in humour—that has made " Punch " such an amazingly complete and happy expression of the humour of the English people. Here, as else- where, democracy is given precisely what it asks for, neither more nor less—for " Punch " is the organ of democracy in a far more real sense than some of the journals that definitely lay claim to that august position. One hears by chance of a particularly • rich- mot by Some Tommy in the trenches, and the best compli- ment one can pay it is to declare that "-it's good enough for ' Punch.' " It is to Mr. Punch that we look for an epitome of the national humour at each moment of the national life. He is a kind of licensed jester at the court of the people. Of. course, he is a good deal more than this. He can be a stern and practical critic of affairs; a master of the true word deliberately spoken in jest. _ _ _

div.head: Bully in the Stocks.
div.p: The Bully in the Stocks.

I suppose Prussianism and all that it stands for has never been so finally and ruthlessly ex- posed as in that extraordinary series of cai- toons in which. we see the Prussian bully in the pillory. But what strikes one so forcibly, in these dark days, is that we have here a repre- sentation or, if you will, a condensation of the spirit that is going to carry us through the even darker days that may be ahead of us. It is the brave determination, not only to carry one, but to keep smiling. It is the moss English thing in England. That is why I have 'chosen to re- gard " Punch " at the present moment as being, in a very real sense, a national organ which should be in every patriot's home. One may as well admit it at once that it is not always easy to offer a brave face to troubles that

come so nearly home to us. Thai is why Tye have such good use for a spokesman, one who,,e voice reaches everybody, to expreP,s the national determination. True, it is possibly easier to keep smiling in England than in Germany; one does not laugh at a Prussian drill-sergeant. it least, I should not like to try. But I think one of the most hopeful signs of the spirit of a-i€, nation at this time is the brave and genuine ring of our national humour, of which I hal,o taken "Punch" as the expression. and, as were, the summary. Everybody needs the tonic of cheerfulness, and where-is it td be -feund.in. such potent draughts as in the pages over which Sir Owen Seaman presides?

div.head: Keep Smiling:
div.p: Keep Smiling:

- For I do not think there can be any doubt that our humour does ring true—perhaps truer than it has ever done. Possibly, too, we a o drawing nearer than ever to a common stan- dard of humour, without sacrificing our .taeto hi- the process.

As I% glance again through, the copy et "Punch" which inspired thesa reflections I seem to detect the hint of a more dr„gnite appeal, a greater certainty of response that could ballo been found, even in this journal, in thane pip- ing times which already seem so many years age. The change is not, I think, so much in 'Mr. Punch" himself, as in his audience. lie always provided something for everybody. This is only to say that our humour has grown more sure 4-1 itself, and that our best humourists, both writers and artists can reflect it with a gret.t certainty of appealing to everybody. And believe this is what is happening. At any rate they deserve all our gratitude just now, these men who can make us laugh in spite of ourselves. They help to keep us the mark in our great task of smiling, for it in laughter that overcometh. They fill us with the spirit in which our soldiers in Flanders are able to crack jokes standing in three feet of freezing mud. And it is just this spirit which will help us, more than anything else, to pull off the j(113 weliave in hand. At this time, more than ever before, when shadows creep close to everyhody's threshold, I want to see " Ptinch " more an more widely read. Open your home to him— you can introduce him freely to your wife, to, your sons and daughters. The radiant face cf "Mr. Punch" is our best friend whatlier the sky is silver or whether it is heavy as lead. 3 t is the cup that cheers.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 20, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY. FEBRUARY 20, 1915.

being unable to gather together in. any appre- ciable degree the sympathy of the town, and to crystallise that feeling into adzquate action. A committee in such a position ought, by the faith and enthusiasm of Its units, to stimulate action in every class and in every quarter. This is no matter for sectional interest; we all recog- nise the need and all desire and have the right to help. Mr. Roberts mentions that they have only what is left of the 042937 subscribed, a very small sum considering the wealth of the town and the needs of the cause. Hence Mr. Roberts tells us that they desire to husband their resources and to go cautiously. Caution is a praiseworthy quality, but, without faith and enthusiasm, its effect in this connection is paralysing. Mr. Roberts tells us that "the committee are willing enough to extend their operations if the support of the public is continued." This of itself is a somewhat luke-warm appeal, and is not likely to elicit much response, especially as Mr. Roberts has already told us that there is • np cause for dissatisfaction with the Warring- ton response. It is as if Mr. Roberts had said, "We consider Warrington has done quite enough, but if you are anxious to give more the committee will spend the money for you." I hope. I have not misinterpreted the com- mittee's attitude and so done the members an injustice, but this is the general impression I gather from the interview with the Chairman.

div.head: MORE BELGIAN GUESTS.
div.p: MORE BELGIAN GUESTS.
Another Refugee Home Opened in Bewsey Street. CORDIAL WELCOME FOR FRESH ARRIVALS. [SPECIAL TO "THE EXAMINER."]

Another, and third, little Belgian community has been formed in Warrington; tins time at No. 47, Bewsey-street, where refuge has been found for., and where hospitality is to be dis- pensed to, a further coterie of nineteen of the men, women and children who have lost their all in the terrible disaster which has befallen their beautiful country. Seventeen members of the party arrived at their new home late on Thursday afternoon—two having been left be- hind, as they were not well enough to travel— and they were driven in a 'bus from Bank Quay Railway Station, where they alighted, to the commodious residence—which is to form their abode until such times as peace is restored, and they may with safety be repatriated. In the main the little party is ;nade up of women and children, but it also includes two men, one of whom, in happier days, was a schoolmaster, and is obviously a man of wide culture.

div.head: WORDS OF WELCOME-AND OF GRATITUDE.
div.p: WORDS OF WELCOME-AND OF GRATITUDE.

Upon arrival at their new home the party (were given a most cordial welcome by represen- tatives of the local Belgian Relief Committee, which body will, of course, make itself respon- sible for the feeding and general care of the guests. Mr. J. Upson (a member of the Refugee Committee and president of the Warrington Co-operative Society) briefly addressed the members of the party, after they had been assembled and accommodated with chairs in the well-lighted and comfortable sitting-room, which forms one of the apartments placed at their disposal. One lady member of the party, however, was so demonstrative in her expres- sions of gratitude that the address was more in the form of a dialogue and. ran after this wise Mr. Upson: Ladies and gentlemen, boys an girls: On behalf .of the local./ Refugee Committee I beg to offer you a very cordial and sympa- thetic welcome to the town of Warrington._ _

The Lady (after Mr. Upson's greeting had been translated to the guests by Mrs. Hertzog) : Merci, m'sieur; merci Mr. Upson: I need not say that, in common with those of all the rest of the people of Eng- land, our hearts bleed for you in the dire calamity which has overtaken you, and the other people of your nation. The Lady: We are all very, very grateful!

div.head: WARRINGTON'S TANGIBLE EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S TANGIBLE EXPRESSION OF SYMPATHY.

Mr. Upson: By doing what we are doing for you, and intend to do for you, we are adopting the only way in which we can express that sympathy in tangible form. The Lady: We will all try and show our gtati- tude to you for your great kindness, in every way that remains to us. Mr. Upson: It gives us, the people of War- rington, the very greatest pleasure—whilst re- gretting the necessity—to show our apprecia- tion, and the appreciation of the whole of the people of England, for the great sacrifices you, our good friends of Belgium, have made in the common cause of the Allies. _

The Lady: We are proud of what our men have done to help yours. Mr. Upson: Personally, I would like to add an additional word of welcome, because I under- stand that among you is a teacher, and I am a teacher, too! We hope that you will be able to make yourselves comfortable here. We have done our best to make you so. The Lady: And you have done very magnifi- cently! Whenever one does his• best, he does all that he can do; one cannot do more than one's best!

Mr. Upson : We are glad not only to offer you this measure of hospitality, but we hope and pray—as we are sure-you do—that the cause of your exodus from your own country will speed- ily be removed, and that the time will once more come when you will be happy and con- tented amongst your own folk.

div.head: PARTED FROM HER HUSBAND.
div.p: PARTED FROM HER HUSBAND.

The Lady: It is terrible, mes amis, to be exiled from one's country, and I feel the exile more keenly, because I have had to leave my husband over there. He holds an appointment under the Mayor of our town and he has had to go back again. Mr. Upson: We hope to become personally acquainted with all you ladies and gentlemen, as well as the little folk, as time goes on, and we shall. do all we can to make you comfortable, and, if possible, happy, whilst you remain with us.

The Lady (after a chorus of expression of gratitude had ceased) : We will be worthy of the kindness that I know we shall receive. She added that she and her husband had been deprived of 20,000 francs. worth of goods by tho Germans, to say nothing of their furniture, &c.; indeed, they had nothing left. Their funiture was broken up, and the house had "gone"; in short, everything they were possessed of had been lost as a result of the war.

The members of the Belgian party then shook hands warmly with Mr. Upson; and with Coun- cillor and Mrs. Roberts, and Mrs. Geary and Mrs. Voisey, who were also present to assist in helping to attend to their wants and to make them feel happy and at home. The formal welcoming ceremony at an end, the refugees were shown over their new home, and they went into ecstasies of delight as they noticed the practical way in which all their wants had been provided for, delight in which the smal- lest of the children joined, for even their toys had not been forgotten.
TROUBLES FORGOT OVER THE TEACUP.

The tour of inspection of the house completed and sleeping arrangements duly made, the com- pany repaired to the spacious and cosy kitchen, where they endeavoured to forget, over steam- ing culls of tea, their past sorrows and the hardships of their recent adventures. The house, it should be added, has kindly been placed at the disposal of the Refugee Com- mittee, rent free, by Mr. Houghton, and has been furnished throughout in the most substan- tial manner by the Warrington Co-operative Society.

div.head: IS WARRINGTON DOING ITS DUTY?
div.p: IS WARRINGTON DOING ITS DUTY?
Mr. Parker And Our Debt To Belgium.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—The published interview with Councillor Henry Roberts, the acting chairman of the Warrington Belgian Relief Committee, calls for comment. It is not a congenial task to criticise the action of those engaged in good work, but the interests of the Belgian people and the credit not only of the town, but also of the nation, are at stake in this issue. Mr. Roberts is of opinion that Warrington, in this matter, compares favourably with others of a similar population. I am not concerned with such com- parisons. Too often, we err in measuring our I duty not by the needs of the case, but by the I action of others. Mr. Roberts says: "Warring- ton has risen fully to our request." But the request, or, as it might be termed, the call, for help does not primarily come from Mr. Roberts or his committee, but arises out of the great need of the Belgian people, and our national, Christian, and humanitarian obligation to min- ister to this need. It is not, therefore, for this committee to set limits on the response which the Warrington people may be disposed to make to this call. The facts out of which this Call arise are these: The Belgian King and people met, and met unaided, the first fury of the german onslaught. Humanly speaking, the holding back of the .German hosts by this little vanguard of liberty at the critical period saved France, and possibly saved England from inva- 'Sion. But the Belgians, if strong in purpose, were weak in power, and their courageous de- fence was in time broken. This courage cost them dear; they became the victim of a merci- less and brutal foe. Belgium was trampled in I the dust, the houses, churches and workshops I of her people destroyed, their means of liven- I hood taken away, their country devastated, al- most every house made a ruin, and almost every garden a sepulch,re. Consider the weakness of the victim thus outraged,' her innocence in the quarrel, the justice of her cause, and the great- ness of her suffering: These things have moved the pity of the world and are the basis of the claim we are proud in Warrington, as else- where, to recognise.

div.head: All Must Help.
div.p: All Must Help.
The existing Town's Committee no doubt relti:as al: tbis, but it ails:nib ttgaulu I“

div.head: Action by Groups.
div.p: Action by Groups.

But in any case, is it not well to look for the enthusiasm and generosity to those groups in the community who are already linked together by some common interest, such, for example, as the Co-operative Society, or the different Christian Churches? Some little has already been done in this connection, and done well; more homes might be so arranged and financed. Each group would thus have close definite asso- ciation with a family of Belgians, have the in- terest of administering their own funds, and the joy of feeling that they were not only giv- ing, but that they were also ministering to representatives of the suffering nation whom they wottld get to know as personal friends. This connection is far more likely to be fruit- ful and productive of wise and generous help than the present plan of subscribing money to be administered by a Central Committee, over which the givers have no control and no close association. The Central Committee would still occupy a useful and necessary office in giving a general oversight to the several homes. They would arrange, as now, for the arrival, form the connecting link with the London organisa- tion, interpret the law, as far as it is advisable, bring about unity of action in general policy. For such work I think the pergonnel of the Central Committee specially adapted, because of its judicial and cautious character. There would still be left ample scope for the House Committees in the management of the buil- vidual -homes.
CHARLES E. PARKER. Penketb, February 18, 1915.

div.head: ABSENTEES AND DESERTERS.
div.p: ABSENTEES AND DESERTERS.
TELEGRAM WAS TOO OLD.

At Monday's Police Court, Driver Thomas Somerset was charged with having been an absentee from the South Lancashire Brigade Army Service Corps (at present stationed in the North) since Monday, February Bth.—lt was stated that on Saturday afternoon the police arrested Somerset, information having been re- ceived from the military authorities that he was absent without a medical certificate.—Pris- oner produced a telegram which said "Call on your own doctor, if necessary," but it transpired that he had receivbd this from the,officer upon a previous occasion.--He was handed over to an escort.

div.head: ABSENTEE IN FREE FIGHT.
div.p: ABSENTEE IN FREE FIGHT.

Private Andrew John Jordan was—at the Borough Police Court on Monday—charged with being an absentee from the 6th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, stationed near the South coast.—P.C. Barr stated that at 12.15 the pre- vious morning he had stopped Jordan in Butter- market-street and asked him for his pass. He replied that he did not belong to Warrington, and bolted. He was found later, however, and admitted that he belonged to the 6th Battalion South Lancashire Regiment. —The thief Con- stable said Jordan had been with some other men in a house, where a fight took place, and he got a kick in the eye. [Prisoner's face was discoloured all round his left eye.}—The de- faulter was ordered to be handed over to an escort.

div.head: SURRENDERED HIMSELF.
div.p: SURRENDERED HIMSELF.

At Monday's Police Court it was stated that Private Thomas Blenkinsop Jackson—who was charged with being absent from the 4th South Lancashire .Battalion (stationed in, the South) 'since February 13th-had surrendered himself at the Police Station that morning.—He was placed under the charge of an escort.

div.head: AN ABSENTEE SERGEANT.
div.p: AN ABSENTEE SERGEANT.

Before the Borough magistrates on Wednesday John Collins, a sergeant in the 4th Battalion of the Lancashire Fusiliers, was charged with having been an absentee since February 11th.— The sergeant, a smart-looking soldier, said that he and an escort were sent to Stafford Gaol with three prisoners. They handed the prisoners over on Monday, and on the way to the station one of the escort slipped away. He was a Man- chester man; and thinking he might find the man in his old haunts he went in search of him, subsequently slipping over to Warrington on a brief visit.—Detective-Sergeant Reddington said that on Tuesday the police received a tele- gram asking them to go to 6, St. Peter's-place, and arrest the sergeant. Witness went to the address given and there saw the sergeant and told him of the telegram. The sergeant then explained that on Monday he went with an escort of two men to Stafford, for the "purpose of taking prisoners to the gaol there. After the prisoners had been lodged one member of the escort gave him the slip. He and the other escort went to Manchester to search for the man, but they could not find him. He (the sergeant) left the other member of the escort in Manchester and came along to Warrington, re- maining here in the expectation that the two escorts would turn up. He Added that he in- tended going back last night.—Prisoner was remanded pending instructions from his regi- ment.

div.head: "GO BACK AND MAKE UP FOR IT."
div.p: "GO BACK AND MAKE UP FOR IT."

"You must go back to your regiment and make up for it," said Mr. J. W. Hayward, the presiding magistrate at the Borough Police Court on Wednesday morning to Michael But- ler, a private in the South Lancashire, who was before the Bench on a charge of having been an absentee from his regiment since the 11th inst. Mr. Hayward added: "We are sorry to see you running away at a time like this, you know !" "I am sorry lam absent, myself, sir !" replied the soldier, "but I should like to say that I was going back last night, only the police would not let me."—He was remanded to await the arrival of an escort.

div.head: TOOK FRENCH LEAVE.
div.p: TOOK FRENCH LEAVE.

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday, Corporal Charles William Seymour• was charged with having been a deserter from the 3rd Battalion King's (Liverpool) Regiment since Monday.—Detective Holland, described how Acting-Sergeant Whitby and himself had visited 19, Edward-street, the previous after- noon, and charged the prisoner. He replied: "I admit it. I applied for leave and they re- fused to give it me."—lt was stated that a tele- gram had been sent to the military authorities, and the defaulter was ordered to be handed over to an escort upon its arrival.
"A COCK OR A HEN?"

Joseph Heslip, collier—formerly of 7, Ger- trude-street, St. Helens, but now of no fixed abode, and Shaving come from Bury—was brought up at Monday's Police Court for having been, found wandering in Bridge- street at a quarter-past one on, Sunday morning, with no visible means of subsistence.— P.C. Harrison said lie., had asked Heslip what he was doing. Not receiving a satisfactory answer, he brought him to the Police StAtion, where he was searched.—lt was stated that he was found in possession of some letters, apparently , ad- dressed to soldiers, and in them he said that he was one of the Bantams. The Sergeant asked him: "Are you a hen or a cock?" and prisoner replied, "A cock !" (Laughter.) As a matter of fact he had joined another branch of the Army, at St. Helens, some weeks ago. He was undoubtedly weak-minded.—The case was ad- journed for a week, it being stated that pris- oner might afterwards be escorted back to his :(4:iiietiL if tiles wanted him.

div.head: WHO SHALL APPOINT?
div.p: WHO SHALL APPOINT?
Medical Inspection or Health Committee?
A CHAIRMAN RESIGNS.

At the monthly meeting of the Warrington Education Committee, held at the Town Hall on Monday evening yr. HOLMAN KINGDOM sought permission to make a statement upon a matter which, he said, did not directly arise out of the minutes, but which was very closely associated with them, viz., the relationship between the Education Department and the Health Committee of the Corporation in regard to the appointment of officials.

div.head: DELAYED OFFICIAL INTIMATION.
div.p: A DELAYED OFFICIAL INTIMATION.

Permission having been given, Mr. Kingdon went on to disclaim any desire of being in the slightest degree personal, and then proceeded to detail at length the steps which had led up to the present difficulty, which was concerned with the recent appointment by the Health Committee of a whole-time dental officer for the schools, an appointment which, he said, was supported by the town, and was one in which the Education Committee were essentially interested, and in which the Medical Inspec- tion Committee, of which he had the honour of being chairman, should most certainly have had a voice. "But," he said, "the members of this committee will hardly credit it when I tell them that the first official intimation my committee had that the dentist has been appointed came to-night, or that we, officially, knew hia name and qualifications, or anything connected with him. I feel that that cis an intolerable posi- tion."

div.head: RESPONSIBLE BUT VOICELESS.
div.p: RESPONSIBLE BUT VOICELESS.

If we are to be responsible or the work of these officers, it is surely necessary and only right and proper that we should have some con- trol over the appointment of them. (Hear, hear.) In January of last year we felt so strongly about these appointments that, we asked to be allowed to meet the General Pur- poses Committee by a deputation, which. in due course, appeared before the committee. They, naturally, did not tell us what they thought about the matter, but they gave us the impres- cion that our views had been sympathetically received. I have not the slightest objection to the Health Committee retaining these appoint- ments, but when they appoint an official and ask us to be responsible for the result, they ask us to do something which is impossible. I thought the result of the intervlew would have been either the appointment of a joint com- mittee for making these appointrhenfs, or that at least in the selection of an officer such as this dental officer we should have been asked to give our views, and, possibly, our advice, because we as a committee' mils% know more about dental work in the schools than the Health Committee. (Hear, hear.) WHAT IS DONE ELSEWHERE.

Mr. Kingdon went on to say that he had asked the Director of Education to collect in- formation showing how these things were done in other towns, and the Director had done so, with the result that it had been found—leav- ing out London, which would be the very best instance to quote, from his point of view— that among thern county boroughs of the country there were three only—Burnley, Bury and St. Helens —in which the appointment of officials who were really to work under the Education Author- ity was mach) by the Health Com- mittee of the Council, and out of the three, two of them actually made an exception in the case of the dental officer. That was to say that so far as their researches went there was only one county borough in the whole of England that did what Warrington did to-day. The county boroughs in which the appointments were made by the joint committees of the members of the Education Committee and the Health or Sani- tary Committee, and subject to the usual ap- provals, were Barrow, Bolton and Chester. In Bradford the appointments were made by the Education -Committee, subject to the approval •of the Health Committee. There were twenty- four county boroughs in which the school medical officers, the dental officers, and the school nurses were appointed by sub-committees of the Education Committee, subject to the usual approval by the Council, viz., Barnsley, Birkenhead, Blackburn, Blackpool, Derby, Gateshead, Huddersfield, Hull, Leeds, river - pool, Manchester, Middlesbrough, Newcastle, Oldham, Rotherham, Salford, Sheffield, South- port, Stockport, Sunderland, Tynernouth, Wal- lasey, Wigan and York.

div.head: THOSE WHO APPOINT MUST ALSO LOOK AFTER.
div.p: THOSE WHO APPOINT MUST ALSO LOOK AFTER.

"If this present position is going to obtain," said Mr. Kingdop, by way of conclusion, !! if it was the desire of this committee and also If it is the desire of the authorities of this town, that the 'Health Committee should retain the power of making these appointments, then I ask this committee to make it quite clear to everybody concerned that the Health Com- mittee must not only make_ the appointment, but must also do the work of looking after the officers when they are appointed. My com- mittee have no objection at all to that. I assure you that this is not a personal matter at all. I have learned enough during my 'business experience to enable me to keep, personal animus out, and I am simply looking at the matter from a business point of view. There is not a man in this room, if he has to be responsible to a conimittee, who would not have some share in the organisation of that com- mittee and in the selection of the people who have to do the work. What would my friend, Canon Stevenson, think, for instance, if the Borough Treasurer was allowed to appoint all the teachers in the town and leave it to the Education 'Committee to be responsible for the results?. This is rather a painful statement for me to have to make, but I feel that it is abso- lutely impossible to continue to go on in this way. . I think in the circumstances the only course open to me is to ask to be allowed to retire from the chairmanship so that I may at least leave the way open to someone more in sympathy with the existing regulations."

div.head: FURTHER DISCUSSION DEFERRED.
div.p: FURTHER DISCUSSION DEFERRED.

Mr. Jonx lipsoN inquired if a member of ,the committee had a right to speak on the subject. The CHAIRMAN replied that while the com- mittee had been quite regular in allowing Mr. Kingdon to speak, he thought it would be much better to defer any discussion until the next meeting Mr. TlPsog : Very good, sir; I quite agree. I was only going to say "ditto" to What Mr. Kingdon has said; except that if I had been permitted to do so, I was going to say it with more emphasis. (Laughter.) Answering Mr. R. T. Fairclough, the CHAIR- MAN said the matter could be discussed at the next meeting, or on a special motion, Mr. C. H. UNSWORTH thought that the ventila- tion the subject had received that evening would show the Health Committee what a strong feeling there was on the matter. , Alderman JAMES EvANs said it was not the Health Committee who were responsible for the arrangements, but the Town Council. Really, these charges seemed to be levelled against the Health Committee, who had done nothing ex- cept what their regulations authorised them to do. (Hear, hear.) They had never overstepped their bounds, and Mr. Kingdon had not stated that they had done so. Mr. KINGDON : I don't suggest that you have done so.
The CHAIRMAN: It would he ,better to have the matter specifically discussed as I have sug- gested. (Hear, hear.)
The minutes were confirmed

div.head: PREPARATORY TRAINING CORPS.

div.head: LATCHFORD WARD.
div.p: LATCHFORD WARD.
At the rifle practice of the Latchford Com- pany at the Whitecross range on Monday even- ing, the six highest scores were: Warburton 63, Wilkins 57, Bayley 54, Broadbent 60, Wilding 55, 38.

div.head: (rAjurth grim.
div.p: (rAjurth grim.
THE JUDGES OF THE WORLD.
Mr. A. Mounfield and the Saints.

A United Free Church service was held on Tuesday of last week in Friars' Green Chapel, being one of a series which have been arranged during the period of the war. Mr. A. Holland presided, and the Rev. H. Ogden led in the opening prayer.:

iiL A.-Mo-unfield gave an address upon Paul's dictum that "The saints shall judge the world." If Paul's letter, he said, had strayed into the outer world the statement that the saints were to be the judges of the world would have been regarded as very curious and un- likely. For the saints .were not the intellec- tuals of the earth; they consisted of small and obscure communities, who were not enjoying a very good time. What would the learned ones who climbed the steps to the great Law Courts at Rome have thought of the assertion that the Christians would judge the nation? Yet Paul was perfectly serious. Ile believed that they had learned.trutbs which would make them the masters of the destiny Of the whole earth; that they had found the truest light, and, having found it, had found the highest moral authority. Rome was famous for law; indeed, it had taught law to all the nations, but, as Paul saw it, the Church was teaching laws which were God-given and would transcend in power and influence all other. influences. In a very real sense the Church was set for the rising and falling of many, both of men and institutions.

div.head: Rome Judged by the Early Christians.
div.p: Rome Judged by the Early Christians.

The Roman Empire was judged in a way that it could never have expected. The Christians learned the value of human life. They gathered in the infants which had been left in the streets to die, and at their gatherings the slave and slave-owner sat together. When Christians set up the orphanage for other people's abandoned children, when they established the hospital, when they denounced the gladiatorial show and the theatre, they were judging the institutions of the day, and those institutions began to crumble. Slavery and infanticide, perished be- cause they were judged by the light of Christian teaching and found to be bad. It had been so down the ages. Francis of Assisi had judged both the church and the world by a life and teaching learned from the Gospels. Mr. Glad- stone became a "public institution" in Eng- land because of the high principle upon which he acted, and the pure soul of Josephine Butler was a high court of justice which shamed and condemned an evil thing. When superior people ,teered about the "Nonconformist conscience," let them remember that it was first used on an occasion when a saint judged the land and raised it to a higher moral level—when Hugh Price Hughes pronounced moral judgment upon Mr. Parnell.

div.head: Latent Powers of the Church.
div.p: Latent Powers of the Church.

In times like the present, when material forces seeded to count for so much and spiritual forces for so little, they must turn back to learn the truth that Paul had taught—that the children of light would say the effective word and be the deciding factor in everything. Did the Church realise that by making the most of is Sunday and treating it with the fullest reverence, it would decide the fate of the Sabbath? Did it realise that it could decide the fate of the drink trade to-morrow, and that armaments stood for judgment, not in the court of nations, but in the court of Christian truth? Jesus said that his followers would "sit on thrones and judge the tribes." It was for them in all humility to realise that Christian teaching and the life of Christian service would make them masters of the destiny of the world. It was a truth in which they must "rejoice without trembling," and a fact which, while it made them humble, should make them strong. At the close Mr. Mounfield was heartily thanked for his address.

div.head: "SERVICE, NOT SERVILITY."
div.p: "SERVICE, NOT SERVILITY."
The Importance of Being "On Duty" Emphasised at Legh-street.
MAYOR OF WIDNES IN THE PULPIT.

The Legh-street Primitive Methodist Church was filled to its utmost capacity at the services on Sunday. The occasion was the Church anniversary, and it was celebrated with special discourses and music. Councillor D. Lewis, Mayor of Widnes, occupied the pulpit. The Mayor of Warrington (Alderman Peter Peacock) attended the evening service. AN IMPERATIVE COMMAND.

Councillor Lewis took his text in the evening from the concluding passages of Matthew— "Then the eleven disciples . . . when they saw Him (Jesus), worshipped Him: but some doubted. And Jesus . spire unto them, saying: All power is given unto Me in heaven and in earth, Go ye therefore and teach all nations . . . to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you: and, 10, I am with you alway, even unto the end of the world." The preacher went on to say he would consider that command of Jesus from three standpoints. It was, first, an imperative command. Consider the significance of the word "therefore." Jesus' cause had been defeated, it was supposed. But God had exalted Him, and that was the great fact preceding the command. The instruction was one not to, be set aside. _ _ _ _

People to-day'admit-ted the truth of the Bible, but did they obey it? They knew the danger of militarism, but did they deprecate it? They let the ways of men override the ways of God. Jesus never indulged in small talk; His words dealt with living subjects; He spoke as Lord and King, and must be obeyed.

div.head: Cross of Discipleship.
div.p: Cross of Discipleship.

Again, the command was one given to the disciples who in those days had lost heart and hope, but who now beheld Him living before them and believed afresh with a new passion, a new hope, and a new love. That was good— very good! But devotion must be proved by service. " Ich Dien" must be the motto of the true disciple, for service was the cross of discipleship. And Jesus did not call His dis-' ciples from their service, but out of it. It had been said that "unadulterated _slack- ness "—rather than intellectual difficulties— was the reason for the Church's condition to- day. And who should say that was wrong The true spirit of worship would permeate their services just by each being "on duty"; it was the one thing that Would make life worth living. And there was no exaction in this command. It was not servility, but service, for which God called.

div.head: Altrtlism.
div.p: Altrtlism.

Lastly, the command was to do a specific work —" Go and .teach all. nations."- What was . the object? A universal brotherhood, bound to- gether by a converging in Jesus, independent of race, country, social distinctions, or creedal differences. "That is Altruism," they would say. It might be Altruism—it was Altruism. But that that was the meaning of the Gospel he did not doubt. The Gospel had a wider meaning than their own personal salvation. To .the whole' human family upon a higher plane—that was its purpose. The Gospel was the most optimistic thing upon earth; it preached the fellowship of man, and pointed to the time when conflict should cease: And that was "The flay" towards which they looked; that was "The Day" they should toast. How else were they to be "the salt of the earth"? No influence was more. potent than that. of the Godly life. Let them then pause to listen to the command, and lo! He would he with them even unto the end of the world. CHORAL SELECTIONS.
The choir ably rendered the anthem "Hark,

hark, my soul" (Shelley), Mr. A. Spruce con- ducting. The solos were impressively sung by Mrs: C. Worthington and Miss M. Jones, the latter lady also giving "Whither thou goest I will go."—Collections were taken at each ser- vice on behalf of the Trust Funds.

div.head: WANTED: A NEW CHURCH. The Vicar of Burtonwood's Hope.
div.p: WANTED: A NEW CHURCH. The Vicar of Burtonwood's Hope.

Writing iu the current issue of "Excelsior". —the Burtonwood Parish Magazine—the Vicar of the parish (the Rev. A. M. Mitchell) alludes to the project of a neiv- church foi the parish, and says of the existing edifice: "St. Michael's, an old and condemned chapel (it was never really 'a church% is, as it has been ar- ranged internally, for worship, a House of God very dear to the faithful, for, its dilapidated state notwithstanding, tip? .a is a w:trnith and homeliness about it whico 28 4:Alculated iu evoke

the spirit of devotion. The new St. Michael's, when it comes, must not fall far short of that which the old St.. Michael's possesses in such a marked degree. It is asked by some among usr Why build a new St. Michael's?' Alas! there is no alternative—it is a new St. Michael's or no church at all, and this in the near future. The old is done, it has had its day, it is beyond redemption: as a building the old ,must give place to the new, erected on common- sense liiw. not to gratify the pride of classie architect n re• but to provide a building which Will be at once a House of God and the people's home. Another reason which makes necessary the provision of a new St. Michael's is that the present building is no longer cen- tral. As to population, it is now rather out of the way. . . . The site for the new hall and _

church was chosen for this very 'redson7ti;a.t- the _buildings might be equi-distant from the- two Tillages [-of Burtonwood and Collins Green].) that both might enjoy equal opportunity, that there might be no dissatisfaction, no jealous- at either end. When centralised as to popula.- Hon, the work of the church will be'rconsider-- ably •strengthened; with church and hall (and' vicarage, '• too) all on one central site, the nor..: mal work of the parish could easily be doubled. It is not too much to hope that this note may he read by some wealthy people, clerical and lay, who will be glad to come to the help of the church at the outpost of Burtonwood."

div.head: PAROCHIAL GATHERINGS.
div.p: PAROCHIAL GATHERINGS.
thonal Social at St. Peter's.

The annual- congregational social in connec- tion with St. Peter's Church was held in the John-street Schoolroom on llondaY evening, when there was a good attendance, though not so large as in former, years, owing no doubt to the war.- The evening was pleasantly spent irr music and games, dancing following and light refreshments being 'served during an interval. Miss Sherwood saw, a number of songs, being accompanied on the piano by Miss Martin.;. whilst Mr. E. A. Padmore played the dance.

HOLY TRINITY SOCIAL. great success attended the annual congrega- tional social in connection with Holy Trinity Church, which was held in the Patten Hall on, Monday evening. There was an excellent attend- ance, the Rev. E. • C.• E. Carleton (the vicar) occupied the chair, giving a brief and suitable address. ,

Afterwards a splendid concert was provided. Mrs. IT. Smallshaw, being twice encored after a fine rendering of ." Angus McDonald," sang in turn "Little .grey home in the West" and "The Dear Homeland." Mr. Booth sang " hear you. "The owd side-ear," am! "Two little eyes of grey," treating all three of these favourite songs very expressively. • Mr- Dutton gave • "'Young Tom. o' Devon" and " Glorious Devon" with great success, whilst Mrs. Dutton rendered "Bird of love divine,'" "Forget-mw-not," '" Seventeen," and "Budding bloom of May." Mr. and Mrs. Dutton also earned hearty applause with that favourite duet "The spider and .the fly." The various Heims. were efficiently accompanied on the piano by. Miss Longdin, and Miss Newall also gave sev- eral enjoyable pianoforte _solos_ - • .

Miring" the evening light refreshments wero. f served. Dancing was then indulged in in the Hall, whilst a whist drive—held in the Infants" School, Miiseum-street—pleasantly passed the. time, for the older folk. WHIST AT ST. BARNABAS' PARTY., The annual parochial tea in connection with St. Barnabas' Church was held in the Bostock- street Schoolroom on Monday evening, and; proved to be both successful and enjoyable, a goodly company sitting down to the well-laden tables, whilst many more turned up later , to join in the whist drive, which was the piece 'de resistance of the evening's entertainment. The prize-winners were :—Ladies: 1, Mrs. Smith; 2, Miss ,Starkey: • Gents: 1, Mr. Waring jun.; 2, Mr. Attlivell. The Vicar ithe Rev. J. H. 'G.. Hollitigworth acted as M.C.

treacherous east winds. When arranging ,:he place ilpon which chickens are to be reared, it is of the utmost important that it be quite apart from the ground upon which the adult fowls exist. As a matter of fact, if the land is not sufficiently extensive to allow of this separation, it is inadvisable to rear chickens. The rearing ground should therefore be a piece of land that can be especially kept for the hatching period, and in the interval between the seasons it should be sufficiently sweetened to obviate all danger of contamination from the previous year's work. The grass should be kept short in the immediate vicinity of the coops, for if it is long the chickens are liable to become wet and draggled, which certainly does , not tend to their well-being. The greatest diffi- culty that the poultry-keeper who rears his chickens out in the open has to contend against is cramp. This is caused more frequently by allowing the chickens to run in among long grass than by anything else. If, therefore, the coops cannot be placed sufficiently far away from this danger, the only way to overcome the difficulty is by keeping the hen shut up in the coop until the chickens have got beyond the very early stages, when the tendency to cramp is not so great. MARKET QUICKLY. The practice of holding back eggs in the hope of obtaining a higher price cannot be too strongly condemned, and is against the interests of the producer in every way. Eggs should be marketed at least once a week; if the highest class trade is to be secured they must be mar- keted three times a week in spring and suinmer, and twice a week in winter.

If a little gum arabie is dissolved in the rinsing water when cotton voiles have been washed, this will prevent them from Lsing that slight crispness which is such a feature of the material. , If your feet are, large you can give them a smaller effect by wearing shoes with rounded toes and with a proper toe-cap. 41. boot or shoe cut without a toe-cap, or with very pointed toes, adds length to the foot. Plain shoes with- out straps are more suitable for a plump foot; straps accentuate the plumpness. Fried Fish. Clean well, removing the head, and, if quite large, the backbone also. Slice the body cross- wise in five or six pieces, season with salt and pepper. Dredge with flour, brush each piece with beaten egg, roll in breadcrumbs, and fry in hot lard or dripping. Be sure to have the fat hot, as it will not be absorbed so quickly. When the fish is browned turned carefully, to avoid breaking, and brown the other side. Garnish with slices of lemon. Palistria Soup (a Parisian recipe). Ingredients: One pound and a half of arti- chokes, one ounce and a half of butter, one ounce and a half of flour, a quart of milk, a gill of cream, salt, pepper, and cayenne to taste. Method: Parboil the artichokes, then put half the milk into a clean saucepan, to- gether with an equal quantity of water, and let the artichokes finish cooking in this. When tender, pulp them through a wire sieve, using the liquid in which they have finished 000 king. Mix the flour and butter, add salt and pepper to taste, heat the remainder of the milk, pour .gently on the flour and butter, and boil this mixture gently till it thickens. Then add the artichoke. pulp and liquid, heat through to within boiling point, add the cream and serve in bowls with a French roll to each person.— "The Lady." At Swinton; meet at Central Station at 1.45 : Rylands' : F. Horrocks; J. Griffiths, A. for- rocks, F. Potter and C. Povey ; J. Gallop and W. Stretford.; J. Brandwood, W. Shaw, A. Penn, E. Smith, F. Baguley and A. N.' Other. Re- serve, J. Dumbell. SALFORD CIL‘RITY SHIELD. RYLANDS' RECS. v. BRADFORD AND CLAYTON. This match, in the second round of the Shield Competition, took place on the Gorsey-lane en- closure on Saturday, when Rylands', winning the toss, decided to start with the wind. Shaw kicked off. The Bradford full-back punted well up the field, but the wind carried the ball back when Baguley. Paced up, and, securing, scored under the posts, Shaw adding the goal points. Later on J. Gallop got his backs going, and C. Povey. put on another try for Rylands', the goal-kick failing. At half-time Rylands' led by 8 points to nil. The second half commenced in rare style; both sides playing fast and vigorous football and neither of them ,making any headway until the Bradford mep eased off, when tries were scored for Rylands' by F. Horrocks, A. Horrocks and W. Shaw, all the goal-kicks failing. The final score read : Rylands', 1 goal 5 tries (17 points); Bradford and Clayton, nil. , Overheard.
